   The Temple of Syrul leered down onto the courtyard like a crouching gargoyle.
   Made  of scarred black stone, the building looked more twisted than built.
   Magistrate Bao was no follower of Syrul. The Suel Goddess was as distant as a shadow, but she was the god that every ruler followed.
    Bao needed to foster as much unity as he was able.
   He smiled reassuringly at the assembled ambassadors, although he was churning with anticipation.  Each one was a representative of a king, queen, prince or princess. A couple glared back, and two were gesturing angrily at each other.
   Some wore elaborate lacquered armour, others were nearly naked. A number wore white or grey togas.
   Hair was raised, hair hung down, hair was bunched up, hair was tied up into blonde plaits.
   Some wore bracelets of gold, some wore necklaces of silver, some dazzled with jewels.
   There must have been thirty of them, men and women, smiling, scowling, apprehensive.
   All different.
   All diverse.
   All Suel.
   Magistrate Bao, limping but embodying dignity, led them through the gaping square doors that opened up into the bowels of the temple.
   The whole place was lit up with guttering torches, great shadows projecting onto the walls like watching giants 
   Such a gloomy hall.
   Ahead, atop a dias were two priests ready to commence the service. They wore black masks that resembled the faces of ogres.
   The delegates took seats and Bao sat at the back. 
   Two hours of chanting later and the priests had retired from the hall, leaving behind the whiff of sulphur and ammonia and prayer.
   The Temple of Syrul, suitably mollified, was now consecrated.
   The Magistrate stood up, a small white figure near the back wall. 
   Now he could begin.
   The First Suel Senate was in session. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2 
Part 24
1187 SD
   Queen Dully waited at the top of a hill. 
   The raiding party would be back soon.
   Hopefully.
   She cast an Eagle Eye spell and scanned the far banks of the wide river that flowed lazily between the two Suel lands.
   Nothing yet.
   Queen Dully felt a cool breeze ruffle her axe beak feathered hat,  The Beast Masters below the hill stood at attention, fearing to turn their gaze to the flowing scarlet plumes writhing in the wind like a living animal.
   Two Suel lands.
   The Suel across the river, diverse kingdoms and forts, war ruined by centuries of rivalry and hate, were at peace.
   United by a Senate.
   Difficulties between the Suel nations were negotiated and overcome.
   And they were no longer kings and queens. 
   They called themselves "Royal Prefects."
   They had all begun to dress in grey togas, their blonde and white hair clipped back into dense buns.
   Their dialects blended together, and the Suel across the river spoke with exaggerated inflections that sounded more like parody than dignity.
   The Senate was led by  a young Beastmaster who had been mentored by the late Magistrate Bao.
   Jacq he was called.
   The new Magistrate. Perhaps the most powerful person in Western Oerik.
   Queen Dully was still a queen of course, not a "Royal Prefect."
   She had not been invited to the Senate.
   She was of the "Suel to the East."
   The "Cursed Ones" the western Suel said, "the Suel with the "Drow taint."
   They were craven. They were pathetic.
The eastern Suel had merely returned to their ancestral lands.
   The Drow were gone and the old cities were repossessed.
   Queen Dully had access to magic and knowledge the other Suel could only dream of.
   She had asked to at least visit the Senate, or negotiate with the new power.
   She was rebuffed.
   The western Suel wanted the eastern Suel to wither away like a dead branch of their new tree.
   Did they not know who Queen Dully was?
   Did they think that the Sorceress of the East would accept a united empire on their borders?
   She scanned again.
   Ah! There they were, making their way to the boats.
   Her magnificent raiders.
   And they brought with them prisoners.
   Syrul wish that the Magistrate was among them! See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2 
Part 25
   Queen Dully 's raiders were back, and they brought her prisoners.
   The fierce warriors looked haggard, and their eyes were bloodshot.
   There were seven less than the original party.
   And the prisoners were disappointing. Who were they? Low level officials and servants.
   No high Ambassador. No Royal Prefect.
   And no Magistrate Jacq.
   "What happened?" she asked them.
   The leader of the raiders, a muscular Beast Sorcerer who normally had a voice of steel and a neat blonde beard, had a cut near one eye and half of his beard had been torn off, leaving a bloody chin and jaw. He spoke hesitantly and the Queen struggled to understand him.
   "Say again?"
   He spoke again, urging her that they needed to go back to the city. They were not safe here in the wooden fort.
   But what had happened?
   The other raiders were only half listening to her. They kept looking out over to the distant river. 
   Were they expecting someone to be coming after them?
   Yes! Yes! That's what we are saying.
   We have to get away.
   Defend the city.
   The Magistrate is coming!
                    ***********
   Magistrate Jacq wore his platinum blonde hair like a mane. Underneath him was his mighty steed, Grolok, a titanothere with an enormous nose horn and a frill of small spikes around his head. 
   Behind him were his Beast Masters, riding an assortment of brontotheres, rhinos, mastadons and elephants.
   Four hundred Beast Masters, Soldiers of the Senate, Servants to the Magistrate.
   They were crossing into the east.
   The fabled east. The land of Spiders. The land of Drow.
   The Magistrate was determined to punish the raiders and rescue the prisoners but he must be very careful.
   Drow webs shimmered and snared.
   Spider gods roamed the dark forests.
   And the Suel who chose to live in this Forbidden place were tainted with shadow.
   At the edge of the river he stopped the Beast Masters. 
   They must pray, let the Goddess of the Suel imbue them with the fortitude they needed.
   Oh Syrul, let us go into the east and let us do what needs to be done.
   Avenge our assault.
   Rescue our beloved people.
   But, O Syrul. Most important of all.
   Let us Return from the East without becoming Drow. See less

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 48
1236 SD
The halflings wore heavy scale mail, their helmets and shields were bronze and they wielded short, grey swords.
Were they supposed to be intimidating?
Baba Yaga was still not fully grown but she towered over the halflings.
She was a giant. An ogre,. A blue girl.
A Witch.
Baba Yaga had left Ull, for there was nothing for her there.
Ull was too warm, and her False Mother haunted the place.
Baba Yaga didn't hate Ulaa, but her earnest nurturing nature was irritating.
Baba Yaga didn't need to be coddled, or even loved.
She was a wild beast, a monster!
She was as whimsical as the wind.
And she had an athema for the Ulluans, ignorant villages full of fools.
Boccob had suggested she go north.
He had told her of forests of fir trees, of northern wyrms - Linnorm dragons, with teeth like daggers and treasure that shone like stars.
Bears and tigers encased in white.
And wild gnomes who could change into giants.
The sky would be grey, and the ground thick with snow in Winter.
Blizzards of ice lashed the edge of the Burneal forest and clashed against the frozen sea.
Baba Yaga had to admit, this land sounded like heaven.
And so, Baba Yaga had crossed the Yatil mountains, travelled through the windy plains of nomads, bugbears, centaurs and norkers, dwelt for awhile in the Cold Marshes, where indeed, she found a northern Linnorm and stole its most valuable treasure, and then, finally, came to this barren place called Blackmoor.
The halflings had seen her and had come to investigate.
They lumbered. They staggered. Armour didn't suit them
Baba Yaga hoped that they weren't as stupid as the Ullites.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 49
1268 SD
Fharlanghn and Celestian were on the Moon.
They were upon Luna, amongst stunted grey fruit trees, below a lavender sky.
Celestian, skin dark as midnight, wrapped his star covered cape around his distraught brother.
High in the sky glowed Oerth, and the smaller moon Celene began to rise in the west.
The sight was beautiful, but Celestian knew that Fharlanghn wouldn't appreciate it.
Fharlanghn was too preoccupied with one world; Oerth. The sky, the stars and the planets were abstract, and Fharlanghn was a practical god.
Being attached to one world had its problems.
If darkness touched a part of it, and there was always darkness somewhere, it would bring Fharlanghn down.
Fharlanghn wanted Oerth to glow. To shine. To outstrip the stars with its radiance.
Who was being abstract now?
Celestian patted his brother on the shoulder.
He comforted him as best as he could.
If only Fharlanghn hadn't returned to Oeridia.
Oeridia, the great island of their childhood, had fallen into utter anarchy.
Every hill held a fort or keep.
Every farm, every village, were surrounded by walls.
The city of the Uplands was gone, broken into miniature kingdoms ruled by miniscule war lords.
And the Lowlands?
The pirates were back.
The sahuagin were back.
The fish people had set up permanent settlements on the beaches, and there they held slave markets, the slaves taken from the Lowlanders.
Fharlanghn couldn't understand what happened.
The evil Death Cult with their oppressive priests had been defeated.
Hadn't the good guys won?
He knew that there would be instability at first.
But generations had passed, and finally Fharlanghn had gone back.
Only to find Oeridia broken, crushed beyond recognition, an island of jetsam.
Celestian had heard Fharlanghn"s cries.
And amongst the grey fruit trees, under the lavender sky,
Celestian enfolded his brother with stars.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 50
1288 SD
Music like bells.
Music like thunder.
Melodies of lightning.
Melodies of fire.
Harken, people of the Adri.
Make some noise!
Dance for joy!
For the Bard and Elf are wed!
(Flan folksong)
********
Heward and Ye'Cind had decided to get married.
They had been fond of each other for a very long time.
Both had been young when they first met
They were now both thirteen hundred.
Heward aged almost imperceptibly, looking less than sixty.
Ye'Cind the same, her silver complexion now lightly burnished with brown.
It was on a whim that they decided to wed.
Heward was drunk. Ye'Cind was tipsy.
Why not? they thought.
Their affection should be eternal.
And so, they organised the wedding, a big and beautiful ceremony on the Bardic grounds of the Adri forest.
Heward's Mystical Organ was there.
Let it play. Let it thunder.
For Heward and Ye'Cind are wed!
*********
It was dark now. The children had been taken home
The hardiest adults were left. A clutch of Bards and elves, a red flushed Boccob, a red nosed Garl Glittergold., a red faced Heward and a red cheeked Ye'Cind.
The Organ was playing quietly, it's shortest pipes murmering like flowing water.
It had been a good idea to get married, thought Heward.
An excuse for good food and excellent drink, partaken with old friends.
The Organ was soothing. The air was still.
Ye'Cind was beside him.
He gazed into her eyes.
He smiled.
The rumbling vibration made him jump.
What was that?
Garl was laughing, which Bard had drunk too much? Get someone else on the Organ!
Yes, the sound had come from the Organ.
It wasn't melodic anymore. Big pipes were belching deep groans. Crazy harmonies collided with dark dissonences.
Heward's Mystical Organ was playing a Burlesque.
Which idiot was on it?
Heward looked around. All the Bards were here, drinks in hand.
Boccob?
Here he was, looking as confused as the rest.
Heward ran out and onto the stage.
And then he saw who it was that was playing, a cold grin upon his pale face.
It was Boccob.
Old Boccob.
The old Boccob, Boccob's older self, wearing a battered hat and an old robe of moons and stars, noticed Heward and smirked.
"Oops," he said, "did I play a wrong note?"

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 51
Heward rushed up to throw Boccob off the Organ, but Boccob was already climbing off the seat.
Boccob shook his head, giving Heward's nose a playful tap.
"I hope you weren't thinking of inflicting bodily harm upon me?"
Heward was livid.
"What are you doing here, Boccob?"
Ye'Cind, Garl and the young Boccob had made their way to the stage and were standing beside their friend. Young Boccob had lost his rosy glow. He looked scared.
If old Boccob was at all fazed, then he didn't show it.
"Didn't you invite me to the wedding?"
What could Heward do? Boccob was always too flippant. Why Was he here, really? And why did he play the broken pipe? The pipe that he had broken himself?
Boccob was smiling broadly.
"Hello, young self," he said to his younger self," "not yet my true self, but getting there. I liked your idea of a Grand Council."
Young Boccob glared at his older self, despite his fear. He wasn't the intimidated boy he used to be. He had travelled the Multiverse. He had seen terrible things. He had bested terrible beings.
Quietly, he mumbled the beginning of a protection spell.
Boccob knocked him down with a punch.
"It's been a pleasure," he gushed, "but it looks like I have outstayed my welcome. Did you like my little Wedding March? No? Oh well. No harm done."
A pause.
"Probably."
Old Boccob blinked out of existence.
********
Several weeks later, Ye'Cind grievously ill and confined to bed, her stomach bloated and distended, her hands cramping into fists, Heward remembered the encounter with old Boccob and wondered whether the wizard had anything to do with Ye'Cind's illness.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 52
Ye'Cind laid an impossible egg.
The egg was as red as ruby, leathery and slightly squishy, and quite large.
And elves did not lay eggs.
Ye'Cind was unconscious, as she had been for weeks now. Ulaa was giving her all the care that she could, but clearly Ye'Cind was afflicted with a malady entirely supernatural.
Damned Boccob!
Heward was convinced that the egg must be destroyed. Whatever was going to hatch out was clearly evil.
But was it?
Ulaa wasn't sure. The egg was Unnatural, disturbing, but the contents were unknown.
She cast a spell to detect evil.
The results stunned her.
"Everything," she murmured, "everything."
"What's 'everything?' What are you saying?"
Ulaa looked into Heward's crumpled face, her eyes dark and confused.
"Everything shows up as evil. You, me, the floor, Ye'Cind, the bed... everything."
She gestured with a shaky hand.
"Except for that."
Ulaa was pointing at the egg.
********
Boccob couldn't help but feel guilty.
Of course, it hadn't been him that had played the Mystical Organ and had ruined the wedding party.
Not yet, anyway.
But he still felt responsible and, he could see that Heward thought so too.
Heward's expression was cutting.
So, Boccob locked himself away.
He wasn't sulking. He was trying to fix everything.
In a quiet little pocket dimension, in a room at the top of a small, simple tower, Boccob bent over a desk, poring over a black scroll.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness.
The evil that the Scroll radiated was palpable. It had sought to corrupt Boccob, turn him demonic.
Boccob had been too strong willed.
He had seen his future and he would resist. He refused to become what he was fated to become.
Boccob would hang on as long as he could.
Despite its evil, great magical insights lay within the Scroll. Through diligence and experiment, Boccob had learned to tame the Scroll and discover ways to utilise magic that even the gods didn't know.
Boccob would find out how to cure Ye'Cind.
He had to.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 53
1293 SD
The mysterious egg was placed in a dark chamber in the bowels of the greatest Bardic college.
The egg hadn't changed at all, and eventually Heward forgot about it, concerned mostly about Ye'Cind.
She slept still.
Heward had tried to wake her, but nothing had worked.
Ulaa 's preparations had preserved her but had not improved her.
Boccob had tried all sorts of spells, but something seemed to block them from awakening Ye'Cind.
There was malevolence in the air.
In fact, malevolence blanketed everything.
Everything was radiating evil.
Heward thought he knew what was happening.
Tharizdun was back.
That would explain it. He had escaped from his prison and his invisible mists covered Oerth.
He was too strong to be overcome.
Everyone was heading towards decay and ruin.
Boccob didn't agree.
He had been the one to trap Tharizdun.
There was no escape.
And, if somehow, Tharizdun had wriggled free, then he would know.
Really? What has your magic done lately?
Heward was far from convinced.
*********
The years flowed on.
The Sun shone. The forests grew. The rain came. The rain went.
Day became night. Night became day.
If Tharizdun was here, he was letting Oerth run like usual.
Boccob still didn't think this malady was the work of Tharizdun.
It was he, himself, the older Boccob, who had done something terrible.
Boccob didn't know why.
Old Boccob hadn't said.
And he was gone. Lost in the ether.
But he had a reason.
Boccob always had a reason.
And the evil aura surrounding Oerth?
Boccob fancied that it wasn't real. It was a dream of evil.
A premonition.
Something terrible was coming.
Not Tharizdun.
Something else.
The evil was a ghost of things to come.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 54
Why won't you please me, my love?
Don't you want me to be happy?
We can go away together.
Would you like that?
Can't you see what I see in you?
Such potential. Grasp it!
Take us away from here.
Let us dominate Oerth.
***********
Boccob sighed, trying to block out the words in his head.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness was becoming more treacherous, more devious.
It was courting Boccob, seducing him.
He knew that if he fell he would be lost.
But the Scroll held immense power, power that he needed.
Somewhere, somewhere, hiding in a maze of incantations and spells, somewhere in the Scroll, somewhere he had yet to look, he would find a way to bring Ye'Cind back from the brink.
*******
Can you see it, my love?
You a king.
A crown of platinum upon your head.
Me, clutched tightly against your warm breast.
Come with me, my love.
Let us leave this place and fly to your destiny.
********
And there it was!
The answer.
Oh no, Heward isn't going to like this.
*******
The forest floor was carpeted with snow.
The trees above had lost their leaves, and the sky was white and cold.
The egg had been placed to the left of the Mystical Organ and Ye'Cind lay sleeping to its right.
Heward was here, as was Boccob, Garl Glittergold and Ulaa.
Heward was clearly angry. He kept giving Boccob dirty looks.
Boccob didn't let it get to him
He understood.
This procedure was dangerous, even absurd.
To play the Organ again, and not just the Organ but the damaged pipe...well, why would this fix anything?
Boccob had explained.
Heward would play it. And not just play it. He needed to create a masterpiece, a symphony of sound.
And then, at the height of its power, at the culmination, the broken chords must sound.
And the fractured notes, the dissonence and the chromatic chaos had to somehow fit with the rest.
And the Symphony would then become profound.
And magic would happen.
And how was Heward supposed to accomplish this?
Boccob, you ask for the impossible.
No, Heward, I don't.
For you are the Magus, the First Bard.
Compose for your life.
Compose for Ye'Cind.
********
Heward took his seat upon the stage, and his dextrous fingers and his agile feet began to play.
The air was bitingly cold, so he made the keys play a warm melody in a major key, and before long a cloud of warmth covered Heward and the Mystical Organ.
And now the Overture over, the Symphony could begin.
Heward played with an intensity even he had never attained before.
This was not entertainment.
This was life in music.
Dark times. Joyful times.
Melancholy. Despair.
Comedy. Drama.
Fear. Laughter.
Yearning.
Desperation.
Success.
Failure.
The Fugue in the Fourth Movement began in an orderly fashion, building up into a octave spanning frenzy
And now it took on a life of its own!
Bang! Bang! Bang!
The long pipes blew out an anthem of longing.
The short pipes shrieked.
Cacophony! Frenzy!
And now it was time to play the broken pipe.
Success or Failure.
Chromatic Chaos!
Ye'Cind's eyes opened.
The egg cracked.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 55
Heward took his fingers off the keys.
The vibrations from the last dissonant rumble faded into silence.
The Magus had finished the Symphony.
Had it worked?
Has the magic cured Ye'Cind from her eternal sleep?
Heward had done his best.
The Symphony had flowed into reality.
He had felt the emotions reverberate around the stage.
And then that last chord, when he activated the enormous, broken pipe...
Heward had ridden it like a bucking bull.
But there was no containing it. Heward had held on, but the fractured noise had its own will.
And now it was over and...
Ye'Cind's eyes were open.
And she was smiling.
*********
"I don't remember the egg at all..."
Ye'Cind was sitting up on cushions, the cold air stinging her cheeks.
The sharp cold kept her awake.
She knew that she had been asleep for a long time, but she didn't remember why.
She had layed an egg...!?
There it was, on the other side of the stage, beside the Mystical Organ.
It was large and wrinkled like a baby crocodile.
There was a hairline crack and a wisp of acrid air emenated out from it.
Why was it here? Why hadn't they destroyed it?
And they explained, her friends, gathered around her.
What was growing inside the egg was unknown, and Boccob was convinced that the egg would be part of the cure.
The egg had rested just as Ye'Cind had rested
If Ye'Cind woke up, then the egg must wake up too.
The egg had cracked at the very same moment that Ye'Cind awoke.
The magic had worked.
Heward had created the Miracle Symphony.
That was all well and good, thought Ye'Cind, but she wasn't convinced.
Whatever was in that egg wasn't supposed to exist.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 56
The egg was taking its time.
Day by day, more cracks appeared, but nothing emerged.
Yet, the egg itself was changing shape, as if the being within was trying to work itself out.
Would it emerge as a monster or would it hatch out an innocent baby?
The Bards watched over it, ready to alert Heward, Ye'Cind and Boccob should it break fully open at last.
Ye'Cind was lightheaded and pale after her long sleep.
Heward was worried about her. Sometimes he fancied that she was growing translucent, turning into a ghost.
Could he see the shape of his hand underneath her own?
He didn't give a voice to his fears.
He was grateful that Ye'Cind was back.
**********
The Winter had been particularly cold this year, and it was deep into the month of Sunsebb, in the gloom of an early evening when the egg suddenly split open.
With a resounding crack, a little fist smashed through the egg, splintering it apart.
Heward and Ye'Cind and Boccob rushed to the stage.
Ice had formed on the pipes of the Mystical Organ and the ground was blanketed in snow.
The egg was broken, and sitting amongst the ruins was an infant with slate blue skin, white spidery hair and bright violet eyes.
By the gods...!
The baby was Drow!

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 57
A Drow? How?
Heward's immediate instinct was to kill it.
But it was a baby.
It began to crawl towards the Organ.
Heward grabbed it and pulled it away
Its skin was soft and warm, despite the cold.
The baby was real.
********
In a small music room room within the College, the friends were having a meeting.
Heward was pointing at Boccob.
"This is your fault."
Boccob shook his head. It wasn't him. It was Old Boccob. The Boccob from the future.
"I know that," snapped Heward, "but Old Boccob is still you. You will become him!"
"Not by my choice."
Heward grabbed Boccob's cloak.
"Is it in your robes?"
"What?"
"Do you carry it everywhere? The Scroll of Vile Darkness?
Ah, the Scroll.
Boccob pulled it out. Yes, he always carried it.
Ye'Cind gasped. She knew how evil the Scroll was. It had once belonged to Tharizdun.
So that was why she had been cursed.
Ye'Cind had grown to trust Boccob. She had been wary of him at first, as was Heward.
He seemed friendly and well mannered, and he was enthusiastic for a bright future for the Flanaess.
She didn't know he still possessed the Scroll.
Garl Glittergold and Ulaa were the other two friends in the room. They told Boccob to throw the Scroll down. He must get rid of it.
Boccob said no.
He understood their fears.
And he did feel guilty, even though he hadn't done anything bad yet.
But the Scroll was not his master.
It whispered to him, cajoling, seducing...but he was not human. He was a man made out of magic.
He could and would resist. He had learned to harness the Scroll, to unwrap its secrets without falling to his doom.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness was a tool to be used and Boccob was strong enough to wield it.
What about the baby?
That was really what all of this was about.
The baby. A Drow baby.
Ye'Cind looked at Heward with frightened eyes.
And were they really the mother and father?
Ye'Cind was no Drow, despite being born an ancestor of those corrupted Olves. And Heward was Flan, more or less.
The baby was sleeping, being looked after by the Bards. It was helpless even if it wasn't innocent.
It didn't seem right to kill it.
But what if it grew up and became a Tyrant?
Boccob then smiled.
His face was warm, compassionate.
Despite being much much younger than Ye'Cind, he was still much older than any ordinary mortal, and his expressive eyes glinted with fatherly love.
He didn't blame Heward and Ye'Cind for hating him.
And he was wise enough to not resent it.
"Why should the baby become a tyrant?" he asked.
Garl Glittergold snorted with exasperation. Was Boccob being serious? The baby was Drow. There were no good Drow.
Do Drow usually hatch from an egg?
Do Drow usually have two stalwart heroes for parents?
Boccob suddenly looked larger than he ever had before.
Large and almost menacing, as if he was evoking his power as he made his point.
And is the baby a Drow?
It has never seen the Spider Queen.
it does not creep under the ground.
The baby might look like a Drow, but what it really was...
... Potential.
The baby was pure Potential.
Give him love. Give him good experiences.
Lead by example. Show him the power of good.
The baby will be the responsibility of the Grand Council. Together, with our care, he will reach his great Potential.
And let that Potential delight the world!
******
So the baby was named Potential, or Vecna, in the Flan language of that time.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2 :
Golden Age
Part 62
1313 SD
The Empress walks through walls.
She could be anywhere.
Beware Stranger!
The Suel Imperium is ruled by a ghost.
--------------
From the Book of Syrul. Chapter XXIX
*********
Empress Dully died long ago.
But Syrul wasn't willing to let her fade away into mist.
The Goddess was still angry with Dully for burning down her temple, and despite the deep gloom that surrounded her, her transparency hung on to a semblance of substance.
Blood still pumped through her veins, though it looked pale blue.
Her heart still worked, more or less.
Lurch...thump. Lurch...thump.
Dully was glad that she had become the first Emperor of the Suel Imperium, but she had hoped to be alive to enjoy it
She couldn't eat and she couldn't sleep. She couldn't make love or enjoy the company of friends.
Everyone and everything plotted against her.
They obeyed only because they had no choice.
Her Will was Law.
And because she was Misery, so should they feel pain and loneliness.
'They', her Subjects, her Suel.
They plotted against her.
She didn't blame them.
**********
The Maures were proud that one of their own was Empress.
Who would have thought that when Lemmik Maure left to investigate the Drow jungle, that her Granddaughter would Inherit Everything.
Only a few decades ago, the Maures were considered amongst the fringes of the Great Families.
Other Houses were manoeuvring.
If only Empress Dully had made clear her succession plan.
Then they realised, to their horror, why there was no succession plan.
Empress Dully was the First Emperor.
And she planned to be the Last Emperor.
Empress Dully would be the Only Emperor.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2 :
Golden Age
Part 63
Where is our God, Syrul?
Is she in the Temple?
Is she in the Palace?
Does she Court the Empress?
I know where our God, Syrul is.
She is the Temple.
She is the Palace.
She is the Empress.
(From the Book of Syrul. Chapter XXIX.)
**********
Dalt Maure had been born on a pirate ship.
His hair was a shock of red, which indicated some Flan ancestry, or perhaps even Mystaran.
But he was a Maure.
Dalt would have been called a prince before the Suel Imperium was formed. Perhaps as a bastard he wouldn't have reached the pinnacle of the Senate.
Perhaps he would have become a Beast Master.
That time was over.
Who cares if you are a bastard.
What mattered if you were prince or count or baron?
A ghost haunted the Imperium.
*********
Dalt was clever. Dalt was quick. Dalt was reckless.
His god was Norebo, the God of Luck.
He had been a handful, growing up in the Maure household. Always restless, always up for pranks.
Dalt Maure had been born on a pirate ship.
He would have made a good one.
**********
The Maures were increasingly worried.
The Empress held onto the Imperium and she wasn't going to let go.
Surely, one of their own was next in line, but the other Houses were jostling.
The other Families thought that they had more right to rule the Imperium than the upstart Maures.
Of course, they faced the exact same problem.
Empress Dully wasn't going anywhere.
********
The priests of Syrul were of no help.
Syrul had appointed Dully as Empress. She was there by Divine Right.
To plot against the Emperor was to plot against Syrul.
Blasphemy.
Syrul had transformed herself into the palace itself. To enter there on false pretences was to enter her realm.
The palace was a maze, a deathtrap.
To attempt to breach it, to defy the Goddess and slay the Empress was impossible.
Impossible.
Say you did make it through the stone guards. What then? You go left and you actually go right.
You go up, but you go down.
You reach the throne but you are trapped in a pit.
Impossible. It can't be done.
Dalt grinned.
This is quite true, he agreed.
But what if one entered the Palace for the right reasons?
What reasons?
To ask for her hand in marriage.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 64
Down steps.
Down. Down. Down.
Winding. Winding.
Down. Down.
Why are you here, Dalt? Why are you here?
I have come to the Palace to seek the Empress.
Why have you come to seek the Empress, Dalt? Why do you seek her?
I have come to offer marriage.
Marriage? Why should the Empress marry you?
Spikes rising from the floor.
Spikes in the walls.
Be careful, Dalt, be very careful now!
I am Dalt Maure, and to marry her is my destiny.
I have travelled far, across rivers and jungle.
I enter the palace with a proud heart.
Let me see her, Syrul.
Let me come to her and propose!
I don't believe you, Dalt.
I don't believe you. You shall die here. The spikes will impale you and then I shall collect your Suel blood.
So Dalt did sigh.
Then so be it. No better place to die than here in Syrul's palace.
So close, so close to my dear Empress.
Shall I close my eyes or die admiring you?
So Syrul did sigh too.
What was truth to her?
So she relented.
A door opened.
Proud Dalt passed through.
(The Book of Syrul. Chapter XXIX)

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 65
Empress Dully heard the door creak open.
She was looking out a tall glass window, gazing at the brown and grey land outside, even though the throne room was deep below ground.
The brown and grey land was framed by white sky streaked with pale yellow clouds.
Dully knew that it wasn't the Empire that she was looking at.
Hades was stalking her.
Then the door creaked open, so the Empress turned to face her intruder
It was a ghost that she saw.
The ghost of a young man with red hair.
She was a ghost too.
So they had that in common.
They both floated around each other.
"Hello," said the ghost boy.
"Hello," said Dully.
"I have come far to find you.'"
"I suppose you have," said Dully.
The ghost boy paused speaking for a moment. He bobbed up and down in thought.
"You are the Empress..." he ventured.
"Yes," said Dully, "and you are...?"
"Dalt Maure. I wish to marry you."
Oh, yes.she had heard about this plan, but then, she heard about nearly everything..
"Oh," she exclaimed, "you're Dalt? I expected you to be taller"
Dully simpered, "and more alive."
Dalt looked down, finally noticing that his body was translucent and his clothes were pale grey. And his feet were not quite touching the ground. Oh, no...
"I would rather not marry you, if you don't mind," said the Empress, " so if you would please go back the way you came, that would be well for you."
But Dalt wasn't listening.
Was he dead?
Syrul had tricked him.
What did he do now?
"Please go," repeated Dully, "I do not require marriage at this juncture."
Dalt felt for the chain in a fold in his toga.
It was still there.
He pulled it out from his toga and produced a shining locket.
"Before I go," he asked the Empress, "may I please give you this one gift?"
Dully frowned, but she took it.
Dalt indicated that she open it. She did, with a click. She looked inside. On a tiny ruby coloured cushion sat a small golden key.
"You are the key to my heart." said Dalt.
The Empress felt the air between them cool. Her simmering anger was chilling the room.
The presumption. The presumption of this little man.
No one manipulated Empress Dully.
Suddenly her face was distorted, demonic.
"You had best meet my friend," she snarled.
And she opened the window.
A corpse climbed through.
The corpse of an old man, ravaged with rot. One hand was gone, the other hanging by dry thread-like veins.
He was bald, save some tufts of bristles, completely white.
His chest was exposed, and a black heart wheezed within a splintered ribcage.
It was the broken shape of a very aged Magistrate Jacq. The Magistrate engulfed by Win-Daled.
The Suel Lich was back.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 66
The body of the Suel Lich was breaking down.
She must find a new body. Dully knew this!
Dully had summoned her, but where was her body?
Dully pointed to the ghostly boy.
Him? He was not suitable.
How was she supposed to take over an insubstantial body?
Black flames erupted.
"Dully..." the Suel Lich wheezed, "Dully...shall I burn your palace down, just as I did the temple?"
Empress Dully glared at the rotting corpse.
"Lich, you will follow my commands. The Goddess Syrul flows through my veins, and she will have you obedient."
But the Suel Lich was still unhappy.
"Release me, Syrul, I beg. This body is dissolving. I am the first Queen. I deserve respect."
Dully pointed again at the young man with red hair. He seemed frozen on the spot. Perhaps he was.
"He is a ghost," whined the Suel Lich, "how can I live as a ghost?"
Empress Dully sneered. She was a ghost herself, and still she managed to live.
The Suel Lich looked glumly at the ghost boy. She must try, for the body she inhabited was spent.
She rushed across and embraced him.
Sheets of black flames crackled around the couple, then the old, dry body of what had once belonged to Magistrate Jacq collapsed into sand.
Dalt hadn't moved, for he couldn't move. Had he been substantial flesh and blood, the story of Dalt would be at an end, and Win-Daled the Suel Lich would now be young and strong, with sweeping auburn hair.
But Dalt was already dead, and as the Suel Lich took over his ghost-form, slimy ectoplasm slithered down an arm, falling into the open locket, for Dalt had frozen offering the gift.
The ectoplasm fell into the open locket and pooled around the golden key.
"It is hurting me!" cried the Suel Lich, "this body is no good!"
"It is the only body you shall have," said the Empress. "Go back to Hades. You need not have a proper body there."
Win- Daled was enraged. Her new body burned black and bright.
"I shall burn down the palace!" she ranted, "Syrul. Hear me. I defy you!"
Dully flung herself at the Suel Lich, translucence versus translucence.
Mist and vapour coalesced.
Ghostly fire burned.
Dully felt her heart scorch.
The Suel Lich through her off. The First Empress bested by the First Queen.
Racked with pain, enduring the agony of Undeath, Win-Daled the Suel Lich was nevertheless too strong for any ordinary phantom to match.
Dully Maure; Witch, Drow, Suel, Ghost, Empress, twisted into fibrous ether, and snatched by a stray wind rising out of the open window, was plunged wholly into Hades.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 67
The locket and key were magical.
Of course they were magical.
Would Dalt have dared bring the Empress a gift that wasn't magical?
********
The Suel Lich was alone in the throne room.
Black flames rose and flickered, ghost-like, because she was insubstantial and her body was already failing.
The dead body of Dalt Maure.
It was agony, this existence.
She supposed that it would end soon.
The Suel Lich looked out the window at the bleak and barren wastes of Hades
There was no trace of Empress Dully at all.
She sighed and prepared to dissolve.
Then, out of the corner of a grey shadow of an eye, she noticed the golden key, glistening with ectoplasm.
It looked beautiful.
Perhaps the key would be the last beautiful thing that she would ever see.
Impulsively, she bent down to pick it up.
The Suel Lich expected her fading hands to pass through the key, but they grabbed it and brought it close.
The key was smiling at her.
How can a key smile?
(Because I am in your thoughts)
Who? What?
(I am Dalt. I am in the key)
Yes. Dalt. This failing body she haunted had once belonged to Dalt.
(You are breaking up. You are losing existence)
The Suel Lich nodded. Her time had come.
(I want my body back)
It is mine now. Such is my curse.
(We can do an exchange. You be the key and I will be me)
How?
(Pick up the locket. Put the key back in it. Before you close the lid send your black flames in. Then close)
And what shall happen?
(I will be a ghost again. Too bad, I liked being alive. But if we don't exchange then we both die forever)
And me?
(You shall be in the key)
I want to die forever.
(As long as the locket stays closed, you will)
*****
The house of Maure had always known that Dalt's plan was foolhardy, and they fully expected his proposal to the Empress to lead to his death.
They also knew that Dalt had a plan to rid them of the immortal Empress.
So two things happened, both not unexpected.
Dalt never returned.
And the Empress disappeared.
Once the Suel Imperium realised that Empress Dully was gone, the Royal Houses began to plot in earnest.
But the Maures were one step ahead.
They had a huge Beast Master called Llerg.
He rode a cave bear.
He smashed heads.

A History of Oerik
Book 2
Part 87
Llerg awoke.
But not the Barbarian Bear.
The true Llerg. The Llerg inside.
He could think with crystal clarity.
The Demon Prince, Demogorgon was about to end his life. What a magnificent creature, tormented in the steaming acid vats of the Abyss, quenched with mercury and lashed with vitriol.
Such is the suffering of demons.
All the knowledge, all the learning given him in the Imperium, it was all inside him now.
It had always been inside him, but something blocked its absorption into Llerg's awareness.
Llerg had been emotion and instinct.
Honed muscle and animal strength.
The Beast Master of Beast Masters.
The Suel Emperor had been a bear!
******
Head Two's eyes narrowed. What was happening? The Sacrifice had succumbed to his confusion gaze.
Now he looked anything but confused.
He was smiling at him.
Demogorgon couldn't remember the last time that he saw anyone smile. Not a genuine smile anyway.
It was disconcerting.
Head One lunged, his enormous canines plunging down.
A fist struck him hard in his teeth, one seven inch tooth dislodging from the blow.
Head One reeled, unconscious. The shock of the impact shook the entire demon prince.
Head Two should have been happy with finally being in complete control of his body, calm, rational malevolent thought working as one, without the chaotic static from Head One.
But his head throbbed.
"Go back to the pit," growled the Sacrifice, his body relaxed, his face calm, "Go, if you value your abhorrent life. For the Missing Emperor has returned."
*****
The Obsidian elementals gathered around Burble and Fharlanghn. The lights that blazed from within harsh and blinding.
The City of the Orb must be protected.
The rain had slackened, the clouds nearly spent. Fharlanghn communed with the stones. He was on their side.
The response was a rebuke.
The City is not for you, Fharlanghn. Wander elsewhere.
And then the stones spoke to Burble.
High priest of the Orb Troglodytes, your ancestors found us, long ago.
Your people walked out paths, gardened the plants, admired and added to our art.
We thought we were whole again.
Our city was returned to life.
Why did you then seek more?
Why did you seek Power?
******
Llerg landed blow after blow, his fists and legs springing forth in an unstoppable dance.
Demogorgon retreated.
The enormous, tentacled, simian headed reptile had never encountered anything like this.
Demogorgon's own attacks passed through the Sacrifice as if he were mist.
Head One lolled upon its neck, dead to the world.
Head Two felt like it was carrying the world.
Yes! Return to the pit. Return to the Abyss!
Emerge again some better day.
********
Fharlanghn dipped his bread into the cheese then took a bite.
Best cheese he'd ever had.
How he came to Adarus he didn't know. The continent was mild, temperate and a very, very long way from Oerik and the Amedio.
He had left Llerg wandering his own path. Llerg didn't want to return to the Suel Imperium. He relinquished his crown.
Llerg explained it quite simply.
He was free.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 88
1347 SD
Baba Yaga looked up into the sky and saw nothing but skulls.
Every cloud was a skull. Large grey skulls or ghostly pale skulls.
Tormented skulls.
.Pleading skulls.
Some still had eyes in their sockets, rolling bovine eyes, focussed upon Heaven.
Or Hell.
When Baba Yaga turned away,, glancing down upon the white, powdery snow, every crystal was a skull staring right back at her.
It was the jar she still kept on her shelf.
The jar that contained Death.
********
What to do about Death?
Baba Yaga couldn't open the jar. If she did, Nerull, the Death god, would escape its prison and show the only merciful action available to it;
Grant Baba Yaga a quick death.
Yet, Nerull was not fully trapped. Somehow his power was leeching out from the jar.
Why else was Baba Yaga seeing skulls?
.Baba Yaga was intelligent, resourceful and independent, but she had never been particularly imaginative. The skulls weren't manifestations from her own mind.
Now then, why was the power leeching out? Nerull had been entombment within the jar for hundreds of years.
Why now?
Baba Yaga's den held a number of magical or arcane items varying in potency, could one or more of them be causing the leakage.
And if the leakage continued, would Nerull be freed?
There was somebody out there who might be able to help her.
The very next morning, Baba Yaga put on her strongest boots and took her longest snow pole then began trekking south across the crisp snow.
She still saw the skulls, and some of them were grinning.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 89
Boccob was feeling more like himself every day, and he didn't like it.
His future was calling.
(Bbboooommm)
Leave the Grand Council.
Spread your wings.
Boccob, don't you know that you are Magick itself?
Don't wish
Be the wish.
********
The Scroll of Vile Darkness wasn't much help either. Boccob had long gotten used to its whining, cajoling, seducing.
He was in control, not the Scroll.
But the Scroll had changed its tune.
(Bbboooommm)
It was sulky and spiteful now.
It burned Boccob's fingers whenever he unrolled it.
And the things it said!
I don't want you anymore.
You are cruel to me.
Let me go! Let me find a new Lover.
You are boring. You don't know what fun is.
Release me!
You disappoint me. You have grown ugly.
I don't love you anymore.
*******
Between the Scroll and himself, Boccob felt caught up in the middle.
His future was angry with him.
(Bbboooommm)
His past felt betrayed.
Boccob knew that he was no regular man.
He was old, but he didn't appear to be over sixty. Spells came to him unbidden. And if he chose to think upon a particular spell, the formula rose into his consciousness in one slow breath.
The Grand Council was an institution he established to create some sort of order for himself, apart from any good it might do for the Flanaess.
That too was under threat, caught between the Olven nations who refused to recognise its authority and the Flan nations who no longer accepted its authority.
The Council met infrequently now. Boccob still had some hope. Ulaa and Heward and Ye'Cind were strong advocates still, but as the years flowed by, the new generations were becoming indifferent.
Was this why Boccob was becoming more like his future self?
He had done all that he could.
Boccob had earned some selfishness.
Yet, he wasn't quite convinced that that was all it was.
(Bbboooommm)
And why did he hear the bass throbbing of a pipe organ ringing inside his head?

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 90
Someone was playing the organ.
Rumbling chords groaning like rusty iron gates shattered the air.
Yet, who or what was playing it couldn't be seen, and nor could the organ be seen either.
"That's because it is out of phase."
Heward looked sad. His brow was creased and his silvery hair looked greyer and paler.
Boccob, Heward and Baba Yaga stood where the Mystical Organ should have been. Blistering broken harmonies continued to belch out from nothing.
"Obad Hai did this," continue Heward, "he is an idiot."
Boccob realised the danger. The Mystical Organ was an extremely powerful artifact and taking it out of reality had rendered it unstable.
But that wasn't explaining who the player was.
"I don't think anyone is playing it," said Heward, "I think it's playing itself."
Boccob shook his head. Someone or someThing was definitely playing it.
Baba Yaga looked up at the sky.
Death peered down.
Was the organ connected with her visions? Was the out of phase instrument affecting the urn that held Death?
Boccob didn't know. The important thing right now was to find out how to get access to the organ and then stop the noise.
Where was Obad Hai?
He was the one who took it out of reality. He could bring it back.
Obad Hai isn't here, explained Heward. He spends most of the time in Fleeth.
The old Druid has become a politician.
******
Boccob seldom felt fear, but his rapid breaths introduced him to that emotion. He could enter the rift, but if he did...
Boccob wasn't afraid for himself.
He was afraid for everyone else. It was very likely that the rift would change him for good.
His future wanted him.
Yes! Go in.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness as well!
Boccob hesitated. He didn't want to become as dissonant as the organ chords.
Baba Yaga saw the fear in Boccob's face. She was gifted with magic too. Let her go instead.
******
Baba Yaga felt the strange feeling that she had left her body at home.
She floated through the rift like a wandering cloud.
A cloud in the shape of a skull.
She was all skull, only skull. Grinning Death itself.
And then she was back in her den in Blackmoor.
She was trapped in a jar.
On a shelf.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 91
Stag men were everywhere.
At the gates, in the streets, manning the watch towers.
Fleeth had become Obad Hai's city.
Obad Hai welcomed them into his quarters. He supposed that he could call them guests, but in reality they were thorns that needed to be plucked.
He led Heward and Boccob to their seats, then asked them what they wanted to drink.
Obad Hai made the drinks himself. He didn't believe in servants and he was quite willing to get his hands dirty.
He liked to work.
Once everyone was settled, Obad Hai asked them the obvious question.
Why were they here?
Oh, the Mystical Organ. You could hardly blame him for that. Obad Hai hadn't built the thing.
"You're the idiot who put it out of phase," snapped Heward.
"I'm an idiot, am I?" asked Obad Hai sardonically, "because I moved an unnatural artifact out of reality? Who was the idiot who built it in the first place?"
Heward's fist clenched. He wanted to punch Obad Hai in the face, but he held himself back.
How dare the arrogant druid criticize the making of the Mystical Organ. The god Pelor even sacrificed himself in order for it to be built.
Heward and the Company used the Organ against Tharizdun. If they hadn't fought him, nothing would be everything.
How dare he!
Obad Hai tried to mollify Heward. It wasn't as if he was against the Organ in principle, but that dark time was over.
Let Oerik return to its true nature.
The Organ, like so much allowed to continue to exist, spoiled the harmony of reality. That was why he let it go.
"But it isn't gone," said Boccob, "it's playing itself between dimensions. Slowly but surely, the Mystical Organ is warping this reality. Your precious nature is bending to its will. Do you remember the storm, Heward?"
Heward nodded. The lightning and the rain was normal, but the thunder had sounded like organ chords.
"Baba Yaga went into the rift to stop it," continued Boccob, "and she is gone."
Obad Hai raised an eyebrow, "Gone?"
"The Organ still plays. She never returned."
Obad Hai wanted to say that she never trusted that witch, but the expressions on Heward and Boccob made him pause.
Perhaps sending the Mystical Organ into the ether had been a mistake. He didn't like the fact that it was leaking its power.
"I suppose I can bring it back," he said, "but it must be locked away if I do. Locked away and sealed off."
Obad Hai stood up, his eyes aglow.
"The dark age of magic is over. Let the Golden Age begin."
"

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 92
Boccob retired to his room.
Fleeth was growing larger by the month. It had a harbour and there were lots of sheep in the meadows around the city. Artisans and craft people of great skill were attracted to its affluent lifestyle.
Obad Hai claimed to love nature, but he clearly loved commerce and wealth too.
Still, Boccob could agree that Fleeth was a beautiful city. It was well laid out with wide paths, the poorest areas were huddled over in one corner, and natural patches of woodland attracted a large number of birds.
The buildings were functional but well made and the Stag Men kept the cities lawlessness to a minimum.
Was Fleeth the model that Obad Hai aspired to? Was the future Flanaess going to become a mercentile empire, filled with Free cities controlled by druids? Cities surrounded with natural beauty, but also regimented farms and pastures?
Boccob had invisiged a freeer society, ruled by transparent leaders of great intelligence and skill, who knew what was best for everyone, open to debate but wisely having the final say.
Boccob went to his bedroom and began to change into his night clothes, when he felt warm air brush his neck.
He turned to face himself.
Old Boccob. His future.
The intruder was smiling, smirking, eyes twinkling with malign intent, leaning on a glowing staff.
"Go away!" hissed Boccob to his unwanted self.
"How can I go if you stay?"
"Don't play games..You aren't me."
"Who am I then?"
Boccob seethed. Whenever his future self came, bad things happened. This was the first time they had met all alone. Boccob was theoretically younger and stronger than his older self, but he knew that his older self had bested him every time.
Calm down, Boccob, talk it through.
"Well," he said at last, "why am I here to see me?"
Old Boccob laughed.
"That's better. Why am I here? To see me, of course.'
"Why? . Why bother me? You know that one day I will be you. Can't you just wait until I am?"
Old Boccob pulled a face.
"Apparently you have made it known that you don't want to become me. I can't have that."
"But I will be you eventually. I can't escape my fate, I know it, but I will delay the inevitable for as long as I can."
"And now you know the reason of my visit. You really must stop resisting me, you know. Why didn't you enter the rift? You and me and the Organ and the Scroll are interconnected. There I was, playing the Organ more beautifully than ever..."
"It was you!"
"Of course it was me! But you resisted. You didn't come to my show. So the witch did instead. She wasn't a fan."
"Excuse me for sounding obvious, but you were me, the me right now, once. Didn't you remember that I didn't go across?"
Old Boccob looked aghast.
"Oh, is my memory playing up again? Of course I knew you wouldn't come across. But you really should have."
"I don't want to become you, remember."
"Oh, there are worse things out there than little old me. You should think it over a bit more for next time, or there may not be a next time."
Old Boccob yawned.
"I suppose I will go on my way. Only came to provide some much needed self care."
"Wait one minute. I'm trying to understand."
"Yes?"
"You, I, played the Organ just to trap me?"
Boccob laughed again.
"Don't be silly. You know that I know that you were never going to go."
"Then why did you play it?"
"Ah, the.hundred gold coin question why not take a guess?"
Then old Boccob was gone, leaving Boccob alone with his thoughts.
"

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 93
1352 SD
It was good to not be alive.
Nerull revelled in being back. His keening howls even terrified the winter wolves. Blackmoor was an agreeable land, why hadn't he visited it before.
He had emerged from what was little more than a black crack in the ground, into a barren, frosted vista, lightly sleeting.
He had been dust!
Dust. Dirt. Sediment.
An afterthought trapped in an urn.
Trapped in a jar.
How many centuries had he been dust?
Crumbled and crumpled.
Forgotten.
Worthless.
And then the stopper eased. Just a tiny amount, just enough to let the sound in.
The sound of a distant organ.
Nerull's mind awoke, but his body was still dust. He tried to gather himself together but his body trickled away like running sand.
His body was running sand.
Then he sensed the witch.
He could smell the magic in the air.
The witch was investigating him. She wanted his power
Nerull didn't want to give it to her.
Will the witch give in?
Will she open the stopper?
Will she release Death?
Nerull didn't know what had happened.
The witch did not release him.
There was an enormously dissonant blast of sound, and here he was, standing in a low cave, bedecked in his black, billowing robe. His skull grinning wildly, his eye sockets glowing green.
The witch was in the urn.
He emerged into sleet. He trod through slush.
He howled. He keened.
O, it was good to not be alive!
*******
Oerik was charged.
Nerull planned to pick up where he had left off, but the Death temples were gone. The Ur Flan had forgotten him.
And where was Dread Tharizdun?
He was destined to rule the Oerth, but he was nowhere to be found.
Nerull found Tharizdun. There was still a temple for him in the Yatil mountains. The Ur Flan there did remember!
The priests prostated themselves to Nerull. They would take him to Tharizdun.
There! Can you see him? The floating mist within the frozen chamber?
It is Our Tharizdun.
Worship with us, dear Nerull, god of the dead.
He hears our prayers. He will hear yours too.
*******
The mist had been Tharizdun?
He was inert. He may as well have been dust.
What had they done to him?
Nerull turned from the priests in disgust. He smote several of them down.
The fools worshipped nothing but a husk.
Oerik was a lost world. Nerull had to find a new purpose.
He was independent.
But he was also lonely.
******
Finally he found them.
Loyal followers of Nerull. Tucked away on an island south of Oerik.
An island called Oeridia, still remembering the old ways.
Here Nerull could rest. The constant wandering was tiring. The animals fled from him, even the monsters.
And the humans, humanoids and demi humans would run, fight and ultimately die.
Let this priest be his eyes and ears and legs.
High priest Dahlver-Nar, arise! My chosen one.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 94
1354 SD
Tovag Baragu glinted in the distance like white mirrors.
The stone circles spread across the shore of this portion of lake Urdukankar, white pillars in wide circles. He had reached his destination.
Dahlver-Nar sat down on a sandy hillock and took a long pull from his water gourd. He wasn't yet thirty, but he looked closer to forty. His eyes were weak and watery, his cheeks sunken, his forehead pasty and lined, and his mouth and teeth were prominent with a strong overbite, but framed with lips thin as wire.
His head was awkwardly triangular, the top of his skull almost hairless already. His arms and legs were long and twiggy and he hunched over when he walked, as if he were ashamed of his tall size.
But he was a great man, and he knew it.
He was the Chosen One.
*******
As he came closer to the stone circles, he saw boats on the lake and a number of pilgrims further off, coming from the north (Dahlver-Nar was coming from the south). Then he saw the steps he was lookin for.
Strong, reinforced steps leading down into the underground. They were freshly hewn as was the straight, torch-lit tunnel.
Dahlver-Nar followed the tunnel and within a hundred feet he reached an alcove with a locked metal door on the other side. Written in a Pyanor dialect was a small sign that said "Wait for Admittance."
There were two pilgrims in front of him, sitting on stools. They wore dusky robes and smelled of sandalwood.
Within a moment the pilgrims were melted puddles on the floor. Dahlver-Nar took a stool. He was next in line now.
Dahlver-Nar waited for three more hours before the door unlocked itself, opening with barely a creak.
The High Priest of Nerull went through. The room on the other side was gloomy, lit only by a few candles. He wasn't alone.
A girl possibly right years old, smiled up at him, her face brown, her eyes white clouds.
"Welcome, Dahlver-Nar," she chanted, "I cannot see you, for I am blind, yet I see everything. I am the Seer of Tovag Baragu. Let me show you what you wish to see."
Mirrored white stone in every direction.
Dahlver-Nar and the Seer were within Tovag Baragu,, and it was a glorious day.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 95
Dahlver-Nar looked up at the stones.
"What do you see?" asked the Seer.
The High Priest of Nerull saw the mirrored reflection of the stones change. Tovag Baragu was showing him someplace else!
Golden domed turrets. Flags of strange design. Soldiers in scale riding unfamiliar animals.
"They are called horses," said the Seer. They are found all over Western Oerik, over the mountains."
"Where is this place?" asked Dahlver-Nar.
The Seer didn't take a look, for her eyes did not work, but she said; "Here. Or near here."
She stuck out her tongue, tasting the air, "but not yet. Not for a long time."
Dahlver-Nar was annoyed. The Seer was playing with him. That would be a mistake.
"No, High Priest, I do not. The stone circles show many things, sometimes the past and sometimes the future. Sometimes it shows things even I cannot understand. Be patient and concentrate. Why did you come here?"
Yes, why had he come here? Dahlver-Nar was sent here by Death. What did Death want with the standing stones? With Tovag Baragu?
He looked again. What did Nerull want to see?
The images changed. He saw dusty plains with no trees or grass. What was this?
"Ah," said the Seer, her face as wise as an old woman despite her looking eight, ",, Tovag Baragu shows you the desert .far from here and across many more mountains it lies. It is the Desert of Lynn."
"Lynn? I have never heard of such a place."
"Truly, it is over there, if you walk on for several weeks. The people of the Colours dwell there, on the other side of the desert. The Empire of Lynn."
Dahlver-Nar turned back to the stones and now he could see the empire.
Triangular stone buildings. Squat brown trees with feathery leaves. More of those 'horses' and other animals too, sandy gold with long legs and long necks and humps on their backs.
And the people. Yes, they were the people of the Colours.
They dressed like butterflies. Some even flew on butterfly wings.
They were a multitude.
"What manner of creature are they? Fairy folk?"
The Seer frowned.
"You ask too many questions. Stop talking and just look. They are as human as you, but they have learned how to fly.'
Dahlver-Nar held back his urge to strike the Seer down. She was just a tool, but an irreplaceable one. Once again he gazed upon the stones.
Why was Tovag Baragu showing this empire, so far away? Did his master, Nerull, really wish to see these things?
The pictures blurred, then changed.
A face, mouldy and rotting, black scabbed and partially covered by dun coloured rags.
The face loomed out from every stone.
It was the face of pestilence. It was the face of disease.
The Seer was giggling, clapping her hands with evident glee.
"Yes,yes! This is what your master wants. Your Death God, Nerull. His old friend lies way over there, across the mountains and across the deserts."
The Seer cursed in her native tongue.
"Behold, Dahlver-Nar. It is Incabulos."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 96
1355 SD
Several weeks? More like several months.
Dahlver-Nar was riding atop one of those creatures called 'camels.' His long legs dangled down into thin air. His knees, thighs and back hurt.
At least the camel didn't spit at him anymore.
The camel knew who was master.
The desert stretched on and on. Surely no place on Oerth could be drier? His guides knew how to find hidden springs of water. Without them, Dahlver-Nar's quest would be over.
The guides were on camels too, but they were inhuman. Pale they were, despite the sun, and their eyes were bright blue.
Desert elves. Who knew that they existed way west, past the Suel Imperium?
Another range of mountains grew slowly up from the ground as the small group travelled on. Another mountain range with an unfamiliar name. Dahlver-Nar didn't even bother to remember half of the strange names he had heard since entering Western Oerik.
The names were as hard to decipher as the people. Scattered Pyanor nations, hordes of ring -mailed orcs and blood -matted gnolls.
All spoke different languages. All had different customs and foods.
And they were all armed to the teeth.
Western Oerik was at war.
Nation against nation. Bandits and thieves raiding lost battlefields as if the forgotten supplies were carrion.
Dervishes on horseback. Nomads herding goats. Pilgrims marching. Elemental Jann on their black camels selling goods and clothes.
The rivers were deep and blue. The forests light green breaks from the grasslands.
The hills were brown and imposing. The mountains walls of forbidding stone.
And now this desert. Hot in the day and freezing at night. Dahlver-Nar thought that the atmosphere fled Oerth once Sol went down to warm instead the stars.
The night sky, black and vast, sprinkled with winking stars, was the only peace he found.
*******
The elf guides were gone. They did not traverse the mountains. So too the camels.
Dahlver-Nar employed new guides. Large brown skinned people with brown curly hair and grey eyes. They knew the mountains well, and they were excellent trappers. The hare here had horns like unicorns and were uncommonly tasty.
.beyond the mountains, they said, lay the Empire of Lynn.
"What are the people like?" Dahlver-Nar had asked one evening, roasting a hare on the fire.
"The people of the Colours?" The mountain man paused in thought.
"We deal with them as little as we can. Everyone knows that they are all insane."

A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Part 97
Huber soared through the air on butterfly wings.
Sol had begun to fall, sending orange light spiralling through the clouds. Just above Huber was a faint rainbow still hanging in the moist air.
The rainbow was pretty, but not as colourful as Huber was. Her wings were orange, white and black, and her scaly armour glowed with fantastic colours of many shades.
Huber looked down upon her magnificent city, triangular buildings glowing white.
She was really enjoying this day. It was her first solo flight.
She was now an adult.
How high was she? Thousands of feet high, she guessed. Huber had flown across Lynn city, and the time had flown faster than she had.
They would be expecting her back soon.
But she was so happy being up here. Her colourful scales streaking across the sky.
She was a dragon now. Not literally a dragon, but as close as a human could come.
Huber was a person of the Colours, the greatest people on Oerth.
******
The sun was dipping ever lower. The rainbow had faded away and the ground far below was indistinct with shadow.
Huber was going to be in trouble.
What could she do now? If she returned to her parents now they would likely punish her, even take away her wings. But if she stayed out after dark, the danger increased.
Broiden had been grumpy lately. She had taken a dim view of intruders in her territory after dark. The brass dragon complained that the people of the Colours scared away the game.
Huber had to descend.
Still, it had been an amazing day, and any punishment wouldn't be forever.
She dropped down through wispy clouds, and below her the land looked unfamiliar.She had drifted too far. She tried to make out landmarks but the darkness was near completion. Huber had never flown the night before. She had become disoriented.
The only choice she had was to come down to Oerth and then walk. Someone would be able to direct her.
There! A single man riding a camel.
Huber landed just in front of him.
"Traveller," she said, "I have lost my way. Is Lynn far?"
The stranger stopped the camel, then looked her up and down. He mumbled something Huber couldn't quite catch, then the man spoke, "how many damned languages do they speak here?"
It was Dahlver-Nar. He was close to the empire now. The girl would be helpful.
"Will you help me get back home?" she asked again.
"Well," said Dahlver-Nar, "if it be the city of Lynn you seek, I believe it's not too far now. You may accompany me, if you will."
Huber smiled. Once she was back home she could blame the stranger for her tardiness. She would say that he had attempted to abduct her.
******
They marched on, the darkness cloaking them with gloom. Dahlver-Nar found it comforting. The land was becoming fertile again, it had even rained a few hours ago. And the people of the Colours didn't seem insane at all.
Then they reached the city.
"

A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Part 98
Dahlver-Nar snarled in Huber's ear,
"You had best co-operate with me, little girl. I can read your mind and I know what you plan."
Huber went pale, though in the darkness no one could tell. The man on the camel was dangerous. She tried to bluff it out. She was a woman, after all.
"I don't know who you are, stranger, but I am Dragon. I will scorch you dead!"
Dahlver-Nar hesitated, but only for a moment. This girl was no dragon. Even if she had changed her shape, her aura was wrong. She was just a human gir...
What was that? A gust of wind touselled his fringe of hair, and Dahlver-Nar felt his muscles contract. A huge black shape soared across the sky, great wings outstretched and luminous .
That was a dragon!
The girl struggled in his grip, for he suddenly grabbed her.
She shrieked when Dahlver-Nar threw her onto the camel.
Brutally tying her up, he scolded her as he pulled rope around her arms,
"Did you summon this dragon? Tell me true, for your mind is too splintered to read clearly"
Huber felt her last ounce of defiance dissipate. When the dragon crossed the sky, she really thought that she was there to save her.
But the dragon had come and gone.
Huber wasn't worth saving. She was fooling herself.
An adult? A woman? Dragon?
Huber was a child, and she was in the hands of a stranger.
*******
They entered the city. There were no walls, no towers. Was the great city of Lynn undefended?
It was pitch black, but the white buildings glowed faintly, lighting the wide road with grey light.Thick cloud covered the moons, and the stars as well. It began to drizzle.
"Do you know how to get to your house from here?" Dahlver-Nar asked.
"Yes."
******
Outside the house, Dahlver-Nar untied the girl and helped her off the camel.
He leaned close to her face.
"You know what to do?" his voice was low and almost gentle. Almost.
"Yes."
"Then let us go in," said Dahlver-Nar, adjusting his mace.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 101
Xxarr opened the door. A tall man in black, wet from the rain, came into the room, and with him was Huber.
Her hair was matted, her eyes wide.
Reinecke frowned. Who was this stranger? What had he done?
"Good evening," said the man, his accent strange., "I found your daughter, lost out in the rain. Her wings had broken."
He pulled from his robe, Huber's butterfly wings. They were both snapped in two.
Reinecke frowned. The breaks looked deliberate to him.
"What happened?" he asked Huber, "who is this man?"
"He found me," said Huber, "I'm safe now."
The man began to warm himself up by standing next to some candles.
"I am Dahlver-Nar," said the man, "I have come from very far away, but I have come for a reason."
Reinecke inched towards his scimitar. He felt very unsure of this stranger. Meyer began to get out of her rocking chair.
"Stay where you are, both of you.," said Dahlver-Nar, very calmly.
The ophidian servant looked over at Reinecke.
"You, whatever you are, don't move either."
"Please don't hurt them," said Huber.
Dahlver-Nar glared at the girl.
"Who's hurting anyone? I just want a little chat with my hosts."
"Did you really rescue my daughter" growled Reinecke.
Dahlver-Nar shrugged, "here she is, safe and sound. So yes, in a way, I did."
He pulled up a chair and placed it near the candles. The candlelight was warm and bright, more than what Dahlver-Nar would expect.
"Should I organise refreshments?" asked Meyer.
"No. Not yet. I want everyone to stay where they are until I know I'm safe. You don't trust me, and I don't trust you." Dahlver-Nar turned to Reinecke, shaking his head, "I see that scimitar. Leave it be."
He gestured for Huber to go to her mother.
"Stay there, with her," said Dahlver-Nar, "you see, we are all friends here."
He paused, passing his eyes across the frightened family. So these were people of the Colours, the people of Lynn? They appeared very normal, not insane at all.
They were clearly decadent.
They looked soft.
And the eel creature? It hadn't moved. The poor thing was scared stiff.
"Good. We're all calm. We're all relaxed. I have come a long way in service of my god."
"What God?" asked Meyer.
"The only god that matters. The one who has cursed us with continuing life, you and me. Until he blesses us with sweet death."
Reinecke grew very afraid. This man called Dahlver-Nar was unhinged.
"We don't know of any god like that."
"No? How about Incabulus?"
"Who?"
"Come now," said Dahlver-Nar, "I wasn't sent here for no reason. Your daughter was fated to lead me here. What I need you must have. Or, at least, you know where it is."
Reinecke looked over at Meyer, who looked over at Huber. Huber was very pale. If that man had done anything to her...
Dahlver-Nar was getting impatient. Incabulos was trapped somewhere in Lynn, and this family held the key.
The scimitar flashed.
Reinecke had reached, grabbed and struck with almost supernatural speed. The scimitar sliced...
... And broke upon the mace that was suddenly in Dahlver-Nar's hands.
"I told you to leave the scimitar," said Dahlver-Nar.
He stood up, wielding his mace.
"I am the High Priest of Nerull. Now you will feel his Wrath."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 103
Dahlver-Nar was being taken somewhere, probably to the ghoul lair.
The ghouls had brought him down, but the bites and claws had not torn him apart. The wounds were deliberately shallow, but the ghouls had injected some kind of necrotic venom.
Dahlver-Nar was paralyzed.
He couldn't move, not even turn his head, so he could only see glimpses of things as he was carried through the dark streets.
Corpse-like skin.
Leering eyes.
Questing fingers.
And his other senses were even more disturbing.
He felt the ghouls clutches, cold and clammy.
He smelled rancid meat.
He heard high pitched squeals and squeaks.
They moved on. Why they didn't kill and eat him on the spot, Dahlver-Nar didn't know. There was no point speculating. He couldn't move or speak. He was completely powerless.
Is this what death was like?
Would he feel the cold soil?
The clammy worms?
The smell of his own flesh slowly rotting away?
The excited calling of crypt rats?
And then he felt the air change, becoming musty and deathly still, and he knew that they had entered a tunnel, and they were winding down into the catacombs below the city.
The ghouls held him up, and a ghastly green glow illuminated an arched vaulted chamber.
The ghouls were everywhere, and they were restless.
White, blank eyes stared up at him, gleaming with hungry lust.
Dahlver-Nar knew that whatever power or fear was holding the ghouls back from a messy feast was losing its hold.
His paralysis was slowly wearing off too. He could move his neck a little, and bending slightly, he could see that the chamber was cavernous and that he and the ghouls were not entirely alone.
On the floor of the chamber were five enormous strong-boxes, rectangular sealed chests. Each was shaking, as if something massive was inside, alive and desperate to get out.
Somewhere beyond the chamber a gong sounded, and black skinned eels with arms and hands slithered in from openings on all sides.
They were like the butler in the girl's house, ophidians they were called, though they glistened as if they were covered in oil.
Perhaps they were.
There must be thirty of them or more. They formed a half circle then one came forward. She looked no different from any of the others as far as Dahlver-Nar could tell, but the others bowed to her in seeming reverence.
She faced the ghouls.
"What iss thiss?" she asked, "why have you brought uss thiss gangly creature?"
She slithered closer.
"What, not even good enough for you to bother eating, yet you present thiss... Thing... To uss as if we would sacrifice it to God?"
She glared with baleful wrath.
The nearest ghoul burst into dust.
The rest began to whimper.
Then one ghoul, perhaps more brave, or more foolhardy than the rest, pointed to Dahlver-Nar's neck.
Around his neck was his pendant, the symbol of Nerull.
The ophidian saw the pendant. Saw the symbol.
And her eyes gleamed with understanding.
"Begone now, ghoulss. Back to your bedss. Food is waiting for you there."
The ghouls retreated, vanishing into the darkness.
The ophidian reappraised Dahlver-Nar, looking him up and down.
"We are glad that you are here," she said, "for your god must be punisshed."
Ophidians swarmed Dahlver-Nar, grabbing him and taking him forwards.
Before the rattling chests.
"Priest of Nerull, " the ophidian intoned, "you must be judged by the five aspectss of Tiamat."
Tiamat?
Dahlver-Nar had heard of Tiamat.
Tiamat, the goddess of the first level of Hell.
Tiamat, the Chromatic dragon.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 104
Tiamat. Dahlver-Nar had heard the name.
She was the Grandmother of Tharizdun.
Tharizdun, once the pinnacle of godhood, had reduced Tiamat to a wyrm.
As written in the Doctrine of the Unrepentant, Tiamat the Chromatic dragon had cursed the Unholy Pyramid of Tharizdun, Nerull and Incabulos, condemning them to dust.
Tiamat was no friend from Hell.
Her judgement would be terrible.
******
Dahlver-Nar was still very weak, so he couldn't stop the ophidians from dragging him up to the first box.
The chest was larger than an ogre, and whatever was inside was causing the entire strong box to shake and thrash.
The priestess of Tiamat touched Dahlver-Nar's face, her oily hand damp and cold.
Then he winced with pain. His mouth forced itself open against his wishes, and his large teeth began to wobble.
Five teeth launched out of his gums, landing bloodily into the ophidian's palm.
She smiled.
"The Firsst asspect of Tiamat is White " she intoned.
A small hatch opened on the top of the strong box.
A shriek, the clash of teeth, then a blast of freezing air shot up from the hatch, striking the vaulted ceiling and leaving there a clutch of icicles leering down.
With no apparent concern, the Ophidian priestess calmly deposited the five teeth of Dahlver-Nar into the hatch.
The hatch closed with a snap.
The chest settled, barely trembling.
They moved to the next box.
The priestess stroked Dahlver-Nar's cheek. Once again, five teeth flew out, landing in the ophidian's hand.
"The Ssecond asspect of Tiamat is Black."
A hatch opened and a shriek of pure rage echoed throughout the cavernous chamber.
A burst of steaming acid streaked out, striking a pillar and leaving a scorch mark.
The priestess dropped in the five teeth.
The hatch shut.
All was calm.
The next chest was bulging and shaking.
The ophidian stroked Dahlver-Nar.
He lost five more teeth.
"The Third asspect is Green."
The hatch opened and the rumbling roar actually knocked two ophidians over. They slithered in oil as they tried to right themselves.
Then a billowing acrid cloud of gas enveloped them, searing their flesh.
Their shreaks bounced about the walls.
The five teeth went in.
Snap went the hatch.
The chest went calm.
Dahlver-Nar felt dizzy and his mouth ached. He tasted blood. What kind of torture was this? Why was the ophidian taking his teeth? How many did he have left?
Five more teeth jerked out from his gums.
"The Fourth asspect is Blue."
Another strongbox.
Another hatch.
Another roar.
A crack of thunder.
A blast of light.
The teeth dropped in.
Hatch closed.
Silence.
Then the ophidians all began to sing, swaying as they sung.
Tiamat. Tiamat. Tiamat.
The final box.
Made of gold.
Five more teeth gone.
Only two left inside Dahlver-Nar's mouth. The two canines.
He was spitting blood, almost choking in it.
Head spinning, he barely knew what was happening.
Grant me Death, O Nerull.
Grant me Death.
"The Fiffthh and Ffinal asspect of Tlamat iss Red "
This time, when the hatch opened, there was no shriek, no roar.
A calm bass voice echoed out from within.
"One day I shall escape this prison. I will burn you all."
"Hussh, young Red," said the priestess tenderly, "you are sserving the misstresss of the Colourss. Your Ssacrifice will alwayss be remembered. I have five teeth for you."
The teeth fell down the hatch.
The hatch snapped shut.
The strong box thrashed.
Then it was still.
Everything was hushed.
Only the drip of melting water from the icicles.
"The Judgement iss Concluded," said the priestess, "Dahlver-Nar, I know who you are."
"

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 105
The ophidian priestess of Tiamat knew who Dahlver-Nar now was.
He was nothing.
He was broken.
