He was wretched.
He was Spirit but not Flesh.
She curled her lips with contempt.
The tall human looked anything but defiant. Did he really think himself a worthy vassal for Nerull?
Teeth are the strongest substance in the human body. By taking his teeth, she had taken away his power.
Five teeth in each box.
Five teeth for each Aspect of Tiamat.
Let the teeth bathe in the Colours.
Let the Strength of Nerull bleed into Dragon.
Dahlver-Nar wasn't even looking at her anymore. His head was downcast, his back bent and crooked.
"I know what you are," hissed the priestess, "and I know what you want."
The ophidian poked his hollow chest.
"You sseek Incabuloss. I know where he iss."
********
Dahlver-Nar had been taken through the chamber and down a rabbit warren of tunnels.
There he was met by young Lynn women wearing white, who bathed him with scented oils and cleaned up his mouth with fragrances of ginger and mint.
His clothes were replaced with bronze- banded mail, reflected in colours of blue, red and green, and he was given a round bronze shield.
He kept his mace.
Dahlver-Nar was lightheaded and he felt as if his body had become displaced. Of course, they had drugged him.
But what were they going to do with him now?
*******
Outside once more, the city bathed in light, armoured men on camels took Dahlver-Nar and tied him onto a camel.
Then they led him away, out into the desert.
..******
At the base of a low mountain, weathered into a long ridge, the knights of Lynn halted in front of a large cave.
"Stranger, this is the place you seek." said the captain of the dragon knights.
"Inside is a rare treasure, collected by Broiden."
Dahlver-Nar couldn't speak, for his mouth was ruined.
The captain answered for him anyway.
"Broiden is a brass dragon. Incabulos is part of her treasure horde."
The captain's mouth under his gleaming helm smiled with malice.
"Dahlver-Nar, foul cleric of Nerull. Enemy of Tiamat. Murdererer. Thief. If you want to retrieve Incabulos for your master, then you must enter the cave and slay the dragon."
Dahlver-Nar was united.
The knights drew great swords.
Dahlver-Nar entered the cave.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 106
The interior of the cave was pitch black.
Dahlver-Nar ignored his aching shoulder and stood upright, shield in one hand, mace in the other.
Was there really a dragon in here?
He vaguely remembered an encounter with a dragon on the way to Lynn, a dark shape with translucent wings.
Was this the same dragon?
The air was still and musty. There was a faint smell of charred flesh.
Dahlver-Nar moved on.
His mouth was a mess.
Most of his teeth were gone.
They had broken him.
No. Nearly broken.
He still had Nerull.
He prayed , Dahlver-Nar attempting to speak the words out loud, but his toothless gums couldn't form proper sounds, and they were still leaking blood.
He said the words in his head.
Dahlver-Nar's eyes shone like a cat.
He could see.
Nerull granted him a gift.
He would need many more.
The tunnel was mostly straight and fairly wide, and cleared of stalegtites and stalegmites, broken remnants were all that remained.
Dahlver-Nar pushed on.
A gust of warm air breezed over his face.
A deep rumble.
A voice.
"Drop your mace, little man."
The voice was deep, like earth and stone. Dahlver-Nar knew that this was the dragon.
"I am Dahlver-Nar, the Vessel of Nerull. I come to seek the one who is trapped here."
Far ahead, in the gloom, with his glowing eyes, Dahlver-Nar could make out the form of a large lizard with a long neck and alligator-like jaws. Two wings lay mostly folded next to its body.
The body was a dull golden colour.
Brass.
And the dragon was scaled and spiked.
"No one is trapped here," said Broiden, "I don't take prisoners."
The dragon sniffled.
"I smell your blood. Drop your mace. You are not from Lynn. You are not of the Colours"
Dahlver-Nar held the mace even tighter.
"Go to sleep," said Broiden, and a hot blast of orange and yellow gas billowed out from the brass dragon's gullet and exploded around Dahlver-Nar.
Dahlver-Nar felt very sleepy.
Go to sleep, said his mind.
Go to sleep.
But Dahlver-Nar had had enough.
He had been paralyzed by ghouls.
He had been tortured by eels
Ridiculed by a seer.
Laughed at.
Scorned.
Judged.
Dahlver-Nar brushed off his sleepiness.
He would sleep when he died.
He began to run, lurching, staggering steps.
His arms trembled, but he held onto his mace with a death grip.
There was an intake of breath, then a searing blast of superheated air struck him in the face.
Dahlver-Nar fell, clutching his face.
His face was on fire!
The mace dropped, ringing as it struck a small rock.
The dragon came forward, slinking on four legs like a panther.
The priest of Nerull was grovelling on the ground, writhing in pain. Silly man. Why didn't he just go to sleep?
Broiden sighed. Time to kill him, she supposed.
Then she paused. His smell was unfamiliar. He was a very odd looking man.
The flames had gone out, leaving his face hideously burned .One eye glowed no more.
"Tell me something" she asked, "for I am curious. Who did you think I was holding prisoner?"
Let me die, lizard! thought Dahlver-Nar, but he answered thus;
Not a man. A god. Somewhere amongst your treasure lies Incabulos."
Incabulos? Broiden had heard of this god. A god of disease. An ally of Tharizdun.
But Incabulos wasn't here. She would know.
"Let me look for him, " said Dahlver-Nar, "let me show you."
Broiden nodded in agreement. Luckily for the man, she had eaten well last night. Not that he appeared remotely appetising.
"Get up," she commanded, "follow me to my museum. Let us see if we can find your god."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 107
The brass dragon turned, then headed down the tunnel.
Dahlver-Nar followed.
He had picked up the mace again, and he briefly considered attacking Broiden from the rear, but her tail twitched and it was spiked.
And he was weak and wounded.
The tunnel opened up into a great cavern.
The walls and ceiling shone like gold.
Here was the treasure horde.
"Welcome to the museum," said the dragon, as you can see, I hide no god here."
What did Dahlver-Nar see with his one good eye?
Bars of gold and silver.
Coins of all kinds, some spilling from sacks, some loose in piles.
Statues. Figurines. Paintings.
Pieces of broken architecture. Pillars. Doors. Steps.
Weapons. Swords. Axes. Hammers. Many that glowed with magic.
Armour of course. Shields. Helms. Gauntlets. Bracers.
And the gems. Diamonds. Rubies. Sapphires. Emeralds. All bigger than a hand.
Broiden smiled, showing her razor teeth. She liked impressing visitors.
Although she didn't particularly like this one. He was not of the Colours.. He was not from Lynn.
And he stank of death.
"Many beautiful things are here in my museum, " said the dragon, "but no captured god."
Dahlver-Nar continued to study the piles and piles of treasure. There. Against the back wall.
He pointed.
The dragon frowned. Some jars. Some ingots.
Broiden felt a chill travel down her brass scales.
One of the jars was very strange. She had found it half buried in the sand not so long ago, maybe a hundred years, maybe two?
She had taken it back to the museum, and went to open it with her claws when she felt a rumble that sounded like the tilt of the Oerth.
So she kept the stopper sealed and stored it with other like items.
Then the jar, the urn merrily sat amongst the other jars and ingots, undisturbed by her or anyone else, until she had forgotten all about It.
Until now.
Dahlver-Nar saw the dragon's changed demeanor.
That jar. That was the one.
Incabulos was trapped in there.
"I am not giving you the jar," said the dragon.
Dahlver-Nar stared into the dragon's lizard eye.
What could he do against the dragon? He was more than half way to death. His mouth and jaw throbbed. His face and hair was burned. One shoulder ached. His back creaked.
He cried out to his god, Nerull, but silently, in his head.
Here is Incabulos. The one you seek.
Dear Nerull, give me the strength I need to bring him to you.
Dahlver-Nar advanced on the brass dragon, shield defending his face, his mace in position to strike.
Broiden was bemused. She would have to kill the stubborn man after all.
She took a deep breath, steam shooting out from her nostrils.
Dahlver-Nar crackled.
Black lightning surrounded him. Black throbbing power.
The lightning surged, then struck, leaping out and clashing against Broiden's scales.
She roared. One scale had caved in, revealing tender skin.
Crack.
Another strike.
Broiden fled.
*******
Tears ran down Dahlver-Nar's ruined face.
Nerull had come at last.
He had vanquished the dragon.
But the price was heavy. His life force was fading.
And pain clung to him like a heavy cloak.
His last two teeth were gone, his gums too loose to hold them any longer. They had fallen somewhere behind him before he reached the treasure horde.
Dahlver-Nar was only a shell.
The black lightning still whirled about his body, perhaps the only thing keeping him from falling into dust.
The last gift of Nerull.
He clambered over the piles of treasure until he reached one particular jar.
This was the urn he sought
Dahlver-Nar grasped the stopper and pulled.
It opened with a pop.
And Incabulos stood before him, a wretched body wrapped in dun coloured linen. Part of his mouth was exposed, revealing a rotting smile. in one hand he held a wooden flute.
"I am free," said Incabulos.
Dahlver-Nar bowed.
He couldn't speak, but his thoughts could evidently be heard, for Incabulos replied,
"Stupid cleric. You think that I am grateful to Nerull? Nerull is dead."
He reached out and touched Dahlver-Nar's arm with his black, gangrenous hand.
"All this time, you thought you served Nerull, the Death god, even though you were bathed in pain."
The laughter sounded like softly beating timpani.
"Bathed in pain. Baptised in it."
Incabulos put the recorder to his mouth and blew into it.
No sound came out.
The god of Pain leered down at the pile of dust at his feet.
"Dahlver-Nar, " he boomed, "Dahlver-Nar. All this time you were really serving me."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 120
1387 SD
Vecna returned to Fleeth, but not to spy or run the Library.
He went back to drink.
He had given up. His talent was largely untapped and it would seem that fate would keep it so.
His physical form was dying and only his mind remained untouched by time.
Why was life so hard? Why was he opposed at every turn?
Obad Hai was too strong.
Boccob was too strong.
Heward was too weak.
There were some very good inns in Fleeth , so why not spend more time in them? The Scroll of Vile Darkness and he were star crossed lovers, fated to never be together.
The Scroll would grow more and more dissatisfied and then, broken hearted and unfulfilled, it would diminish into shadow.
And Vecna? His heart or his lungs or his liver would give in and then he would be dead.
*******
"Hello, Vecna."
Vecna looked up. Did he know this gentleman?
His companions, Ravid, a middle aged woman thief and Gamon, a sometimes -pirate scowled at the old bearded man. He looked like he could be a druid, though his blue robes and floppy hat were covered in moons and stars. But his staff was made of strong wood and his beard was long and white.
Yes. He was a druid all right, a friend of Obad Hai, here to spoil their fun.
Vecna did think him familiar though, but his brain wasn't at full functionality at present.
"Vecna? You really don't recognise me?"
"Go away," muttered Gamon.
The old man smiled and Gamon turned into smoke.
At the shocked faces of Vecna and Ravid, the old man shrugged.
"When he said, 'go away,' I thought that he meant himself and not me. Did I do wrong?"
And Vecna knew who he was.
Boccob. But an older Boccob. And he was colder too.
"May I join you?"
Vecna gestured for Boccob to sit.
Boccob settled back in his chair. "Ah, it is nice to catch up with old friends, isn't it?"
Ravid felt uncomfortable with this stranger, so she got up to go to the bar.
"Yes, by all means go," said Boccob mildly, "don't worry, I won't turn you to stone." He tossed her a small bag of coins.
"Have a few drinks on me."
Then Vecna and Boccob were alone.
"What do you want?" asked Vecna.
"From you? Nothing. At least, not yet. I actually have something for you."
And from his robe he pulled out a black scroll.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness.
"Take it from me, young Vecna. It won't bite. Probably."
Vecna was confused, and it wasn't just the absinthe. Why was Boccob giving him the Scroll now, after he had worked so hard to stop him?
Boccob stroked the Scroll as if it were a kitten.
"See, it's quite docile now. The Scroll and I have quite a History. We haven't always gotten on, have we Scroll?"
Vecna reached out...
...and touched it.
The Scroll tingled his hand.
"Ah, good! I knew the Scroll liked you," said Boccob,. "take it, by all means. Put it in your shirt. Have fun with it."
Vecna did so. He felt the Scroll shiver against his chest.
"Why the change of heart, Boccob," he finally managed.
"Who said I had a change of heart? Boccob is as stuffy as ever. I had to take it off him by force. My younger self is still very boring."
Boccob climbed to his feet and took his staff.
"Best be off. Zagyg will wonder where I'm at."
He turned to look at Vecna one more time, a twinkle in his eye.
"Oh, and Vecna. I wouldn't drink anymore. It's not safe to drink and scribe."
Vecna sat at the table feeling stunned.
He felt elated. The Scroll was now his. But he also felt deflated. He hated to be played.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 121
Alone at last!
Vecna's gnarled old hands stroked the black vellum of the Scroll. It was warm and it was trembling.
Vecna couldn't believe that the Scroll lay under his fingers, but here it lay, unwrapped.
Magic sigils covered the vellum, coy to give up their secrets.
Yet.
Would Vecna have to woo the Scroll? Hadn't he proven his love already?
Why did the Scroll remain silent. Why wasn't it eager to receive his gaze? Why were the sigils not yielding to him?
And then Vecna realised the truth. The Scroll of Vile Darkness was as overwhelmed as he was. So long disappointed, dreams unfulfilled, when the fantasy became the reality the Scroll still thought it was asleep.
He would be patient.
He left his Scroll partially unrolled, covering part of his desk in deep shadow, as he went to make himself a drink.
This place was his hideout. Not even the Stag Men knew of this hut. It was so ordinary that eyes passed right over it. Vecna had put quite a bit of magic into that.
So, his Scroll would remain undisturbed.
Still, when he returned, Vecna half expected the Scroll to be gone.
But there it was, a black void upon the desk.
Vecna, it breathed, Vecna my dear. Vecna my love. See what gifts I have.
And Vecna began to read.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 122
1398 SD
Aging was such a pitiful ailment.
The love of Vecna's life had come too late. How could he satisfy the Scroll of Vile Darkness with a failing body? Within the coiled vellum of the Scroll were secrets of the multiverse, secrets that a younger man might exploit.
But not Vecna.
Why was he cursed so? Why couldn't he have been immortal like his supposed parents?
Vecna checked himself.
He knew that he was sulking.
The Scroll lay out on the desk before him, and he knew that it was getting sick of his moaning. The Scroll presented itself as serene and composed, but he felt its pain.
The Scroll regretted the aging of Vecna too.
The Scroll had previous lovers, all of which had quickly become disappointments. Vecna was different. Vecna had the cold, calculated cunning of a true genius, and his ambitions were enormous. He didn't crave destruction for its own sake like Tharizdun, or behave erratically or recklessly like Lolth, or learn but do little, like the Queen of Chaos.
Vecna wanted to put the Darkness into practise.
But to do that, Vecna needed a sound body.
******
For a few weeks, the Scroll recoiled from Vecna's touch. He couldn't unroll it without it shocking his fingers, and if he tried to read the Scroll, the sigils would blur and move around, making study impossible.
So that's it then.
Vecna's time with the Scroll had come to an end.
He would write a letter, a letter that would explain that it was not from lack of want that Vecna had failed the Scroll. It was from cruel fate, forced to house his brilliance inside a feeble vessel. A vessel that had one overwhelming weakness, it could not resist the passing of time.
The letter would explain it all, and at some future date a new Lover of the Scroll, a lover that could finally give the Scroll everything it deserved, would find the letter, read it and understand.
His failure was not his fault.
******
He procrastinated. The words he wanted to write couldn't quite come in the way that he wanted.
He went back to drink.
But some evenings he stayed sober and pretended that the Scroll loved him again. He would unroll it, hoping that this time there would be no scorching pain, that the Scroll would accept Vecna's last weeks on Oerth before his inevitable demise, and let him live out his end as happy as he could ever be.
And then, it happened.
Vecna unrolled the Scroll. No shock. No pain.
And there were new words written there.
The Scroll had found the secret of immortality.
Was there moisture glistening at the side of Vecna's dry eyes?
It was good to be in love.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 123
1399 SD
The party was in full swing.
Cassa Crix was pleased. She had handpicked the guests with a thoroughness that had annoyed her husband. Ninety percent of ambition was social, but he couldn't see that. Then again, he wasn't all that bright. A useful husband, for sure, and he had produced some strong daughters, but...never mind.
Beggars can't be choosers.
There were more Crix guests than any other house, and no Maures at all. The nascent Suel Imperium had suffered growing pains, and Cassa was dedicated to bringing the empire to a stable fulfilment. The fact that her plans promoted the Crix House into the Premiership was a mere bonus.
Cassa moved effortlessly from guest to guest, her ears catching snatches of conversation and gossip from all ends of the ballroom, and orientating her to her next destination.
It was as if her hearing was enhanced.
Of course it was. Knowledge was power, and Cassa was greedy for both.
Cassa breezed past an old cleric in a dark toga. He was the historian of the Suel, at least in his own mind. He would have nothing useful to add this day.
But what did he say?
He was talking to a young man, barely fifteen. One of her nephews, Flipp. Had she heard correctly?
Cassa slid over and entered the conversation.
"Good nephew Flipp, I see that you have struck upon Zola. He can tell you who placed the first stone of the pillars of Risewater if you have an interest in such things, but not so much the sort of things young men usually take an interest in. Would you like me to rescue you?"
Flipp met Cassa's eyes with innocent earnestness.
"Oh, no, Aunt Cassa, Zola is very interesting. He knows so much. He thinks that it is true."
"What's true?"
"Heward is back."
******
Who knew that Heward was real?
Cassa presumed that Heward was a made up folk hero set up by a long forgotten author to give flavour to the old Suel tales of the very early history.
The Rogue and the Magician and the Drow.
Was she really going to meet this man? A man who was over fourteen hundred years old?
Cassa understood that Zola thought him truly Heward, but Zola wanted to believe it.
She would find out soon. He guested at the estate of one of the lesser Maures. Of course they would let her in to see him. Refuse the offer of friendship from Cassa Crix? Unlikely.
Yes, Cassa would pay a visit to the decrepit old Maure, and she would find the truth.
If Heward was real, and if he still existed...
Wheels turned inside her racing mind.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 124
The Suel Imperium sat upon Drow land.
Heward could smell the change in the air. It was an indescribable scent, slightly sweet and slightly foul.
He was close to the Palace, and that great edifice filled him with dread. At night, when he looked out of the window, the shadowed forms of gargoyles flew above the spired roof of the palace, wings beating against the black sky.
Heward needed the Palace.
Evidently, it didn't need him.
Heward could have snuck into the Palace, he supposed. Turn himself invisible and sneak around until he found what his son needed. But the Palace was a God, and he couldn't fool a god for long.
Ah, his son.
Vecna.
He wasn't doing so well. He had become very ill since entering the Imperium, and he said that his body was failing. He stayed in his room and let no one comes near him. Heward had last spoken to him several days ago, and he saw that Vecna's complexion looked like cold stone.
Vecna swore and cursed. Fool of a father! You have failed me again. We have come too late and you do nothing. Leave me be. Let me die!
Heward had sighed, then sobbed quietly once he was alone. He had lost his beloved Lathia. He had lost his beloved Ye'Cind. He was hated by his son.
He was a fallen hero, a broken ruin. Heward's body was marble and it had toppled and fractured.
Heward might as well be a statue. He was as useless as one.
Yes, Heward had almost reached his goal. He could see the Palace, bright and harsh in the sun, cold and sinister under the moons. But he couldn't get in. The guards had laughed at him. The Suel could tell that he was an imposter.
This sad sack our Folk Hero? Ridiculous. He should be stoned or driven out.
And Heward, who felt very uneasy and unsettled, wanted badly to leave and return to Ulek. Vecna, not quite ill yet, insisted that their was still hope. Convince someone father, for you Are Heward!
Rus Maure came across them as they crossed the square. He was old, but his hair was neat and his toga was resplendent red and gold. He was intrigued by the pair. Are you the ones that wanted to come to the Palace? I am a Maure! I am Royal! Come with me to my manor, and let me hear your story. Perhaps I shall take you into the Palace myself.
But he hadn't. Not because Rus Maure didn't believe that the man before him was Heward, but because Rus Maure was rich, and royal, yet of no consequence. His branch was a withered vine and all he had was one magnificent house. No influence. No respect. Rus Maure was an old eccentric cousin of a once great House. If it wasn't for his Aunt, he wouldn't even be a Maure.
Heward was trapped in the house. Vecna lay dying in his room, and he lay sobbing in his.
And Rus Maure promised each and every day, "yes, I am using my influence, and I am pulling my connections. Dear heroic Heward, I will soon have you in our Palace."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 125
Cassa Crix and her entourage flounced into the room.
Cassa smirked at the expression on Rus Maure 's face. He hadn't had someone as important as she come to his house for quite a while, she was sure.
"Madam Crix, a delightful honour, " he said. Cassa acknowledged his words with a slight incline of her head.
"Now, where is he?" she asked.
"Who?"
"Now now, Mr Maure. You know very well to whom I refer. The folk hero, Heward. He is alive and well and staying here at your residence I am led to believe."
Rus beamed. This was good fortune. Cassa Crix could help bring Heward into the Palace. His messages must have been read after all.
"Yes, indeed he is, Madam Crix. I shall summon for him at once."
An old man soon entered the sitting room. His clothes were patched and fully coloured as if the die had faded away. His face was darker than a Suel, almost coppery, and his hair was white. Was this man Heward?
"I am," said the man.
Cassa wasn't convinced of course. Heward might be long dead. It might be that he never actually existed in the first place. How to tell? Well, a little spell was in order. Would Heward consent to an examination?
"I do "
A golden bulb of Divination orbited Heward, then blinked away leaving a flash of light on the retina.
Well! The spirits were in agreement.
This was Heward indeed. Gracious!. The man is real..
Cassa Crix moved about the room as if she owned the place. Rus Maure took a chair as he watched the interloper organise food and drinks.
Cassa wanted to know everything about Heward's life. What was the old Drow lands like? Had he really met the very first Suel? Was the First Queen a long list friend? What had he been up to? What was the world across the Hellfurnaces like?
And Heward, why did you end up in this old place? You don't want the Maures helping you, for that House had faded, and everyone knew that. You should have come to House Crix directly. Three of the last five emperors had been Crix's.
Heward felt a little overwhelmed. His old charm and roguish nature was long gone. He hadn't socialised for decades. He stammered in reply, answering Cassa with few words.
He wished to go into the Palace. His son was dying but had found that old secrets of life lay hidden within that magnificent building.
Secrets of Life? How intriguing.
Yes, old Drow magic, possibly created by the Spider Queen herself.
Gracious me. I wouldn't believe a word you are telling me if I didn't know who you were. Did you ever meet Lolth?
Heward nodded. He had fought her long ago, and helped to bring her down.
"Well," exclaimed Cassa, "I think that I will talk to the Emperor and organise a visit for you. What is wrong with your son exactly? The Suel have strong medicines for most ailments and maladies."
"Old age," answered Heward.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 126
Vecna lay flat on the bed. He had pulled off the sheets because he was feeling too hot. Vecna's skin was clammy with sweat.
This was it for him.
Death was coming.
He wore nothing but linen pants. The Scroll of Vile Darkness partially unrolled, lay near his head like a dark, black stain.
Oh how old I am.
And Vecna looked at his hands, clubbed with arthritis, and blue stoned.
He was becoming Drow once more, Drow as he was when he hatched out of an egg.
What kind of egg was it, that an elf laid?
Olve does not lay eggs
Vecna knew.
It was a spider egg.
*******
Delirium took Vecna at last, and his soul dived down under the bed. There it found a small hole in the floor and descended.
Vecna was surrounded by dark light. The Scroll lay purring in his ghost arms. Down he went, like a cold draft, down and down and down.
Strange creatures, pink and violet, horned and tusked, jeered him as he travelled through a twisted tunnel.
What have you achieved, Vecna?
What have you done?
Nothing.
Nothing at all.
Vecna was a gust of cold air travelling through the Underdark.
*******
Then the passage became clogged with webs. Enormous spiders worked upon them, spinning out ever more web, as if web was life itself.
Time and again, Vecna's ectoplasmic body struggled to continue downward, pulling itself away from the sticky strands that caught in his hair.
Then the web cleared and the tunnel opened up into a network of galleries.
Galleries filled with Drow.
Real Drow. Drow with white and lavender hair, dark blue skin and violet eyes.
They didn't even see him as Vecna fell amongst them.
Well, he was dead.
Still, he looked admiringly at his ancestors. The Drow were beautiful.
They wore little, but what they did wear was ethereal and emphasized their shapliness. Why did the surface world denigrate the Drow?
More striking than any elf Vecna had ever seen, they carried themselves with a haughty self awareness that reminded Vecna of gods.
Perhaps the Drow were gods.
Vecna wanted the Drow to acknowledge him as he fell amongst them, an invisible breeze of dust and decay.
"Here I am!" he called out, "I am Drow too. I wish to live amongst you. Say something dear sisters!"
Of course they ignored him. Even if they could see, or even feel Vecna as he tumbled through the labyrinth, they would ignore him.
Vecna was not Drow. Vecna was a broken chord from a broken spell.
What had he done in his cursed life?
Who cares.
******
Everything opened up. An enormous cavern stretched out under the Oerth, immense and lit with luminous light.
And there she was. The Spider Queen.
Lolth.
"I hear you Scroll," she whispered, somehow high and low pitched together.
"Come to me, Vile Darkness. Leave the crippled thing. Return to me."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 127
Heward was resurrected.
He felt useful again. Cassa Crix was delighted with his wit and his dashing looks. She could see through his marble and observe his diamond heart. It was uncut, unpolished, yet within the stone was untapped light.
Cassa bathed in Heward's brilliance.
Heward was brilliant, wasn't he? He had resisted empires, fought gods and demons, played the greatest instrument and he was the Magus. The First Bard.
And Cassa saw him as he once was, because he wasn't any of those things anymore.
Cassa made him believe again.
"Come with me, after your digging around for the secret of youth. Come back to my beautiful province where the gardens make perfume and the birds eat from your hand."
*******
Emperor H'jax of House Lemera, opened the letter from Cassa Crix. What did that harlot want this time? He read the letter quickly, scoffing rudely under his breath.
The insolent bitch. The deferential tone belied her real thoughts. Cassa saw herself as at least an equal with H'jax, if not his superior. H'jax found this hysterical. What sad losers these Crix's were! They treated the House Lemera as placeholders before their inevitable return to the throne.
The Crix's were rich and influential with the other Houses. Eliminating them would be counterproductive, because instead of one reculcatrant House, he would need to deal with many.
Keep the Crix's close. That was the trick.
Now what to make of the contents of the letter? Allow a long lost myth to explore the grounds of the Palace with his ailing son? Cassa was losing her mind. Good. Demented Crix's were a curse well deserved.
Emperor H'jax would write a letter back to the slut and fool. Let Heward and Vecna come to the Palace. They can move freely through the old rooms and corridors.
If the Palace itself allows.
Syril take them!

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 128
Heward readied himself for his trip to the Palace. Cassa Crix had provided him with a purple toga with a magnificent displacer beast cloak, black as coal and soft as silk.
It was fitting for a great Folk Hero to look his best, Cassa had said.
And Heward looked grand.
Although Vecna was also invited, Heward prepared to go only with Cassa. Vecna had slipped into a coma. Heward hoped that the magic he would find would restore his son to health.
Vecna had assured him that old Drow magic was in the Palace.
His only hope to stave off death.
Heward knew that Vecna was odd, cold and prickly.
But he was his son.
And he would do anything for him.
*******
And the morning of Heward's visit a miracle happened.
Vecna came into breakfast with glowing eyes and with a smile on his slate blue face
He felt much better, he said, almost resurrected. There was something in the air that had rejuvenated him.
See, Heward, I told you that the Suel held the secret of youth. The Palace is on Drow land.
Could they return to Ulek then? Was Vecna cured?
Vecna shook his head, and Heward noticed a new growth of hair atop his head. Hair of pale lavender.
"No. We must search the Palace, " Vecna said, "I have been given a reprieve, no more."
*****
Cassa was delighted that Heward's son would join the expedition after all.
"The Palace owes a debt to you, great Heward. Without your struggle against the Drow, the Suel Imperium would not exist. The Palace would have never grown in the tangled jungle. Monstrous spiders would hunt us down. Yes. The Palace will open its doors to you, I am sure. You, and your dear son."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 129
The Scroll of Vile Darkness had chosen Vecna!
It had been a fever dream, he knew, but somehow he had travelled into the Underdark and met Lolth.
The Demon Queen grasped for the Scroll, but it wouldn't come to her.
It had chosen to stay with Vecna.
What tortures he endured in the subsequent nightmare he would never mention. Finally, Lolth released her hold upon him and he ascended back to his bed.
The Scroll had saved him, and had transformed him. His hair was growing back (a different colour, but so what?) and his arthritis and aches had eased.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness wanted a future with him and she preserved him for what was to come.
Somewhere inside the Palace lay his destiny.
*******
The ghost of Dalt still wandered the endless halls of the Suel Palace.
Emperors had come and gone. Mostly raised by ambitious Houses. Mostly laid low by ambitious Houses.
It had been a chaotic time.
The Palace was a goddess. She was Syrul herself. Dalt could feel her pleasure.
She enjoyed the pain of her children. They tore at each other's throats, yet rather than diminish, the Suel learned lessons that would hold them in good stead.
Ruthlessness.
Deceit.
Persuasion.
Weak emperors were doomed from the start. They couldn't access the treasure vaults and died amongst beauty, completely penniless.
Strong emperors were rewarded with magnificent weapons and magic. There was carnage before their time came.
Dalt had seen it all, a forgotten ghost that Syrul barely noticed.
And now new guests have come to the Palace. Guests invited by the new Emperor. They walked amongst gold and marble.
A Crix. A Flan. A Drow.
What would Syrul want with them?

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 139
1431 SD
They were still called the Stag Men, but they no longer wore stag masks with sweeping antlers.
Their robes were brown or grey or black and instead of masks they wore grey caps. The Stag Men wore simple, neatly trimmed beards with a small moustache. They tended to walk in pairs.
For those not in their inner circle the Stag Men all appeared the same with no discernible hierarchy, but for those in the know, subtle differences of expression, of the placement of a hem or the rise of a collar, indicated sometimes vast differences in status.
Fleeth had risen again, as had most of the other great cities on the east coast of Oerik, but this time they were less populated, more controlled, and the Stag Men were administrators and rulers.
Magicians and Ur Flan were expunged. The only religion allowed was Druidism. The population was almost entirely Flan, with a smattering of Flan with some elf or orc ancestry. Foreigners like dwarves and gnomes could be employed for specific projects, but then they would be paid and sent home.
Boccob was saddened by this.
Although he lived far away in the west, in a multicultural realm called Ulek, the old wizard felt, not for the first time, a growing unease that the new promise he felt after the fall of Tharizdun had gone pear shaped.
The Great Council's gentle guidance of the affairs of Eastern Oerik had been too gentle, stroking with a velvet glove when perhaps an iron gauntlet was needed.
Boccob had high hopes for the basic goodness of humanity. Perhaps he needed that hope, because his future was smirking at him.
If Boccob could resist his own future corruption, then perhaps the Flan could too.
Yes, he had been far too naive for the world.
Two of the greatest heroes were gone, lost to time. The Great Council was hardly great now. It wasn't even independent anymore.
The Great Council was incorporated into the political system of Ulek. Ulaa was the chair. The goings-on in the east barely making the agenda.
Ulaa wanted to concentrate upon Celene, Ulek and the Sheldomar valley. These were regions that were within their sphere of influence.
Boccob, she had said, Boccob, Obad Hai has the east. Let him have it.
Boccob had stayed silent. He knew that Ulaa was right, that no one person or council could control everything, and nor was that desirable.
But Boccob still felt guilty.
No one knew the power that churned his insides. Raw magic filled his lungs. He was a great wizard that had never needed to study.
If he wanted to, he could probably turn Obad Hai into dust.
Could he? Could he really?
And would it be bad if he did so?
The Stag Men were sinister, anti-free will. They said that they were the servants of Oerth,
There was no glory in being a Stag Man, they said, It was a painful duty. They didn't enjoy trying their fellow Flan. They felt sick with each execution. The Stag Men toiled only for Unity and Utility.
Maybe Boccob would free them from their toil.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 140
1447 SD
Incabulos emerged from the hold of the old, scarred trader.
It hadn't been the first time he'd smuggled himself inside a ship, but he hadn't planned on making a habit of it. He lurched through the shadowed harbour, a bandaged vision of horror.
Now, where was he?
Where was Nerull?
This was the Lowlands, a miserable collection of slums and flotsam and jetsom of humanity.
Incabulos would have to move through this unpleasant collection of squalor and make his way to the Uplands.
The Uplands where the Death priests dwelt.
It was a long walk, for Oeridia was not a small island, and the sun was just beginning to emerge as he reached the hill trail that led to the plateau. He sheltered underneath the shrubs growing off the path and waited for night to return.
Incabulos wasn't bothered by light, but he wished to remain unseen because the reactions of humans to his presence was boring. He didn't particularly enjoy smiting imbeciles, and he enjoyed his own company best.
So why, when the shadows lengthened once more, was Incabulos bothering to find Nerull anyway?
Nerull was a dead god.
Incabulos could smell something else apart from Nerull. Another Power, dormant, perhaps alive. Perhaps dead.
And was it really jealousy that caused Incabulos to trek his way to the Southern island? Nerull had set himself up in Oeridia as the only Death god left standing.
Behold my scythe
Behold my skull beneath my hood.
I am Nerull the Only.
The Pyramid is One.
Worship me so that you may Live.
Incabulos was going to scotch that grift.
Nerull was a dead god.
And Incabulos was going to make sure that he was dust.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 141
Incabulos went into the cyst.
"Nerull, show yourself."
The tiny room was black. A couple of chests and a few vials, pots and jars were arranged in a ring on the floor. It was haphazard as if someone was attempting an ancient ritual with only the objects to hand.
"Nerull. Dead thing. I have returned."
The dust within the circle swirled, forming into the outline of a tall robed skeleton holding a scythe.
"Incabulos," it croaked.
Incabulos looked upon his old, old acquaintance. Nerull had once been a cocky boy who thought that he was smarter than anyone else.
He was a dead thing now.
"Nerull, I am reanimated. I am better than you. Go away. This land is mine."
The outline wavered, and motes of darkness tried to fill Nerull in, but he remained largely transparent.
Incabulos gave out a derisive wheeze.
"Nerull. I brought your servant Dahlver-Nar to me. You are gone. You are nothing. I am the last Death god. Begone."
Nerull's eyes would have blazed with fire, had his eyes any substance.
Incabulos was right. He was dead.
But he couldn't leave the cyst.
He was trapped within the circle.
He had watched Dahlver-Nar journey to the far west of Oerik, his disciple, sacrificing himself for Nerull, but hijacked by Incabulos.
And he could do nothing.
He was a dead thing
"Why won't you leave?" Incabulos's bandaged visage was contorted with imperious rage.
"This is all I have left, Incabulos. This circle in this cyst. But here I rule Oeridia. Let me rule it, Incabulos."
"No. This island is mine now."
"I will not go. I cannot go anyway. I am here to stay."
Incabulos bent down, his rotten knees popping with blissful pain. He picked up an old bronze jug.
"Leave the items where they are," admonished Nerull, "They are sacred."
Incabulos tried to smile, but his black lip caught the edge of a loose thread of bandage and split instead. The jug was worthless junk. Everything in the circle was junk, just dusty old forgotten things
But this jar...
It hummed.
Incabulos picked it up. It was very, very cold.
"Put that down, Incabulos. It is not yours."
Incabulos ignored him. He felt power. Should he pull the stopper?
No, he decided.
"What is in this urn?" he asked.
"I will not tell you."
Incabulos blew out from his cavernous chest and long dead air struck Nerull, distorting him into no more than an amorphous shadow.
Incabulos produced a tooth.
A tooth that once belonged to Dahlver-Nar.
The tooth was as warm as the jar was cold.
He placed the jar back into the ring.
He then threw down the tooth.
Nerull felt a surge of hope and fear and guilt and failure rush over him in an overwhelming wave.
His broken form cracked.
His dust cascaded down, settling upon the tooth. The dust smoked.
Incabulos crossed the circle.
The ring was dead.
Incabulos settled himself into a corner.
He would open the jar tomorrow.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 142
1455 SD
Today was particularly cold.
Baba Yaga used to enjoy snow and frost, but that was then, and this was now.
She wrapped her cloak tighter, but it didn't make much difference. Why did she return to Blackmoor? What was here?
Her heart.
What was cold? A sensation, a discomfort, an inconvenience.
Better than being dead.
Baba Yaga looked around for her trap. Where had she put it? That's right, over near that dying tree. Her boots plunged through heavy snow. The trap was empty. No meat today.
The old witch only placed out one trap at a time, for she didn't want to make an impact more than strictly necessary. She had plenty of nuts stored away and a cauldron filled with broth. She'd be alright.
Baba Yaga trudged back to her den. She felt worn out and was looking forward to a long sleep after her meal.
Then, if the next day was a little warmer her head might clear.
And she would return to her researches.
She had Death to ressurect.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 143
Today was even colder.
Baba Yaga was coming to the realisation that the cold was emanating from her.
The cold surrounded her like clammy tentacles.
How was she supposed to work with a head that felt like a block of ice and hands warped with chilblains?
Baba Yaga threw on a thick fur cloak. It made little difference.
Yes, she was the cold.
Baba Yaga tried to light a torch but her fingers were too numb. However, she persisted and finally she created a flame. She fanned a hand against the flame.
She felt no heat, just a sharp pain as if the flame was the edge of a knife .
If anything, the den grew even colder
Baba Yaga slumped down, dropping the torch. Was cold endurable forever? Could she learn to overcome it? Could Baba Yaga rise above it?
She did have work to do.
*******
Baba Yaga checked her trap. Empty again.
Perhaps the cold was keeping the small animals inside their holes.
She went home but the fire wouldn't light at all, and the broth was cold.
Cold belly. Cold heart.
Baba Yaga had to get back to work. Suddenly the inclination to return to her work bench rekindled inside her soul. She would reanimate Death. Perhaps then, Death would retake the cold.
*******
Death. There it was. A pile of dust. It had occupied a jar, an urn.
The same urn that she had resided in for too many years.
There was a kinship now between Baba Yaga and Death. She only needed to wake it up.
But how do you awaken sand?
She pulled out a doll, a little ragged woolen doll, wrapped in linen bandages.
A little toy mummy.
"Is this your doing?" she asked the doll, "are you cursing me with cold?"
Of course the doll didn't answer.
And how could it? It wasn't as if the doll was a living thing.
Not anymore.
Incabulos shouldn't have made Baba Yaga angry. She put down the little mummy and rubbed her blue fingers until she felt her blood circulate again. Then she once again pondered the problem before her.
How was she to harness the dead dust called Nerull?
.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 144
1462 SD
Monk Vrad found the snow covered hill blocked by heavy thickets.
Should he return to camp and fetch reinforcements? No. Vrad was confident in his abilities, and if he was attacked the retribution would be severe.
The vegetation wouldn't be an impediment anyway. He mumbled a prayer to Obad Hai.
The stiff, thorny leaves parted.
The Stag Man moved through.
He came to the top of the hill and saw the outcrop of stone.
Her cave was there.
Vrad stumbled, for the slope was awkward, but he was able to rebalance himself, and soon he reached the outcrop, curiously free of snow.
Two figures emerged, one from each side of the bare stone.
One was a skeleton garbed in dull blue. The other was a skeleton dressed in faded red.
Blue Death and Red Death.
White skulls turned and stared at the Stag Man with empty eye sockets.
"I have come to see your Mistress," announced Vrad, trying to keep his voice steady.
Red Death and Blue Death said nothing. They moved closer.
"You must not harm me," warned the Stag Man, "I am of high rank. Let me pass, for I must have words with Baba Yaga, the witch."
The two Deaths reached out with grinning skulls. Monk Vrad would not see her this day.
*******
A terrifying shape all in black marched down the main street of Fleeth.
Stag men blocked her way, but Baba Yaga tossed them aside like rags.
How strong she was. Since her return to the land of the living her physical strength seemed doubled and her bad temper likewise.
Her bones were almost protruding but they were like iron, as were her savage teeth and talons. Baba Yaga was a hulk, a monster.
And how angry she was.
"Come out, Burgher Meister. I will tear Fleeth to the ground if you don't."
The threat was listened to, for the Burgher Meister did leave his offices and step out onto the street. He was dressed modestly, and his cap was black.
"Why have you come here, Baba Yaga?"
"Because your Stag Men hound me day and night."
"But you have left Blackmoor and are now in Obad Hai's lands. Go back to the ice, hag."
Baba Yaga 's warped face became even more distorted. A hag was she?
"I go where I will," said Baba Yaga, "I will be left alone. Why persecute me? It will be to your peril."
The Burgher Meister couldn't bear to be around Baba Yaga any longer. She was a giantess, an ogre, an unnatural witch.
The Stag Men had to keep her in check. Baba Yaga was playing games with the Natural World. Obad Hai himself had warned the good people of Fleeth and elsewhere that Baba Yaga must be kept contained.
The Burgher Meister didn't know what to do. How could he get her to go away?
"You and your creatures slew a Stag Man," he exclaimed. "You rob our northern caravan routes. You come in and go out, leaving destruction in your wake. Chilling winds accompany you wherever you go. Stay in Blackmoor and I promise you that I will make sure that you no longer will be molested."
Baba Yaga considered the offer. What more could she expect?
Then she summoned her two Deaths.
Then she went back home.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 145
1466 SD
Rebels were amassing in numbers.
North of the Adri forest, on the thin strip of coast between the Rakers and the Grendep bay, and on the other sides of the bay, North and East on the jagged coastline South of the frozen Corusk mountains, Ur Flan forts and settlements were popping up everywhere.
They were refugees from the Stag Lands, foreigners from Kodgeland and mystics from Glantri in Mystara.
They were concerning. Obad Hai left the interrogation chamber. He needed to think.
Obad Hai had ambitions beyond the eastern Flanaess, for he now dreamed of a united Oerik.
That would take time of course, hundreds of years even, but he was immortal and he was a god, so it was a dream that could come true.
The Eastern Flanaess was beautiful. The towns were small and encroached but little upon the parks, gardens and forests.
Neat squares of farmland quilted the land, but skirted natural Brooks, rivers and lakes.
Wilderness had unbroken corridors that allowed the animals free movement across the range.
The balance that Obad Hai sought had come to pass. Now it was time to expand west. The elves of Blemu and Celene didn't understand balance. They worshipped chaos and mess. The Unnatural Fey blighted their lands with dark mischiefs.
And beyond, in Ulek was Boccob.
Boccob the do gooder. Boccob the wise. Boccob the insolent.
Obad Hai still saw Boccob as he really was, a boy that had been kissed by Tharizdun.
Boccob was the most Unnatural creature on Oerth.
Yet, Obad Hai's plans for the west must wait, for the cold north had become hostile.
The Ur Flan gathered and plotted against him. They were building towers and their magic was growing.
If they moved below the bay, and entered the Adri, Obad Hai would have to war them.
Imagine the Flanaess under the Ur Flan? Demons and devils would walk at will. Slavery would return and the Wild lands would be polluted and broken and ruined.
The Flanaess would become a patchwork quilt of monochrome.
The Druids would lose their power forever.
Obad Hai went back into the room. The unfortunate Ur Flan was still conscious but only just. He had lived in Fleeth as a boy, and Obad Hai was fairly certain that he once knew his father.
He had lost a lot of blood.
And his hands and feet too.
But he had been helpful at the end.
Obad Hai took out a small dagger. Time for a little mercy.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 146
1470 SD
Boccob was increasingly restless.
He left Ulek and wandered the stars with Celestian.
He travelled around Oerth with Fharlanghn.
He went to Glantri and saw their impossibly tall towers.
He saw emerging kingdoms take root in Kara-tur.
He saw the Gith fracture into separate peoples.
He went into the homely holes of the gnomes.
He went down into the Underdark, peering up at a vaulted ceiling of light.
Boccob had lost his love.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness had left him long ago, but Boccob couldn't forget her.
There was a time when the Scroll and Boccob were one. He was fused with her, and they kept no secrets from each other. Boccob was the Scroll and the Scroll was Boccob.
He was young and naive, she was old and cunning.
She whispered to him, "do bad things."
Boccob whispered back "but I am good."
"I love you," said the Scroll, "Do bad things so that I can be happy."
And Boccob became confused, because he felt so close to her, and yet so far away.
Boccob chose to be good. It was important. Beyond his horizon his shadow dwelled.
A shadow of a Boccob of What Will Be.
A Boccob that did bad things.
The Scroll of Vile Darkness had fallen out of love with Boccob.
She had taken on a new love.
Yet, Boccob missed her, and he hankered for her. Sometimes he thought that his moral principles had blighted his only chance for happiness.
What had 'being good' done for Boccob?
And why hold onto that good despite Oerth growing dark? Especially when that darkness was waiting to embrace him. His future self.
Waiting for Boccob to come to his senses.
Boccob had lost his love, and he was fated to lose his soul, but he was damned if he was going to idly stand by any longer, shackled to an ideal that was violated by everyone else.
And when he thought of everyone else, he really meant Obad Hai.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 147
So, this was a Stag?
A flabby man, portly, jowled, with watery eyes and dressed in severe black.
Boccob had taken him to the top of a mountain. They were together, alone on a ledge high in the Rakers. Below, the land was obscured by thick grey clouds.
The ledge was all there was, for above was a sheer wall of rock, then sky, and nothing but fog below. Boccob had abducted the Stag because he wanted to know how they ticked.
Isolating one was the best way.
The Stag had been stubborn at first. Boccob was an unauthorised entity. He was not to be submitted to.
Boccob wasn't in the mood for this nonsense.
He struck the man in the mouth.
It had been satisfying, visceral. Sometimes physicality worked better than magic.
The Stag had yelped. Perhaps he had never been struck in his life. A bully that hit others only.
And then he talked. He was defiant and officious. The Stags would come for Boccob, no matter what he did. To take a Stag was a capital crime of the highest order.
Perhaps even Obad Hai himself would seek retribution.
Obad Hai? What did the Stag know if the rogue druid's plans?
" Rogue druid? You blaspheme. Obad Hai is the Highest Druid, the Hierophant. The Father. He will smite you for that!"
"Let him come. I have looked but I cannot find him."
The Stag sneered at the grey wizard, "He does not come to the likes of you. He is everywhere and nowhere. You cannot see him because you have not the faith to see."
******
The more Boccob conversed with the Stag, the less he liked him. He seemed to have no personality, unless that personality was Unitarian.. He called himself an Administrative functionary and he was proud to organise and shape for the edification of the Flanaess. He was also a Guide of Behaviour and an Instrument of Obad Hai.
Finally Boccob had had enough. The Stag had begun to talk of the murders he had committed or organised, justified as mercy killings for an Ideology that Boccob could see was no more than gratification for Obad Hai.
So he did an impulsive thing.
He pushed the Stag off the ledge.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 148
Boccob immediately felt sick. Why had he murdered a man in cold blood?
The murdered man was a Stag, and he had blood on his hands, but he was still a man.
What scared Boccob even more was that he had enjoyed doing it. His hands still felt warm where he pushed the Stag's belly.
Boccob began to feel vulnerable. Should he leave the ledge? The clouds were breaking up below, and the dizzying drop of the Rakers began to manifest.
Above the ledge, across the crags, new clouds were gathering, thick and black.
And then Boccob saw a flash of green and red, and he knew that he was coming.
A comet launching across the sky, flashing in fury.
Obad Hai.
******
The rain came down, shiveringly cold rain that smoked with static.
Boccob knew that fleeing was pointless. He pushed his floppy hat over his nose and looked through the silvery sheets of water, waiting for Obad Hai.
An explosive percussion split the ledge.
There was Obad Hai, looking like a frail old man with scared eyes.
Scared? Yes. Obad Hai was facing Boccob. Some said that Boccob was magic itself.
But the eyes showed fear for only a moment.
The old man blinked, and when his eyes opened again there was a piercing rage.
"You kill my men, Boccob. Why?"
Boccob was defiant. He didn't like the righteous expression of Obad Hai's face.
"What's the point of conversing with you? You don't listen."
The ledge became slippery from the rain. Boccob leapt and rose up to the very peak of the mountain.
Obad Hai followed, briefly transformed as a grey hawk.
The storm raged below.
Landing atop the serene cap of the Rakers, streaked with powdered snow, Boccob thought to himself that this was a better place to fight.
******
Obad Hai was catching his breath.
His arms and legs hurt each time he shape changed. Now he was back, and he would punish the...
Orange bolts streaked against his chest. They threw Obad Hai back twenty feet.
He quickly rose to his feet, holding a sky blue globe. Let the battle begin!
*****
Boccob saw his for rise up. Obad Hai wasn't just a geriatric Flan, but a petty despot. And a god.
How many worshippers did Obad Hai have now? Thousands? Hundreds of thousands?
And they were bent to his will. Unthinking and uncaring zombies.
In his own way, Obad Hai was Tharizdun.
Boccob threw out a whirlwind of fire.
*****
Obad Hai held out the globe, the flames whirling around it like a dancing dervish.
The globe smoked, the fire vanished.
Obad Hai retaliated.
******
Boccob's robes rose up to devour him.
He flung them off before he was constricted.
In his underclothes, Boccob struck back.
*****
Fire and light. Cold and ice. Stones against flesh. Flesh against stone.
Boccob and Obad Hai fought for hours atop the peak of the highest mountain in the Rakers.
How much magic did they have? Would it ever be spent?
Who knows? At the end, it was not the magic that diminished but the will.
Boccob and Obad Hai, for all their failings, were too wise to fight forever to no purpose.
Finally, they both stopped, beards ragged, faces flushed, hair bedraggled,; stopped and faced each other with a stillness that was as discomforting as the flashes of thunder and destruction that preceded it.
They faced each other atop a scorched broken chunk of rock that had once been a mountain.
They acknowledged each other, briefly nodded then turned away., lost in thought.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 149
Obad Hai needed more firepower, something that could break Boccob.
Boccob needed more firepower, something that could break Obad Hai.
Obad Hai frowned upon the Unnatural, but sometimes it was a necessary tool.
Boccob felt incomplete without the Scroll of Vile Darkness, and she was lost, but he had a connection to something else.
Heward's Mystical Organ.
Obad Hai had hidden it himself. Time to bring it out.
Boccob didn't know where it was, but the billion burning suns that powered it powered him too.
Obad Hai didn't know how to play the Organ though, but there were the Bards...
Boccob didn't know how to play the Organ either, but he had his intuition.
Most Bards were hostile or indifferent to Obad Hai, but there were a few that were also Stags. They would do his bidding.
Boccob felt his entire body tingling. The Organ's location was revealed. At last he knew where it was.
*****
Heward's Mystical Organ glowed with the light of the Sun.
Three Bards in brilliant colours were around the contraption, puzzling over it, for they had never seen or heard it played. Obad Hai was explaining its workings as best as he could, for he had heard it played by Heward himself, and the memory of that magnificent concert had never left him.
Then Boccob arrived in a pillar of fire.
Obad Hai was shocked. How had Boccob located the Mystical Organ? He had shielded it with the fabric of the Seasons themselves, veiled in life, laughter, darkness and death.
This Glade within the Adri forest was the perfect hiding place, for even Oerth had forgotten its existence.
Yet, here Boccob was.
"The Mystical Organ is under my control," said Obad Hai, "my Bards will strike you down if you approach it."
Boccob waved a hand. The Bards melted into the grass.
Boccob stepped up to the Organ.
"What do you plan to do, Boccob? Can you even play it? You can go anywhere. Leave Oerik for me. I will make it a Golden Age if you stop interfering."
Boccob could hear a quiver in Obad Hai's voice. He was frightened. Good!
Boccob hovered over the keys. Above his head loomed the enormous pipes. At his feet were giant black pedals.
He had helped to play it once before, but only to pump the bellows.
Obad Hai was gesturing and muttering. A large blue globe appeared, surrounding the Hierophant in an anti-magic shell.
Did Obad Hai think that could stop the might of the Organ?
One finger touched one key.
Electrical energy surged through Boccob's brain.
He felt an incredible wave of joy.
. The Mystical Organ was his family. And Boccob didn't need to know how to play the Organ, for the Mystical Organ would play him.
*****
The first chords were high, wavering trebles of delight, and the leaves of the nearby trees glowed pink.
Obad Hai crouched down within the blue globe. Inside it he could not hear the music, and that was a good thing, because if he couldn't hear then the magic wouldn't affect him.
The second chords were deeper but bright, sending lights shooting up to the sky like fireworks.
The globe distorted but stayed firm.
The third chords were supersonic rumbles that shattered Obad Hai's globe into glass shards.
Boccob looked up from the keyboard sporting a devilish smile. Surely Obad Hai was now helpless.
What to do to him though? Banish him from existence? Turn him into an actual stag? Strip away his connection with the Natural World he loved?
Obad Hai was standing still, eyes blinking in shock.
He knew that Boccob had bested him.
And then Boccob felt sorry for the old Druid.
It had all gone wrong for him, just as Boccob's dreams had gone wrong.
Boccob would show mercy.
He came down from the Organ, approached Obad Hai with outstretched arms.
"You have wronged me, Obad Hai, but I have also wronged you. We both want a harmonious Oerik. Can we perhaps work together once more?"
"No," answered Obad Hai, "my grievances with you are too high for you to pay. And you will not submit to the Stags, I know it. You are too loud for Oerth."
"A truce perhaps? A temporary cessation of hostilities whilst we work out are separate futures?"
"Aye, Boccob. That is something I would consider. But..."
"Are you kidding me?"
Boccob and Obad Hai whirled around.
Sitting upon the Organ was an annoyed Boccob. An annoyed old Boccob.
He pointed rudely at young Boccob.
"You were so close to becoming me, Boccob. I could feel it."
"I could too. And I vowed to never be you."
"What is going on?" asked Obad Hai.
"Quiet, you old goat," snapped old Boccob, completely ignoring him thereafter.
"Leave me alone, future me," pleaded young Boccob, "stop interfering with my life."
"It's my life too. I don't particularly like what you're doing with it."
"Too bad. I am stronger now. You won't bully me anymore."
"Oh, is that so? And how strong do you think I am, boy? Why, I've brought empires down, mocked the gods themselves! I have created monsters and I have tested mortals with puzzles beyond possibility. You..."
The sound was like the tolling of the mantle of Oerth.
A bell, but a cracked bell. A bell made of lead and marble and rage.
The two Boccob's could hardly move, but somehow they had strained their necks around to see what was happening.
Obad Hai was playing Heward's Mystical Organ, but he had no idea what he was doing.
The broken chords vomited out of the broken pipe, wretched, dissonant but highly potent.
And as if the Mystical Organ itself took umbrage at the three gods before it, an enormous ocean of shattered noise engulfed all three with a motif of hideous clashing pitches that sent them howling out into the lost places of the multiverse.

posts.title: ; Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2;
Golden Age
Part 150
1473 SD
Who knew that werewolves could die from old age?
Old Fang had returned to Kodge Land to die. Vecna had nursed him to the end.
It was funny, Old Fang had been the closest thing to a friend that Vecna had ever had, and he hardly knew a thing about him.
Vecna supposed that it was because he never asked.
Old Fang was an Ur Flan, a werewolf, a better administrator than a fighter, and he was very loyal to Vecna.
Vecna would miss him.
Age was catching up with him too. His complexion had turned pale and puffy, his eyes were grey, his hair was receding and white, and once again he looked more Flan than Drow.
The magic from the Suel Palace (perhaps Lolth) that had sustained him for many more decades was waning.
Vecna didn't want to die in Kodge Land.
It was a pleasant enough place he supposed, and the island, strangely shaped like a dog's head, had a particularly interesting form of humanoid.
Fox people, some seven feet tall, and much more intelligent than orcs, goblins or bugbears.
Vecna had recruited them to his cause, and with their protection he had conquered much of the island.
He had grown very wealthy, for Kodge Land was an important nexus between Oerik and Mystara, particularly the growing Glantri Empire.
Vecna's influence stretched across the Solnor sea, out into northern Oerik. It was here that he planned to return.
Oerik would be where Vecna chose to die.
The fox people, the kodge, were excited to see this new land, because Vecna often talked about the endless forests, mountains, hills and plains that made up the Flanaess, and although he had set up pirate forts in the cold north, he had not yet allowed the kodge there.
Vecna didn't actually want to die, but he doubted that he had much choice in the matter.
The Book of Vile Darkness stopped whispering to him. Their love had ended when Vecna had turned her into a book.As a book she was now under Vecna's control, because he could bookmark pages and choose which pages to read. He had domesticated her.
The price he paid was a return to mortality.
Vecna had best make a name for himself before he went.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 151
1476 SD
The Stagmarshal tried to hide the worry on his face.
The Burghermeister wasn't going to like this.
Fleeth had expanded again. The city was the largest in the eastern Flanaess and the wealthiest new shops and houses were coming up all the time, and large manors stretched out into the surrounding forest like wandering fingers.
The Stagmarshal crossed the plaza that led to the Edelhirsh.
The Edelhirsh was an austere block of a building, square, squat and functional. Two Stagi stood outside in their simple black. The Stagmarshal approached them and they quickly saluted, stamping their boots.
The Stagmarshal went inside. The Edelhirsh was a warren or partitions and rooms, cluttered with harried Stagi working feverishly.
The Edelhirsh was the centre of Fleeth, the hub of the Flanaess. It was here that the concequential descisions were made that affected the entire region.
It was a great honour to be appointed a Stagi.
It was also a great responsibility.
Imagine then, how much more so for a Stagmarshal.
******
The Burghermeister was in a good mood. His face was flushed, but his smile was lopsided but genuine.
"Stagmarshal, a pleasure to see you again. Let me order you a beer."
The Stagmarshal declined.
The Burghermeister looked up at the stern looking middle aged Stagmarshal. His nose was almost a perfect triangle and his eyes betrayed nothing.
A good man, this Stagmarshal. An honest man. An earnest man.
He was the perfect fit for his job as protector of external threats, because it meant that he spent most of his time abroad.
The Stagmarshal was built for the outdoors, and that meant that he was at a disadvantage indoors.
Which meant that the Burghermeister had the advantage over him right now.
Offer him drinks, sweets, women. Keep him off balance. Don't let him get ideas. Let him know his place.
"Now, let us get to business," said the Burghermeister, "you have been gone for nearly three months. Have you secured the memorandums of understanding with Gwive and Kenk?"
"They are no longer the problem," said the Stagmarshal.
"How so? At our last meeting I found them quite belligerent."
The Stagmarshal stood as tall as he could. It was time to deliver the bad news.
"It is the north. The Ur Flan have not accepted the payments. They have brought in barbarians from a foreign land, vicious fox men called kodge. They fight with cunning and each one is stronger than two ordinary men. Their fortifications are strong and a warlord has appeared as well."
The Burghermeister stayed composed. The barbaric north was nothing new, and warlords were worth as much as a bag of copper coins.
The kodge sounded a little worrying, but nothing beyond the Stagi.
So why was the Stagmarshal sweating?
"It is the warlord, great Burghermeister. He is one that has been whispered of. An old sorcerer of the old times."
"An old sorcerer? What are these whispers?"
"He is called Vecna, my Burghermeister."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 152
1478 SD
The fijords of the rectangular chunk of land that made up Northeast Oerik stretched out like the hands of a conjuring sorcerer.
Baba Yaga found the warlord Vecna within a cylindrical tower at the talon of the longest finger.
Vecna hadn't seen his cousin for a long time and he was impressed by her appearance. Her skin was a blotchy blue, hanging off bone. Baba Yaga was enormous, a true ogress, and her teeth and claws looked like rusted iron. She wore a thick cloak made from snow tigers and her very form imbued cold.
Vecna shivered. He was wearing a thick woolen jerkin, but it wasn't enough. Should he go get his cloak?
Baba Yaga held out a gnarled warty hand.
"Little cousin," she said, "it has been a long time."
Vecna nodded. When was the last time that he had seen her? One of the Council meetings he supposed. Another world away.
"You dwell in Blackmoor, I hear..."
Baba Yaga interrupted him.
"I dwell wherever I want. Right now I dwell here."
Vecna studied the giant witch's glowing eyes. Was she challenging him?"
Baba Yaga laughed, a light and bubbling laugh as if she were a child.
"You have nothing to fear from me, dear boy. We are kin. We share the same aunt."
Vecna smiled, but his teeth were chattering.
"Well, Baba Yaga, my home is yours "
******
The fire was roaring.
Baba Yaga and Vecna sat close to it, though even the bright warmth it gave off couldn't completely quell the chill.
Baba Yaga pulled out a wooden object. It looked like an old flute.
"Do you know what this is?" she asked.
Vecna took it into his arthritic hands. He examined it briefly. Yes, he knew of this instrument. It had once belonged to Ye'Cind.
"Your mother."
"I have no mother. I am Unnatural, as Obad Hai used to say."
"Tish! Don't mention that name. I am glad that you recognise Ye'Cind's old magic recorder. Do you know how to play it?"
"I know that you blow into it whilst pressing down on the holes, but no more than that."
"Pity. I have tried to play it since I took it from Incabulos, but it won't make any sound for me."
Vecna shrugged. He didn't know anything about that.
A kodge entered the round room. He was tall, lanky and his fur was orange and brown. His face sported a long snout of white with a black nose. He wore a bronze breast plate.
"Great Vecna," the kodge spoke in perfect Flan, "Developments. Three more ships sunk."
"Three? Merchants?"
"One merchant and two pirate ships. It was the Fleeth fleet again."
Vecna regarded Baba Yaga quizzically.
"It's my turn to ask you a question. How should I handle the Fleeth? Pour down from the north? Attack from our bases in Kodge Land? Both? We are strong, but Fleeth has the potential to bring in all of the eastern cities against us."
"You said you would ask one question. I counted four. I wouldn't bother fighting them at all. They are a pathetic race of people who don't know what life is for. Stop building up armies and live out the rest of your days in luxury. You are old, Vecna, though you will always be a boy to me. Embrace what you have left."
Vecna scowled.
"You don't know me at all, cousin. Why should I Age and Die like a mortal? I am Drow. I am Flan. And I don't want to retire. I want my energy to return. I want to work! And I deserve it all."
Baba Yaga laughed again.
"It's your life, not mine. Personally, I prefer solitude to towers and armies and Ur Flan. I just came about the recorder. But I may stay a few days and keep you company."
"Stay as long as you like," said Vecna.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 153
It was just a trip to the fish market.
The Fleeth fish market was the best one in Eastern Oerik, and they offered rare and exotic sea foods. Baba Yaga had a craving for a particular delicacy, Solnor lobster. Grendep bay was too far north and the Ur Flan were not renowned fishermen. Meat was the common diet of the North.
Baba Yaga strode into Fleeth with no cares in the world. Why would she? She towered over the Flan and her magic could turn them into dirt. And she wasn't here to be difficult, she just wanted some lobster.
The Stagi knew at once that Baba Yaga was in Fleeth. Without even seeing her everyone could feel the cold that followed Baba Yaga like a ghost, a chilling breeze that hurt the bones.
The Stagmarshal was quickly informed. He happened to be in Fleeth making one of his reports.
Stagmarshal knew Baba Yaga well, by reputation. His interrogations of Ur Flan had told him much about the giant witch..She travelled throughout northern Oerik, from Blackmoor all the way to the fijords of Grendep bay.
She was kin to Vecna, an ally of the warlord and infested with magic.
The magic of Baba Yaga, the Ur Flan and Vecna was acknowledged as the most pressing problem for harmonious Fleeth.
That's why the Stagmarshal had prayed to lost Obad Hai day after day, and night after night.
The two moons were in eclipse when Fleeth's prayers were answered.
Raw nature came down on a twisted moonbeam and blessed the devout Stagmarshal.
The Stagmarshal thanked the Stagi for their news. He grabbed his cape and cowl. Time to confront the ogress.
*******
Baba Yaga was looking over the lobsters when she smelled an odour of sandlewood. It was stronger than the smell of the sea exuding from the crates of the fish market, and that was very odd. So, she turned away from her shopping and looked down upon a stern looking man all in black. He was dressed as a Stagi, but something about his demeanour gave her pause.
He hardly looked frightened at all.
"Baba Yaga, hag," spat the Stagmarshal, "you are under arrest for plotting against Fleeth. Come with me."
Baba Yaga felt her hackles rise. She cackled with contempt. Won't the Stagi ever learn? She was a free spirit.
Baba Yaga glared down. She pointed a finger of death at the still stern looking Stagi.
The man still stood.
He should have been disintegrated.
Baba Yaga decided then to tear him apart with her claws. She lunged...
A pale blue sphere emerged out from the Stagi and drifted into the ogress.
Baba Yaga groaned, her eyes rolled back into her skull and she fell onto the paved stones like a falling tree.
The Stagmarshal kneeled over the fallen witch.
"I thank you, Obad Hai, for your Blessing. May the garden grow."
The Stagmarshal clicked his fingers, and out from everywhere came the Stagi.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 154
Baba Yaga was tied to a wooden stake in the plaza outside the Edelhirsh.
She was regaining consciousness as the Burghermeister arrived to inspect her. Baba Yaga was diminished now divested from her furs and cloak, a long and lanky scarecrow more than anything.
A pale blue sphere surrounded her, almost as transparent as a soap bubble. The Burghermeister turned to look at the calm and erect Stagmarshal.
"You may examine the witch without fear," said the Stagmarshal, "the sphere has sucked out her power."
The Burghermeister questioned the use of magic to quell magic, but he was not of the Stagi, and the Druidic arts were a mystery to him.
Baba Yaga was straining to look at the Burghermeister but her eyes were darting about as if she had yet to regain control of her nervous system. The Burghermeister reached out through the sphere, which he could not feel, and touched the ogress face. Her skin was dry, rough and nobbly.
"Can you hear me, witch?" he asked.
Now Baba Yaga did look at him. They settled upon his flabby face and would have scorched his nose with the power of her glare if she could.
The Stagmarshal saw the insolence and hit her with his stick. The stick bounced back as if it had struck iron.
The Burghermeister stepped back.
"I see no point in conversing with the witch," said the Burghermeister, "she will tell us nothing. Burn her."
*******
Baba Yaga felt the kindling under her feet. There was a large pile of it. Was she going to burn? Did she not bring forth cold itself? Would the frost counter the fire?
What frost?
What cold?
Baba Yaga realised that she felt no chill at all. The cold was gone.
The blue sphere had smothered her magic entirely.
Stagi with lit torches came to the pile of kindling, setting it alight.
A great orange blaze began to dance under Baba Yaga 's feet. A flame licked her knee and she howled.
*******
Baba Yaga was completely ablaze and the Stagi were cursing her as she ignited into red and blue gas.
"Look at the Unnatural witch!" the Stagi cried.
"She is a monster!"
"Her evil leaks out!"
The blue gas and red gas suddenly knitted into two skeletons, solid and grinning as if everything living was a macabre joke.
Red Death and Blue Death stalked the plaza, forcing the Stagi and the other onlookers to flee in panic.
The Stagmarshal hesitated though. Why was the Obad Hai sphere not stopping this magic?
A skeletal clutch of his cowl forced him to cut off his thoughts, and he broke into as fast a speed as everyone else.
The plaza cleared of the living, the Deaths turned back to Baba Yaga and the burning stake.
There was nothing left of her, just fierce flames guttering white and yellow.
The two Deaths marched back into the inferno.
The two skeletons bathed in fire, became Incendiary fireballs that struck the Edelhirsh, causing that ugly building to burst into flame.
The Edelhirsh lit up Fleeth as if Hell had come.
The heat was so intense that no one could come close for hours, having to settle to watch the Edelhirsh engulf into ash from streets away, the sky bright red though the sun had now set.
And then the fire was sated, and now turned on itself, shrinking and cooling as the night sky turned orange, brown then black.
Where the Edelhirsh once sat was a pile of black flakes.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 155
A cool breeze blew over Fleeth.
The air was scented with salt. The Burghermeister could taste it on his tongue. He looked through the open window onto the street. The sun was low but rising and the sky streaked blue and grey.
Finally the smoke was gone.
The Edelhirsh had burned to the ground, taking the whole block with it. A steep price to pay but there was no such thing as a free lunch.
The witch was dead a week.
He woke his wife.
"Look, dear," said the Burghermeister, "it's a beautiful day."
*******
The Book of Vile Darkness told Vecna what he needed to know, not what he wanted to hear.
Fleeth had burned Baba Yaga.
Vecna reread the passage:
'and lo, a calamity fell upon cousin Baba Yaga, for she was consumed in smoke and flame.
Woe to the people of Fleeth, for surely there would be a reckoning...'
Vecna slammed the book shut.
Yes, a reckoning there would be.
Vecna loathed Fleeth and her Stagi, that was nothing new, why else had he built an army looking over it? But he was too old, too feeble to lead them after all.
Arthritis had ruined his hips and his knees. The cold air from the Corusk mountains had destroyed his lungs.
Death was coming to claim him.
But he had set things up and the Ur Flan would remember him.
Yet, despite the failings of his mortal body, he still did live.
Vecna lives!
********
They built for Vecna a flying pavilion made from spider web, for the Ur Flan loved their warlord sorcerer. It was a platform of silver and weaved within the strands rose the Spider Throne.
Vecna was mobile again.
The old, curved Flan still had his mind and still had his magic.
He owned the Book of Vile Darkness.
The Ur Flan were with him.
The kodge were with him.
Baba Yaga would be avenged.
Then Vecna could die.
.
