posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 156
The Stagmarshal sat under an old bronzewood tree eating his lunch.
It was good to be back in the wilds, away from Fleeth. The forest was home. And his surroundings were as familiar to him as family. For instance, this Bronzewood exceeded forty feet in height, and it was the largest tree of its type in the entire Adri forest. The ground that fed its roots was a rich brown and the Stagmarshal could almost smell the nutrients rising off it.
The air tasted like leaves and the water in the creek tasted of life.
It was here in the Adri that the Stagmarshal was at his most dangerous. He felt part of nature itself and his senses were greatly enhanced. What manner of monster could possibly overcome him here?
******
The Stagmarshal finished his meal then set off again to find the ranger camp. The Rangers were being particularly hard to find, and that made sense since the kodge incursions from the north.
The kodge were tough to kill and they fought like wild boars. They had begun to raid the farmlands around Fleeth and the Stagi and rangers soon learned to regret taking on the fox people in hand to hand combat.
Kodge had been spotted in the Adri too, and doubtless the rangers were being extra careful to stay hidden.
But the Stagmarshal needed to find them, and his oneness with nature would help him.
Where were they?
The Stagmarshal felt his nose itch. He sneezed, quietly and discreetly.
His eyes felt dry. He blinked but they stung and watered pure salt.
The Stagmarshal sneezed again, louder this time.
Now his throat felt like fire!
What was happening to him? It was as if the forest was repelling him.
Obad Hai. I am your servant, Obad Hai.
Why do you forsake me?
The sneezing became uncontrollable, the Stagmarshal fell onto the soil he had earlier praised, and the warm dirt on his fingers cracked his skin.
Obad Hai?
Where are you Obad Hai?
Blood seeped out from the cracks. His throat constricted.
Then the Stagmarshal realised something profound.
Nature was an abomination.
He denounced Obad Hai.
Something snapped inside his mind.
His life had been a lie, for Obad Hai had never been a god.
How could he be a god when there were no gods?
And then, through his pain and blurred sight, he felt reality pour into him, true reality, harsh, cold, indifferent.
The Cosmos itself.
*******
A silver platform with a Spider Throne landed near the Bronzewood tree, then the old, bent figure of Vecna eased himself off, hopping to the ground with the aid of his staff.
He looked down at the body of the Stagmarshal. His kill.
The dead man's mouth was smiling, perhaps he had found his peace.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 157
The Stagi were even easier to deal with.
Vecna turned a mirror to their souls.
What the Stagi saw was shocking.
Their hearts had twisted into antlers, scarlet and black. Their lungs were made of thorns and their spleens were enlarged and engorged.
The four humors flowed together, intermingling and struggling to be free from the rot.
What had the Stagi become?
Noble defenders of the forest no more.
Peculiar ambitions have driven the Stagi into becoming bureaucratic minotaurs, custodians of labyrinthine civil service.
They were policemen of Shadows.
The realisation of what they had become, so different from their childhood visions when the world was light and bright, drove the Stagi into spasms of guilt.
The streets of Fleeth saw the Stagi scramble underground into their dungeons.
The rows and rows of cells, filled as they were with common thieves, beggars, prostitutes, tricksters, fraudsters, political prisoners, and subversives, were opened with iron keys, where the afformentioned prisoners rushed up to the surface, now light and bright since the shadows had slunk away.
And the shadows, the Stagi, desperate to atone for the suffering of Fleeth, threw themselves into their own cells and tossed away their keys.
******
No Stagmarshal.
No Rangers.
No Stagi.
Vecna's army laid Fleeth to siege.
******
The Fleeth men at arms were no match for the kodge, who struck then from their towers with arrows and spears, or bested them at the gates with morning stars and axes.
No Druid prayers to blunt the magic of the Ur Flan war wizards.
The Fleeth army was routed, gutted, and the walls fell.
The silver platform with the Spider Throne glided down onto the burned plaza besides the ash and dust that had once been the Edelhirsh.
Upon the throne, cross legged, was old man Vecna. Moving into the plaza and flanking the platform were Ur Flan and kodge, who took up defensive positions.
More kodge moved through the fallen city, some returning with captives.
Amongst the captives was the Burghermeister.
The Burghermeister addressed Vecna.
"You have conquered us, and we surrender, Vecna. Take our city, but please spare our lives."
The malevolent face of Vecna looked down at the chubby Burghermeister.
"No," said Vecna, "I don't think that I feel like showing mercy today. You showed no mercy to Baba Yaga and my cousin was worth fifty thousand of you. I will see all of the citizens of Fleeth come before me where each will be beheaded."
The Burghermeister was an evil man, but even he had his limits, and he couldn't abide such an atrocity under his watch. He begged Vecna not to slay everyone. Murder him. Torture him, but spare the innocents of Fleeth.
Vecna considered the request.
Then he smiled, but it was a bitter smile that dimmed the sun.
"Let the rulers come to me then, the burghers, the officials, the rich merchants and the diplomats. And bring your wives and children too. Everyone else will be spared."
It was a high price to pay, and the Burghermeister resisted.
Vecna shrugged. It was that or everyone dies.
*****
Some hours later, the ruling classes and their families were gathered before the Spider Throne.
"Good news," whispered Vecna, "for I have decided to show great mercy. I spare your lives. Leave Fleeth and do not go into the southern cities, for they will soon be mine. Go West, cross the great Nyr Dyv. Visit the Rift Canyon. But do not leave until morning. Let the torches be lit, for I have an entertainment for you this night."
The Burghermeister was greatly relieved. He felt naked without his Stagi, completely helpless and defeated. He had prayed that he would be executed before his wife was so that he wouldn't have to see her suffer.
Perhaps Vecna wasn't a terrible and unnatural monster after all.
"What is the entertainment you will give us, noble Vecna?"
"A fitting entertainment for the likes of you. You are going to watch me collect the heads of every man, woman and child in Fleeth."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 158
Only the smaller Celene lit the inky sky, for Luna had already set
Vecna rode his silver platform to the ash that was once the Edelhirsh. He stepped off, the Book of Vile Darkness under one arm, a staff assisting his steps in the other.
He bent down, feeling his back complain, and rose back up with black dust on his fingers.
Was Baba Yaga truly dead?
She had been dust before. Dust in an old urn.
Vecna took his Book from his arm then opened it. The pages blurred with movement, turning on their own volition. The Book settled upon an open section all in black.
Vecna studied the darkness.
And then he felt two presences either side of him.
Two upright skeletons, one red and one blue.
Baba Yaga 's pets.
They stood, impassive, waiting.
Waiting for what?
Vecna looked at the mound of ash. Was it stirring? No. But there was a faint miasma hovering above it, a haze that might be just Vecna's imagination.
The Book had called him here though, and the two Deaths had appeared, so likely the fog meant something.
"Baba Yaga?" his voice sounded high pitched and pathetic. Vecna felt like a child again.
A chill came over him. Vecna felt lost and alone.
And the miasma stretched out and up, until it formed into an ogress shape, insubstantial and transparent but somehow present.
The two Deaths opened up their jawbones into wide grins.
Baba Yaga, a ghost?
"Help me, Vecna," intoned the phantom Baba Yaga, "Release me from the ash."
How was he supposed to do that? Then the black pages burned with ebon flame. Letters flew out like sparks.
Good book! Vecna collected each letter into his mind, reciting them out as words, harsh, dark and deathly.
Instead of Baba Yaga returning to life, the ash of the Edelhirsh rose and spun about the phantom ogress, solidifying into what looked like old wooden planks. The planks collided into each other, forming a shabby looking hut.
The hut stood where the Edelhirsh once was.
Now the two Deaths, one red and one blue, stalked up to the hut, opened a crooked door then went in.
Suddenly the hut lifted and lurched,
Below the hut were two long, bony legs, looking like chicken legs, one red and one blue.
Then, the legs sprung, leaping the hut into the air. The feet came back onto the ashy ground, sprung again, jolting the hut against an astonished Vecna and knocking him over.
Now the hut began to run, faster and faster until the hut raced down the street, turned a corner and was gone.
Vecna used his staff to help himself up, then achingly returned to his Spider Throne.
That was the thing about being dead. You can only die once.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 159
1481 SD
Five kodge moved west through the central Flanaess until they crossed the Jewel River, reaching the borders of Celene.
They were deserters, tired of following the orders of an old Flan.
Cities had been sacked, and Vecna now possessed most of the far east, from the Arctic Corusk mountains to the sub-tropics just above Sunndi.
The kodge were treated like lackeys, common vagabonds. Let the kodge be seduced by gold, but not these five!
Together, although only five members strong, they would make their own way across Oerik until they found somewhere that they liked.
A fast running creek divided itself from the Jewel and the kodge followed it. Before long they reached a clearing curtained by drooping trees.
Elves were playing there; elves and one centaur. They were clearly young and their clothes were garish.
"Let's skirt past them," the kodge language sounded like yelps, whimpers, whines and barks, but meaning was tempered with accent and timbre.
The centaur paused her cantering. Had she heard him?
The kodge swiftly moved behind the trees. They didn't want trouble with elvenkind, not after the last time.
There were thirteen elves there in the field, and they teased the overly timid centaur for jumping at shadows. Soon, they were all back at play again.
All twelve.
"Hello."
Appearing beside the kodge, whose bulky bronze breastplates and heavy morning stars made the fox people even larger than they were, was an elf maiden. Or perhaps she was a human, it was hard to tell. Her ears were pointed, but less so than most elves, and her hair was dark, no, it was golden, no it was dark again.
"What manner of creatures are you?" she asked, twiddling with a plain looking flower.
The kodge didn't speak Elvish. They looked at each other. Was this elf a threat? Do we kill her, or do we leave?
"Hello," the girl said again, but this time in Flam.
The kodge understand Flan. Relieved, they conversed with her, briefly.
They were just moving through, they said, looking for a new place to call home. Did she have any suggestions as to where they could go?
Ehlonna, or perhaps she was called Ehlenestra, thought for a moment.
"No," she said,
"No? What do you mean, no? Nowhere out of the way where we can herd some cattle or settle in a nice town of open-hearted people?"
"No," said Ehlonna, "not for you. You are warriors. You have spilt blood. I can smell it."
We were warriors. Now we just want to live our lives.
"This place is Celene. You are not welcome here. Further to the west are the people of Ulek. They will not welcome you either."
Further west then?
"Dwarves, of the Barrier Peaks, giants of the Jotens and the Crystalmists. Southwest, the Hellfurnaces and the Suel Imperium. Return to Vecna. There is nothing for you here."
They could have struck down Ehlonna with one single blow.
They could have, but they didn't.
And as they left the way they came, they didn't know why they hadn't.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 160
1493 SD
   Vecna was over two hundred years old, and now it was time for him to die.
   Gwide and Kenk and the rest were owned by him and his army (but not Fleeth; that city was destroyed), and he was revered as a master sorcerer.
   Vecna's legacy was established.
   He lay in his bed, enjoying the gloom. 
   His legs were so riddled with arthritis that he could only walk with supreme effort, and he was so weak that he needed help to dress, (although he had a spell to help him with that).
   Yes, Vecna's body was all but destroyed.
   It truly was time to die.
   But he didn't want to go 
   Vecna was confused about his own feelings. Why didn't he want to die? Why put up with agony and indignity longer than he had to? 
   Vecna had proven to be mortal, not inheriting the great longevity of his Drow mother or his semi-divine father. 
   It wasn't as if Vecna was alone with his mortality. Whole generations had born, grown into adults, then deteriorated into wrecks over these two centuries, and most seldom complained about it. 
   Most mortals shrugged and accepted the hand of death when it came.
   Why was Vecna different?
   Because he had been robbed.
   Vecna was greater than both of his parents combined, smarter, more ambitious, more cynical.  He should live at least another millenium.
   There were spells and magic to keep Vecna alive, but they didn't work on him like they were supposed to. His body seemed to reject the effects.
   Somewhere out of sight, Vecna felt that someone or something was laughing at him.
   He called a slave to attend to him. Vecna required the nightshade medicine. Nasty stuff, but it temporarily took the pain away, but he always had bad dreams after taking it.
                             ******
   Here comes the bad dream.
   No Lolth this time.
   Vecna was back in the Palace of the Suel Imperium. 
   The rooms roared at him.
   Vecna felt as if he was inside the mouth of an enormous lion. He was a crumb caught in its throat.
   The Palace shuddered, trying to push him out.
   Vecna crashed into walls and doors. A heavy wooden door was rotten, and when Vecna fell into it the door exploded into damp splinters.
   Vecna found himself in a small room lit with orange and yellow light.
   The jolting subsided, then stopped. Perhaps the crumb called Vecna had bounced out of the windpipe and plunged into the digestive tract where it belonged.
   There was a middle aged man in the room with Vecna, a man in faded red.
   It was Heward, his father!
   "No, I am not," said what appeared to be Heward, 'I have his body, but Heward is gone. I am Win-Daled. I am a Suel Lich."
   "Suel Lich, why do you invade my dream?"
   "It is the nightshade, not me. But since you have come here, I should give you some advice."
   "What advice would you give me?"
   "Do not become a Suel Lich. Such a curse is this! I kill those I care about the most. I am nothing but a demon now, and I never once asked for Undeath. But I know that you do."
   "No," said Vecna, "not Undeath, but eternal life."
   The Suel Lich that looked like Heward laughed bitterly.
   "That you cannot have. You are an anomaly, a break in reality. The Universe wants you gone."
   "Then I will die? There is no escape for me?"
   "Only Undeath or nothing."
   Vecna thought for a moment. Then his eyes widened with sparks.
   "Make me a Suel Lich like you, for I have no loved ones, and murder means nothing to me "
   The Suel Lich sighed.
   "I don't know how, and I would never help you anyway. I was the first Queen. And I cared for my people. You are an old Ur Flan sorcerer who rules for the sake of itself. Go back and die if you cannot understand the pain that I feel with every non existent beat of my non existent heart."
                               ******
   Vecna awoke with a headache.
   There was no escape.
   No one was willing to help him, alive or dead.
   Time to get his affairs in order. See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 161
   Still alive.
   Vecna lifted himself up in his bed and he groaned.
   For three nights he had not taken the nightshade. His eyes had closed but he hadn't slept at all. Now, another day dawned and Vecna had to get himself together.
   He had a realm to rule.
                             *****
   Evening returned. The slave brought Vecna the nightshade.
                              ******
   The silver platform with the Spider Throne glided down into the garden at the front of Ulaa's cottage. Vecna levitated off and floated towards the front door.
   His legs ached so he kept his feet a few inches off the ground when he knocked on the door.
   Ulaa was surprised to see her nephew. She had heard about his exploits in the East, and she was unimpressed.
   Vecna had been a sullen boy, and now? A sullen old man. 
   "Why are you here?" she asked.
   "Can I come in, aunt Ulaa?"
   Ulaa gestured for Vecna to enter her cottage, but she was deeply unhappy.
   Vecna glided down the corridor, quickly reaching the living room. He fell into a seat with visible relief.
   Ulaa asked whether she could get refreshments for him. Of course, he said yes.
   Soon the two were drinking herbal tea and devouring oat biscuits, reminiscing.
   "I have always liked you, aunt Ulaa," muttered Vecna between mouthfuls.
   Ulaa nodded but didn't return the favour.
   "Did you just come because you missed me?" she finally asked.
   Vecna laughed coldly.
   "I don't tend to miss people."
   He poured himself some more tea 
   "No," said Vecna, "I've come to your cottage to look for something."
   Ulaa's eyes narrowed.
   "You're not poking around looking at my things, Vecna. My home isn't a toy shop."
   Vecna attempted to look conciliatory.
   "Now, aunt Ulaa, don't be like that. I believe a mutual friend left something behind last time he was here. I want to give it back to him."
   "What friend?"
   "Boccob."
   Ulaa began to feel a little frightened. Boccob had disappeared without a trace. No-one knew what had happened to him... except for Vecna?
   "Where is he?" asked Ulaa, "What did you do?"
   Vecna shook his head.
   "I did nothing, aunt, and I don't exactly know where he is. But he spoke to me in one of my bad dreams, and he asked me to fetch him one of his knickknacks that he left here absent mindedly once."
   Ulaa stood up. She was feeling very uncomfortable and her nephew was making her skin prickle. Although she was standing, the sitting Vecna still had to slightly look down in order to meet her eyes.
   "What's the knicknack?" she managed to ask.
   "Oh, just a little metal jar. An urn." See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 162
   Ulaa's unguent was helping with the pain, and ironically Vecna had actually slept well the past four days because of it.
   But Vecna stuck to his choice.
   The unguent had been kept in the very jar that Boccob had accidentally left behind in Ulaa's cottage.
   It was the urn that would bring some justice.
                              ******
   Vecna closed the Book of Vile Darkness. He didn't like what he just read. 
   It was terribly risky. And he needed to trust someone else 
   Everything was ready, but Vecna trusted no-one.
   The slaves were out. They did whatever he asked them to, but once he was dust he doubted that they would obey his last instruction.
   Vecna had some very competent administrators that helped run Vecna's little realm (actually a long strip of land running north and south along the coast of the Solnor and including the fjords and peninsula below the Corusk mountains) but he didn't exactly trust them. One young Ur Flan was very bright and extraordinarily helpful and attentive to Vecna's needs.
   Acererak, he was called, and Vecna always recognised him by his elegant black moustache, but he was perversely obsequious and Vecna knew that Acererak 's attention was false.
   If he couldn't find someone or something to rely upon when he was literally crumbs, then the ceremony couldn't go ahead and fate would continue to laugh at him.
                             ******
     Luna was full, and her eerie light cast an enormous shadow upon an old wooden hut striding along on long chicken legs. The hut pushed its way through thick thickets until it reached a grey road. The hut then proceeded down the road, the legs clacking like a bone xylophone upon the gravel.
   The hut stopped before a round, squat tower, the chicken legs disappearing from sight when the hut set itself down.
   Vecna heard the clacking and creaking, and he had gone to the window. The hut of Baba Yaga...
   The crooked door in the hut croaked open and Baba Yaga stepped out. Vecna could feel the chill exuding from her even within his tower. She was all in black and she was hunched over, making her shoulders only seven feet from the ground instead of nine.
   "Vecna," she called, "Vecna, my cousin. Come out and greet old Baba Yaga."
  Vecna came down the stairs, his knees barely complaining, then he was outside, lit pale blue, facing Baba Yaga.
   "You seek Death?" she asked.
   "I seek Undeath, " Vecna replied.
   Baba Yaga shrugged, as if to say that she saw no difference between them.
   "I know Death," said Baba Yaga, "and I heard your call."
   Vecna waited for the witch to continue.
   "You are in a bind, Vecna, for without a soul to help you, you will be lost forever."
   "That I know. Will you help me?"
   Baba Yaga paused, for she was thinking.
   "Me?" she said at length, "No, I cannot. For I have no soul."
   "Have you come to mock me then? Have you come to watch my plans fall into ruin? Is this entertainment to you?"
   Baba Yaga shook her crooked head.
   "Cousin, cousin. We are not of the same blood, but we are kin, and always shall be. I have no soul, but I know two that do. My attendants. They are silent, uncomplaining and always ready to assist."
   And then to Vecna's left was the Red Death and to his right was the Blue Death. They grinned at him.
   Vecna trembled, despite himself.
   "If you have no soul, Baba Yaga, then how can they?"
   Baba Yaga laughed, and it was the kind of laughter that turned milk.
   "Can the Dead not have souls? Now, cousin, go and set up the ceremony. Do you have the urn prepared?" See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 163
1517 SD
   Acererak found the great gash in the Oerth, the Rift Canyon, quite fascinating.
   Magic had created it, and that excited him. 
   Acererak had always been excited by magic. Fortunately he was a very intelligent little boy, and his talents had secured him a very good tutor. 
   The Ur Flan teacher had worked under Vecna in Kodge Land and his connections allowed Acererak to move in elite circles.
   And now, thanks to Acererak's natural charm and good looks, he made himself indispensable.
   Vecna was looking to expand his realm and Acererak had been charged to investigate the possibility and probability of securing the Rift Canyon. 
   Acererak stroked his black moustache, still black although the hair on his head had gone powdery grey. 
   Monsters. There were a lot of monsters that dwelt here. Manticores and basilisks, a dragon or two, hydrae and cockatrices, minotaurs and purple worms.
   Lots of orcs too, and goblins, bugbears and ogres.
   Securing the Rift Canyon wasn't possible.
   Imposing Will upon it was.
   Nobody owned the Rift Canyon, so Vecna might as well claim it.
                            ******
   Blemu, or what was left of a once huge Olve empire, was almost gone entirely.
   Raiders from Vecna were always looking for soldiers and slaves, and the Adri forest was now infested with bands of kodge and bandits. Just the western edge of Blemu remained. 
   Celene had grown and grown, absorbing Blemu refugees, now the central haven of Olve kind on Oerik. Celene were allies with Ulek and the entire Sheldomar. It was a serene and enlightened realm, nothing like the grasping empire it had once been.
   Only Sunndi rivalled Celene, but Sunndi was isolated in the south east, bordered by Vecna's realm and the Vast Swamp directly to its South.
   The Celenians feared for Sunndi, for the Hand of Vecna was always groping for something beautiful to acquire. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 169
   Arik was a short man, but broad with unusually long arms and unusually short legs. He wobbled about in a very aggressive manner and he seldom concealed his rage at everything that displeased him.
   His rage had softened today, because his forces surrounded the Coral Palace, surrounded and conquered it. O, wouldn't Vecna be pleased! The Lich would forget about Acererak and Arik could finally step out from his elder brother's shadow.
   A lot of his army had been slain because the elves were deadly with their bows and their magic, but he himself had directed his war wizards against the defences, and the Coral Palace was finally secured, and the Palace itself was still largely intact, though some of its spires were broken off 
   All that remained was the formal declaration of surrender by the Ierendi Queen. 
                             *****
   Deep below the palace, where the night remained moonless, Erondel knocked upon a stout door. He heard no answer, but he opened it anyway. He was trembling noticeably when he went into the pale blue room of his Queen.
   "Why do you fear me?" said a soft voice, high and flute-like. It was the Queen, Sehanine. She was very small and very pale, and her hair was silvery as were her lips and eyes. She was draped in thin silks of grey.
   "Dear, Erondel, you need not be afraid, for are you not my subject, and did I not swear to serve you all, my kin, my Olve, despite your flaws?"
   "Yes, your majesty."
   "Then sit, my master, upon that chair just there, and tell me how does the war fare?"
   Erondel sat down on a three legged flat chair and continued to shake.
   Queen Sehanine raised a scolding finger.
   "Now, now, naughty elf, I command you to stay still and calm. Nothing can harm you here, I said. What is happening up above? Do they bring back our moon?"
                                ******
She rose up from below the floor, translucent, beautiful and terrible, a frown upon her perfect brow, eyes blinding with light, teeth of pure white, arms outstretched, legs like one single pillar.
   Arik looked at her face and cried.
   The fools had said that the palace was secure. That the Queen was alone with just a handful of servants.
   They hadn't said that the Queen was a god.
   "" Moon thief! ," wailed Sehanine, "Why do you take even more from me? Have I not lost enough?" 
   Arik found himself on the floor. Had he fallen over?
   "Queen Sehanine," he managed to stumble out, "I have conquered this island for Vecna. Drop your arms and you will be spared, as will all the survivors."
   "Fool! Thief! Do I look armed? I am a defenceless maiden, can't you see that? Why did you take my moon from me? Why do you want me to suffer so?"
   Arik began to dare that perhaps he had won after all. Why was he on the floor?
   He climbed back to his stumpy feet  He drew out a curved dagger.
   "Through magic or violence, I will end you, Queen of Ierendi, unless you submit at once."
   "Submit, little man? We get to the point at last. No, I don't think that I shall submit to you. I wish to keep whatever purity I have left."
   And then, surrounding Sehanine like a halo, were pale moons, bright moons, dark moons, crescent moons, full moons, gibbeous moons. They circled around Sehanine, slowly rotating as they did so. 
   Then they blue shifted into streaks of light that shot up and out, illuminating all of Ierendi in a glow that reflected off the coral, multi-coloured walls of the palace.
   Arik now knew that he had lost. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 170
1536-1541 SD
   Arik recuperated in Glantri city, the capital of the Glantri Empire.
   The city was made up of soaring and swirling towers and bridges, some hundreds of feet tall.  The Ur Flan had come to Mystara and made it their own. They had conquered the west and they had cowed the Mystarans to their will.
   Arik was welcomed, for Glantri was an ally of the realm of Vecna. Arik was in a bad way, burned and disfigured. He was blind in one eye, and the other only saw dim shades of blue. His teeth were broken as was an arm and a leg. He was very lucky to be alive.
   Living statues, servants of the war wizards who ruled the Empire, tended to Arik. Most were humanoid and made of clear crystal, but Arik also saw strange moving sculptures of emerald and ruby while he stayed in hospice, geometrically weird and seemingly overseeing the more common crystal -forms.
   The months rolled into years. Arik was rebuilt, a common Ur Flan no longer. One eye blazed with Ruby light, the other was a brilliant Saphire. His limbs were diamond and his chest was steel. Yet, his mind remained Arik, and he felt little difference. His failure to take Ierendi haunted him, and he couldn't help but feel the crushing weight of the realisation that he would never be as great as his brother.
   Eventually he adapted to his new body and he returned to Kodge Land. He would raise a new army and conquer a different region of Mystara for Vecna. Arik must do it or he knew that he couldn't return to Oerik ever again. 
   To the north of Glantri was the Elven realm of Silver Land. Austere and forbidding and isolated within mountainous valleys, Glantri had ignored them, concerned instead with expanding into the east where they engaged ferociously with another young empire, Thyatis.
   Before he left Glantri, Arik had gained the blessing of the war wizards that Vecna could lay claim to Silver Land if he could secure it, without upsetting Glantri, as long as fair trade and relations were maintained.
                              *******
   The Silver mountains had been a difficult barrier to overcome, but the discovery of a large natural harbour and a network of passes and tunnels connecting the valleys saw Silver Land eventually fall.
   This time, there was no angry goddess to thwart him, and no nasty surprises. The Silver elves lacked magic compared with the elves of Ierendi, and their martial abilities were no match for kodge, Ur Flan and bugbears. Glantri had overestimated Silver Land to the same extent that Arik had underestimated Ierendi. Finally, Arik had achieved success.
   All praise Vecna. See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 171
1543 SD
The three great forests of Celene, the Gnarley, the Welkwood and the Suss, were covered in thorn hedges. Behind were rows of Celenian archers ready and waiting for the Hand to strike.
For Vecna's Hand had formed a fist, and he planned to pummel Celene into submission.
******
"I bought us a little time," announced Garl Glittergold with pride, "they are heading South East instead of South West. My illusions have completely befuddled the bugbears."
"Good, for now," answered Ulaa, " but soon they will realise, and we will have to meet Vecna in battle."
The leaves of the Welkwood glowed orange in the sunlight, and Ehlonna could feel the trunks tremble.
Beory, the Oerth mother, was afraid.
******
Lord Spindle had wondered where his main force had gone. The bugbears were to meet up with the goblin army in the Cairn hills just South of the Lake of Unknown Depths, the Nyr Dyv.
The problem with bugbears, decided Spindle, was that they were oafs. Hairy, ugly, oversized goblins with ears like a lynx and eyes too big for their heads. They hated orders unless they could give them out themselves, and they tended to extreme violence as a default.
Celene was a dangerous adversary, Spindle knew, and powerful heroes defended the realm. The bugbears probably blundered into danger out of sheer stupidity.
What should Spindle do now? He needed the bugbears, because what else could absorb elvish arrows? His black eyebrows knitted across his grey face. He would have to send out scouts to find them.
******
As Ulaa had predicted, the army of Vecna eventually came.
Vecna's fist was large and heavy, but the magical thorn hedges covered his wrinkled knuckles with quills.
War wizards stepped out to blast the forest with fire, but Celenians flying hippogriffs soared across the sky, arrows raining like hail.
War wizards fell, riddled with arrows. Lord Spindle frantically ordered them to withdraw, but several were dead already.
Damn! Vecna would not be pleased.
Now the bugbears lumbered in, charging the thorn hedges, taking the arrows, but howling with rage and pain, for the thorn hedges had spikes as strong as steel.
The bugbears ran back, ignoring Spindle's exhortations.
Disaster! The frontal attack on Celene had obviously failed. And now Celenians on unicorns thundered out and Spindle himself fled.
*****
Later, the three heroes, Garl, Ehlonna and Ulaa, discussed the results over a simple meal. Celene was probably safe from Vecna, because there was no clear line of attack that Vecna could make without Celene having time to prepare.
"What do you think he will do next, then?" asked Garl.
Ulaa looked at the old gnome.
Ehlonna looked at Ulaa.
Vecna already had a vast area of the Flanaess, from the Rift canyon to the old Blemu lands, the Flan lands and dear Sunndi.
It should be enough. More than enough.
But what did the undead know was enough?

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 172
Spindle couldn't sleep.
He reached for his Glantri timepiece and stared at its pink glow. Only a quarter past three. He smacked his lips in frustration, ignoring the wet drool that landed on his cheek.
Vecna's words kept ringing through his head. That was the problem, and it was a problem that Spindle didn't have the power to solve.
Spindle had failed the Lich Lord.
Vecna's army was at a standstill, and Celene was too well defended. Spindle had read the histories, and he knew that Celene was battle hardened, having survived turmoil including Gruumsh and the Drow of Lolth.
But Vecna wanted Celene for his own, and Lord Spindle was expected to deliver it.
Expected to deliver it.
And obviously, he hadn't.
So now he couldn't sleep.
Spindle climbed out of bed then padded his way to his dresser.
He put on some simple breeches, a tunic, then took his heavy cloak.
Spindle left his hut and turned left. The road was little more than a muddy track, an out of the way by-way of the new little town on the Wild Coast.
The track wound through the poor quarter, and here Spindle wasn't the only one up. There were a couple of Ladies of the Night returning to their slums with their meagre takings, a few restless drunks, and, somewhere out of sight Spindle could hear lyres and flutes playing dance music.
But the urge that possessed Lord Spindle wasn't to socialise or drink. He kept walking, anonymous in his cloak, until the track ran out. Here was a pile of heavy rocks marking the very edge of the town. Beyond was the beach, and Spindle could hear the crashing waves, and taste the salt in the chill air.
Spindle wasn't here for the beach either. At the base of one of the stones was a lever, crafted to look like part of the outcrop. He pulled it, causing a trapdoor to open. Spindle went down it, although it was pitch black. He pulled out the timepiece, and its pink glow illuminated a narrow tunnel of earth.
Spindle finally let out a sigh. Had he not been breathing? Well, it was time to take off some of the pressure. The tunnel led to Goblin town, and he was nearly at his destination.
The tunnel opened up into a network of corridors, reinforced with wooden beams. It was a warren, a maze, but Spindle knew where to go. Finally, coughing slightly in the stale air, he reached the room he was looking for.
A group of dirty dingy, goblins were sitting in the sand, playing dice.
"Mayi join you?" asked Lord Spindle, and he smiled.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 173
1544 SD
Vecna's ships choked the Wooly Bay. The Wild Coast was inundated with goblins, Ur Flan, bugbears and kodge. War wizards atop pterosaur -like dragonels sparked fires up and down the forested edges of Celene.
Lord Arik the Red Eye and Spindle the One Hand were further south, in the Azure sea, leading the main fleet, for the battles in Celene were merely a diversion.
The northern beaches of the Azure sea were part of Ulek, and Ulek was going to fall.
"You look seasick," said Arik to the green looking Spindle.
"Don't mind me," said Spindle, "we are going to row out soon. I hope you are ready."
Arik's ruby eye glowed sardonically. He had conquered a chunk of northwest Mystara, and here was Lord One Hand trying to throw his weight around. Spindle was lucky to be alive. It was said that Lord Vecna's displeasure had been so great that he himself had wrenched one of Spindle's arms right out of its socket.
Why Lord Vecna had let Spindle live was a mystery to Arik. Arik would have tortured the miserable failure to death.
*****
The battle was brutal, and descive. So that was why Vecna let One Hand live. Arik had never seen goblins fight like that.. Atop their warg wolves, led by Spindle mounted on his own warg, despite having disembarked only hours before, they fought as a team, flowing like a rapidl river, surprising the Dwarven scouts, overwhelming the gnome infantry, and securing the beach before the elves could counter attack.
The great heroes of Ulek were fighting dragonels in Celene. Arik and Spindle would push north, west of the Lortmil mountains and take all of Ulek before the Celenians could react.
Let Celene become an island state, surrounded by Vecna's realm.
Arik looked back across at the moored ships Now, the main forces of Flan, Ur Flan, bugbears and kodge were rowing towards the beach. The only thing that Arik would regret was that he would have to share his victory with Spindle.
He stroked his remade face. Well, there were worse things in life.

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 174
1544-1548 SD
   Scale mailed ogres, Ur Flan, Flan infantry and kodge flooded the lands west of the Nyr Dyv, reaching all the way to the huge Vesve forest, then looping down south to join Spindle and Arik's forces already battling in the Sheldomar.
   Celene was completely cut off,  a narrow strip of forest and meadows encircled within Vecna's palm.
   The Kron hills to the north? Vecna.
   Ulek? Controlled by Vecna.
   The Lortmil mountains? Occupied by goblins and kobolds in the pay of Vecna.
   And now, pouring out from the Hellfurnaces and the Jotens and the Crystalmists, giants. Mercenaries of Vecna, well paid, and with the promise of keeping their kingdoms, came into the Sheldomar from the west, bringing down powerful silver and copper dragons recruited by the gnomes and halflings, and utterly blocking any help from the Dwur.
   The Sheldomar fell within a year.
   Vecna's realm became the Empire of Vecna.
                             ******
   By early 1548, the Empire of Vecna stretched out an enormous Hand, its span encompassing the vast bulk of the Flanaess, Kodge Land and Silver Land of Mystara. 
   Vecna had aligned with the Glantri Empire in Mystara and the fire giant and frost giant kingdoms of the western mountains. 
   Only Celene remained a serious thorn, but they were trapped and contained, at least for now.
   But two realms remained of some concern.
   The Suel Imperium was an unknown quantity. A vast empire lurking behind the Hellfurnaces, if they chose to cross into the Sheldomar before Vecna could reinforce and consolidate, more major wars could follow.
   And closer to home was Lord Acererak.
   Acererak had turned Sunndi and the Vast Swamp into his own personal fiefdom. He refused to look into Vecna's Eye, and he refused to shake Vecna's Hand.
   Vecna had left Acererak alone for he had far more important things to attend to. 
   Not anymore. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 175
The green water was still, framed by sinuous, simian-like black branches of entwined trees.
Then, a slight ripple, and a head emerged from out of the water.
A head, bald, gaunt and sunken.
Acererak.
The water was tepid, sulphuric and clammy, and Acererak loved bathing in it. He was convinced that its mineral properties kept him young.
How old was he? Eighties? Nineties?
What did it matter to Acererak.
After his morning bath he would climb Skull Hill with his bony legs, then stop to breathe in the gaseous mist that lay at the top of the hill spreading out with its peculiar scent, and feel it hit his lungs with each breath (that surely also kept him young), then retire to his hidden cave to write.
Acererak wrote magic spells, but also general reports, fiscal data, purchase lists and inventory sheets. Sometimes the two disciplines would blur and merge into a new conjuration or evocation, never seen or felt before. Then, Acererak would feel a self satisfied glow, that made him glad to be alive.
To the north, in Sunndi, he had his administrators tend to the slave elves and the subsequent complications, but Acererak saw Sunndi more as a buffer zone and the home of a work force than any place of interest.
The Vast Swamp was Acererak's prize.
Acererak felt a shiver, sudden and unexpected. His right arm tingled. He grabbed the sleeve of his robe and saw the material undulate.
Something was moving inside the sleeve.
With a soft squelch, a grey, pockmarked toad leapt out of the robe and landed onto a glowing page on Acererak's work bench.
The toad must have crawled into his clothes when he left it by the pool to have his swim.
Acererak broke into a grin. Funny that such a simple thing startled him. Such a simple, harmless creature. Yet, Acererak, an Ur Flan, a king, had been startled, and just for a moment, he had been afraid.
Acererak looked down at the toad.
The toad looked up at him.
It snarled.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 176
Warning Horror themes
It wasn't the toad who snarled.
Acererak heard the thud of heavy footsteps striking moist ground behind him. He turned to face the Eye.
Vecna's Eye blazed with yellow fire, overwhelming the rest of his body, a dark shadow.
Vecna was here. The Lich Lord.
Vecna snarled again, low, menacing, the air that left his dried up lungs cold as liquid ice.
Acererak bowed.
"My Lord," he said.
Vecna came closer. He wore a black waist coat that glittered with jewels. His body was emaciated and mouldering and his head was a black skull. One eye was like a flaming cat. The other was a sunken grey pebble.
Vecna reached out and touched Acererak lightly on the arm. The touch was so cold that the Ur Flan felt his bones burn.
Acererak gasped.
"I heard you call yourself king?" Vecna croaked, "the king of the Vast Swamp?"
Acererak pulled himself away. His body ached with dread.
"My Lord," Acererak again said, "I take nothing from you. I am a king, yes, but merely over crocodiles and lizards. Do I not supply slaves for you? I make no claims against you."
Vecna stopped. He stood motionless, his feet hidden beneath the murky water of the cave.
"You seem to be very old," he growled, "old and broken."
Acererak protested. No, he was in good health, and he hoped to live decades longer.
"Are you sure?" probed Vecna.
Come to think of it, Acererak didn't feel all that well. Didn't he have a niggling cough that he couldn't shake?
His hands and knees were crippled with arthritis. His teeth were black and his gums were infected.
His eyes saw double. His hearing was going and he had innumerable dizzy spells. In fact, Vecna had just overcome one before his Lord arrived
Vecna was right. Acererak was old, crippled, dying.
Help me, Lord Vecna! Bring me your gift of immortality. Let me live like you.
And Vecna smiled, though one lip gave way.
"Why do you think I am here to visit you?" he cooed, "I will make you Lich like me. But you will be a good servant now, won't you? Sunndi and the Vast Swamp belong to me."
Acererak felt his heart lurch. He was going to die at any minute! Yes, Lord Vecna. Yes! My land is your land. I will be your faithful servant. Please just let me live!
Entering the cave, one on each side of Vecna, was Red Death and Blue Death. Vecna came forward and touched Acererak again. This time the touch was soothing, comforting. The cold was a friend.
Vecna produced an object from a pouch in his waistcoat. A vessel. An urn.
Red Death and Blue Death lurched forward.
"Let the ritual commence," murmured Vecna, and Acererak knew no more.

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 177
Garl Glittergold had lost his shadow.
The great gnome of Oerik has left the Celenian fortress to look for Ulla. She had left to help Ulek and the Sheldomar during the war but she hadn't returned.
Garl knew that she was still alive, because he had encountered her when he too fought against the forces of Vecna. But she hadn't returned to Celene after the war was lost, heading west into Ull.
Garl needed Ulaa back in Celene. The Olve nation was cut off from the rest of the Flanaess, an island amidst the sea of Vecna. Who knew what the Lich Lord was planning next. Garl Glittergold felt stronger when Ulaa was around.
And now he found that he had lost his shadow.
Garl looked across at the sheer cliffs looming above the horizon. The track wound into the foothills of the Barrier Peaks, deep shadows patterning the ground.
But Garl Glittergold cast no shadow at all.
It was very strange. Garl was a master of illusionary magic, so it occurred to him that his shadow was really there, but was hidden from him. A prank by a young gnome perhaps, if a weird one.
Yet when he crinkled his nose and sniffed, the telltale scent of phantasm wasn't there
This was no illusion.
Garl continued on. Shadow or not, he couldn't do anything about it and he felt normal, more or less. He planned to cross into the mountains by the end of the next day, then seek dwur guides to help him reach Ull. And he hoped that the dwur had seen Ulaa and knew her plans.
*******
There was his shadow!
The sun was up and splashing light across a ridge, sparking orange and red across the highest rocks. And dodging the flashes was a Garl shaped shadow, moving impossibly, completely independent of Garl Glittergold himself.
Garl hefted up his axe. The shadow was alive which meant that it was of the undead. Perhaps Garl's movement was noticed, for the shadow paused mid leap. It sank into a hollow in the cliff face, oozing out like black ink.
Garl held out his axe and waited
The black ink spread until the entire cliff was in shadow.
What was going on? Undead didn't behave like this either.
The black stain flowed down and across and onto the trail before Garl. He was confronted by a wall of black. Then it stopped. Garl looked down. The shadow was only four feet away from his boots.
Garl covered his eyes and cowered. A brilliant blaze of orange struck him in his face.
The Eye of Vecna.
Vecna came forward, out from the shadows. He was mouldering, skeletal, but he exuded power. His cat eye pierced Garl's soul
Vecna didn't speak, but Garl could hear every word that the Lich might have said.
Garl was a trickster. An Illusionist. A fraud.
Why, had he ever really been worthy of the company he kept? Heward, the first Bard, the enchantress Ye'Cind.
Ulaa the goddess of two realms. Obad Hai the Hierophant and god. And Boccob, magic itself.
Garl Glittergold was a big nosed little child.
You play with shadows, little gnome, while the world freezes.
Garl Glittergold knew that all of this was true He had been useless against Tharizdun. He couldn't even play the magic Organ. He played with shadow not reality, a master of trickery not power.
And look at Vecna. Garl knew him when the Lich was a mortal child. How could he have allowed that sullen little boy to become this...horror?
Why do you think that you are above the shadows?
You are nothing but a shadow already.
Come forward. Be my Illusion.
Garl Glittergold stepped forward and barely flinched when he felt Vecna's cold Hand curl around him like a talon.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 178
Lord Arik rubbed his ruby eye.
They had said that the Suel Palace was a manifestation of the goddess called Syrul, and they were right, because he could see her.
The Palace shifted, .Rooms came and went, doors appeared and disappeared and corridors suddenly plunged downward into lost shadow.
But not to Lord Arik. He focussed his eye upon the Truth. The Palace didn't exist at all. It was just a stone construction, a shell.
Arik saw Syrul lurking behind the curtain.
He winked at her.
Syrul scowled.
"You are a stranger," she said, "not Suel. I don't want you here."
"Tough," answered Arik.
Arik wasn't alone. Beside him were two fine young Ur Flan and four kodge bodyguards. The kodge wore bronze breastplates and their fur was rich and red in the artificial light. They saw the Palace quite differently to Arik, constantly murmuring with astonishment, jumping back in fear or pointing out beautiful works of art.
Well, they didn't have his ruby eye, now did they?
Arik kept them in line. He was proud of his leadership. He had worked hard for it.
"We are here to see the Empress," continued Arik, "so let us go to her. I am the ambassador of Vecna, and he wishes to reach a concord with the Suel Imperium. Stop confusing my associates, and stop wasting my master's time."
Syrul looked stunned. Her eyes bulged in thought, her dark eyebrows crinkling. Syrul was quite plain looking, Arik thought.
"I have met Emperor Vecna," said Syrul, "long ago, when he was mortal. I let him live. He owes me now. Are you his puppet? Why does he not come himself?"
Arik didn't like being called a puppet. He was a powerful Lord, both in rank and magical strength. How great a goddess was Syrul? Arik's eye exposed her. Did he dare to accost her?
Suddenly he remembered another goddess, Sehanine, and his sapphire eye flashed
The flash was involuntary, a flash of fear.
The ruby eye dimmed, the sapphire eye accendent. Arik shouldn't have come. He should have told Emperor Vecna to send someone else. He didn't want to die in a shed!
One of the Ur Flan, a tall, pale man called Gavron, lightly touched Arik on the shoulder. Lord Arik felt comforted. How good a man was loyal Gavron, always knowing how to calm him down.
The sapphire light subsided, the ruby once again in charge.
"Goddess' Syrul, I am merely a servant of great Vecna the All Seeing. If you forbid my advance then I shall return to my Master. He will decide what he owes you, and how he plans to repay it."
Time stood still.
The Palace reformed into a wide and bright corridor. At the end was an iron door.
"Go down the corridor," said Syrul, "and the door will open for you. You will find Empress Wee Jas waiting for you there."

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 179
Wee Jas. Lord Arik knew of her. He'd probably even met her.
Arik seemed to remember a dark haired Suel who apprenticed herself to the Ur Flan during the conquests. Was this lady her? She looked about thirty, that would be about right, and her eyes were blue green as were those of the apprentice.
The room beyond the door looked like an old Library. Books and scrolls were stacked up on wooden shelves, and strangely shaped objects were scattered about upon benches, chairs and tables.
"Welcome, Ambassador, to my throne room," said Empress Wee Jas, but she didn't smile.
Arik's sapphire eye gleamed in puzzlement. This was the throne room?
Then, his ruby eye saw the ghost.
There was the ghost of a young man hovering in one corner of the room.
"You can see me?" asked Dalt.
"Yes," growled Arik.
Wee Jas, her slaves and Arik's bodyguards saw Arik conversing with nothing. The two Ur Flan looked at each other. Why was their Lord speaking to himself?
Now Wee Jas did smile.
"Another visitor who can see my ghost. Alas, I cannot. What is he like?"
Arik turned from the ghost of Dalt, and returned to the attention of the Empress.
He bowed.
"The Eye of Vecna is All Seeing," he stated.
Empress Wee Jas pointed at the Kodge.
"And what manner of creatures are they?" she asked, "I have never seen fox men before."
One of the kodge now bent his head to her. Through his snout and sharp teeth he greeted Wee Jas in almost perfect Suel.
"You speak the perfect tongue?" she exclaimed in astonishment.
The kodge nodded.
"I speak several languages," he said, "I studied the Suel tongue just before this mission."
Empress Wee Jas of the House of Nehell paused, turning to look at each of her 'guests' with careful consideration. She knew that Vecna would come eventually.
Her slaves went back to their work. They made space for Lord Arik to sit. The ambassador sat down with a metallic creak.
Slaves poured wine. Arik found the wine too sweet.
"What can the mighty Suel Imperium do for your Vecna?" Wee Jas asked him
Arik looked up at her, his face a red glow.
"Stay within the bounds of your realm. Don't take advantage of the current turmoil in the Sheldomar. And supply soldiers to us. You know that we pay well."
Wee Jas sipped her wine. She didn't speak for several minutes. She studied Lord Arik, who was grimacing, fists clenched, face white, ruby eye flashing red. He was a short and ugly man. A brute. And only half a man as well. What was he, part mechanical?
Wee Jas remembered her time as an apprentice in Glantri. The Ur Flan were brilliant magicians and she had learned a lot from them, magically speaking.
But the Ur Flan were emotionally stunted. They believed that the world owed them power. They were spoiled. Entitled. And many Ur Flan were bitter and unhappy. They could hurl thunder bolts and fireballs, but they had no idea why a farmer could live a happy life with his old wife, why a woodcarver would die contented among her grandchildren though she had never even felt the glow of magic on her fingers.
The Ur Flan were dangerous and powerful, but they were still just children.
Wee Jas returned to the Imperium as soon as she realised this. She wanted her magic to make the Imperium strong, not just to help herself. And she loved the purity of magic, the idea of it.
Real wizards spoiled it for her.
And Arik seemed to be even worse than most of them. She had asked about the ghost and he had ignored her. He made demands that he assumed she would follow.He was arrogant, insecure and disrespectful.
Wee Jas stood up.
"I have heard what your Vecna wished me to hear," she said, " and I reject it. The Suel Imperium will do whatever I wish it to do. I am her Emperor, not Vecna. Sheldomar has fertile land. Why should your Vecna keep it all? And our soldiers are for ourselves. Keep your money. Now, this interview is at an end. You and your henchmen will leave my land."

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 180
1549 SD
   Th're the silver dragon had spent hundreds of years in the West. The Empire of Lynn fascinated her, as did the other nations that had emerged from the shadow of Tharizdun in Western Oerik.
   She still remained friends with Ulaa and she periodically flew across the mountains to visit the half dwur. Ulaa kept Th're abreast of developments in the Flanaess. She knew of the rise of the Dark Druids, the Stagi, and of the witch Baba Yaga and the Lich Lord, Vecna. Yet, the dragon remained in the West. The Tarquis city states, the Thytic horse people, the intrigues of Zindia, and Lynn felt more real and immediate to her.
   Th're had crossed the Barrier Peaks once more and had found the Sheldomar ruled by Ur Flan, goblins and fiox people. Farms were worked by slaves overseen by verbeeg giants and bugbears.. Gnomes and halflings lived in remote hideaways deep underground.  New towns were being built, ugly stone constructions that looked more like watchful ogres than homes.
   This was the Empire of Vecna.
   Where was Ulaa?
   Ulek was gone too, crushed within Vecna's clenched Fist.
   Where was Ulaa?
   Not in Celene. The Olve kingdom was overgrown with thorns and weeds, yet it stood strong although isolated, fiercely independent, a last bastion of the Elves.
   Where was Ulaa?
   Ulaa? She had gone into the mountains. Why do you ask?
   Th're went into the Barrier Peaks. The dwur greeted her. They had not been charged by Vecna. Let the Lich come. The Dwur were ready for him.
   Do you know the whereabouts of Ulaa?
   Yes, we do. She dwells deep within a mine, and there she digs for beautiful things. We will take you to her if you like.
   Th're entered the mine, changing her form into a gnome, for the tunnels and galleries were too narrow for her natural silver-scaled hide.
   The mine was erratic, full of dead ends and passageways that crumbled into nothing. Other ways led into hollowed out chasms denuded of their minerals.
   Th're persevered and finally climbed down a shaft that led into a red-lit cave. 
   And there, surrounded by gigantic rubies,.attacking a stone wall, was Ulaa.
   Th're greeted her. Ulaa looked up from her work, a great hammer in her hands. The half dwur looked older than Th're remembered, her gnomish face lined with wrinkles and her eyes were grey and wide.
   "Welcome, dear Th're," said Ulaa, "I am working hard. Will you join me?"
   "I am not a mineworker, as well you know. This is a wondrous cave."
   "You think so? The rubies here are large, but a little bit mediocre. I am hoping for better when I bring down this slab."
   Ulaa hefted up the hammer then returned to pounding the wall. Th're was confused by her friend's behaviour. Ulaa had never been like this before. Ulaa was a healer, an advisor, a spiritual guide. Mining had always been an afterthought.
   "Will you stop for a bit, Ulaa? I came to visit you, and see how you are faring."
   Ulaa stopped, reluctantly.
   "I am faring well enough. I expect better soon."
   "I am not talking about rubies. Why are you here? The people of the Sheldomar need our help again."
   Ulaa began to shake. The huge hammer dropped out of her hands.
   Th're ran to her, and grabbed her, for her shaking was violent.
   "What's wrong, dear Ulaa. You can tell me anything."
   "I...I can't go back, Th're. I cannot!"
   "Why not?"
   Ulaa's shaking subsided, but she looked distraught.
   "Vecna came to see me. Vecna and his Eye."
   "Yes?"
   "I was his auntie once."
   "Yes,.I know."
   "' 'Auntie,' said the Eye, 'auntie, I show you mercy. You are as precious to me as the best rubies,' and then I blinked, and the Eye was gone. Th're, I have been here ever since." See less

A History of Oerik
Book 2:
Golden Age
Part 181
1550 SD
Louse the Black Monk went down into the Lowlands, a stream of ring mailed soldiers marching behind him.
The Lowlanders were dressed in brown and grey, the only colours allowed to them.. There were hundreds of the scruffy people here. Did they breed like rats?
Louse stopped mid tread.
Only brown and grey? A red feather peaked out from that man's slouch hat.
That woman, there! A yellow boot..
And see there? That old man wears a blue scarf.
What do I pay you for? Go do your duty.
The Black Monk waited until the butchering was over, then he continued leading his men to the docks.
******
The Ur Flan saluted. The Black Monk has arrived.
Lord Spindle climbed into the rowboat with seven goblins. He took an oar himself. The spray was cooling, for the day was too warm for him.
Reaching the shore, Lord Spindle lumbered up the beach. What a drab island. Even the seagulls looked bored.
Then he spied the Black Monk. The Oeridian waited with four looking soldiers a couple of hundred yards to the east. Oh, there was a Wharf there. Spindle didn't know that they had one.
Another communication problem. Oeridian was a hard language to translate.
Spindle and his goblins passed grey people flitting about like ghosts. There wasn't one smile among them. Spindle was starting to warm to Oeridia after all.
The Black Monk inclined his hooded head when Spindle approached.
"Welcome to Oeridia," he wobbled in imperfect Flan.
"I should hope so," Spindle replied. "You have the paperwork?"
Louse reached into his robe.
"Yes, I brought it myself." He handed over the scroll. Spindle took it into his greasy hands.
He unfurled the scroll and then read the contents unhurriedly.
"Good," said Spindle when he had rerolled the scroll, "Oeridia belongs to Vecna. I commend you for your dislike of bloodshed."
"Oh, it's not that," said the Black Monk, "you can kill all of these Lowland riff raff if you like. The agreement was to preserve the Uplands."
"Don't repeat to me what I have just read. Emperor Vecna honours the agreement. When will the relics be passed over to him?"
"Once you swear alligeance to the Dead gods, I will take you there."
Lord Spindle pulled back his shirt. Around his neck was a silver necklace addorned with a pyramid.
"I already have," he asserted, giving Louse a cold stare.
*****
The goblins were left behind on the beach. They called from the ship their mates and soon the Lowlands were swarming with goblins, their short, stocky bodies pounding the Lowlanders with clubs and daggers, their flat snouts snorting with pleasure, and they let the air whistle through their thorny teeth as they committed carnage.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 182
1552 SD
   Empress Wee Jas was given reports on disturbances in the westernmost fringes of the Imperium. 
   The nomadic Baklundish people had expanded into the rain forests and plains of the region they called Zindia. Some rode great rhinos like the legendary Beast Masters of old, and others herded black camels. Jann were among them, strange semi-Djinn of mysterious powers, and the Baklundish dressed like them too, all flowing robes. The Baklundish were also said to be painted with glitter of gold and silver, symbolic of barbarous rites.
   Now they moved into the fringes of the Suel Imperium. It wasn't that the Zindian Baklundish were in any position to invade, it was their influence on others.
   Their religion was spreading.
   The Suel priests of Syrul were not happy.
   Neither was Syrul herself. The Palace was more erratic than ever. Usually Wee Jas was granted unfettered access to all parts of the Palace, but yesterday she walked down a corridor that ended in a cell.
   She would need to sort this out.
   Wee Jas made plans to go and see Zindia for herself, but predictably her advisors said no. It wasn't safe. The Empress was needed here in the capital. Finally, the Imperium had some stability and it would be foolhardy to risk it all for a minor matter.
  " It's not minor. Small matters left unattended grow into large ones."
   "With all due respect, Empress, do you want to disappear like Llerg the Lost Emperor? Send in your soldiers. Send us even, but stay in the Palace and rule with wisdom."
                             *****
   Wee Jas was frustrated and she couldn't sleep. She went down a spiral staircase, crossed corridors and soon reached a plain wooden door.
   She knocked and a male voice called her to come in. Wee Jas entered a small room with a bed and a desk and shelves of scrolls and puzzles. Paintings were everywhere. Sitting on the bed was the Suel Lich.
   She was in the guise of Heward, for she had taken the body of her old friend. She had retained the trim beard, and her face was still that of a dashing silver fox.
   Wee Jas hadn't been born when Heward had succumbed to the Suel Lich. She wondered what he was like, for although the body was that of Heward, the mind was Win-Daled.
   "Nice to see you again," said Win-Daled the Suel Lich.
   "You too," said Wee Jas, "I couldn't sleep. I am trapped, Win-Daled. I am an empress in chains."
   Win-Daled scowled,, Heward's face losing its good humour.
   "You dare to complain to me?" wailed the Suel Lich, "I am in one room, lost in the body of a man I held as a dear friend. I have outstayed my life. You cannot sleep you say? I cannot die!"
   Wee Jas returned to the door. Win-Daled was in one of her melancholy moods again...
   "Why do you leave?" 
   Wee Jas returned a look to the Suel Lich, "Really? I came down for comfort and you gave me abuse."
   Heward's stolen face looked downcast.
   "Forgive me, dear. I am bored. I am sad. You know how heartbroken I am. I need something to do."
   Wee Jas looked around the room. 
   "You have been painting a lot."
   The paintings were simple landscapes, but of a land Wee Jas had never seen. The grass was read, the sky was violet, and the Sun was brown.
   "Old memories," explained the Suel Lich, "but scrambled. Anyway, painting is something to do."
   Wee Jas came closer. She touched Win-Daled's/Heward's face. She could feel the stubble.
   "I came here for some comfort," she murmured,
   The Suel Lich nodded. 
   "You will need to prepare the warming spell," she replied, "because I am particularly cold today."
   " See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 183
    The sky was deep velvet and filled with stars.
    Horns and drums and woodwinds soared out, a wall of sound. Dancers  swirled, their billowing robes spinning the air with the scents of the exotic west.
   Nutmeg, cinnamon and other sweet and subtle scents that Wee Jas didn't recognise. The Empress continued to watch.
   The Seven Dancers broke apart and the Lady in the Middle, draped in silver and gold, levitated above the open theatre, arms outstretched, expression exultant.
   No torches or lanterns or fires were lit, but she and her Dancers glowed with luminous halos. Wee Jas was entranced.
   Now the Lady in the Middle smiled, and her grin lit up her entire face in silver light.
   "He is here!" she cried, ""Can you feel his spirit? The sky is filled with his eyes."
   The Seven Dancers stopped, then bowed their heads.
   They whispered a chant, low and almost inaudible to Wee Jas. She couldn't catch their words.
   It was annoying. Wee Jas blinked. The spell was broken. 
   The levitating Lady n the Middle began to slowly rotate, gesturing to the stars.
   She began to name the constellations. The Hungry Dragon. The Serpent. The Four Orcs. The usual names.
   Wee Jas shuffled in her seat. The stone was cool and it's solidity aggravated her lower back. She turned to look at her company. She had managed to wrangle her way to the westernmost province in the end, but she was forced to bring a retinue of fifty with her. Amongst the red leathered soldiers were a handful of her friends including Rindo, who had studied with her in Glantri.
   They were all watching the ceremony with eyes glistening with tears, completely entranced.
   Even Rindo, who had never entered a temple in his life.
   This won't do.
   Wee Jas was apart from everyone else. She could see the manipulation. And now the Dancers began to prance once more. The Lady in the Middle descended, the Dancers moving around her.
   Thirty men burst onto the stage, fifteen a side, brandishing white scimitars lanced with green light.
   A sabre dance.
   The women spun..the men leaped.
   High above, the stars watched.
   This won't do at all.
   Who were the dancers? Who were these men and women recklessly throwing themselves around the open stage, dressed in billowing robes, if they were dressed at all, painted with gaudy luminescence, fanatical, devoted followers of the Star Man?
   They were Suel.
   The House of Crix had let this barbarism happen. They had betrayed the Suel Imperium.
   Only the Lady in the Middle was Baklundish, the High Priestess of the lands of Zindia.
   One Baklundish. Only one.
   And look at the Infection she had created.
   The arena was filled with Suel. The watchers were all Suel.
   Her soldiers were Suel. Rindo was Suel. 
    All poisoned!
   All but her. All but the Empress.
   Wee Jas looked up into the sky, glaring at the stars.
   They weren't looking back at her.
   They were just little lights 
   All of the dancers, all of the watchers.They were wasting their time.
   Wee Jas returned her glare to her soldiers, and to Rindo.
   If they were brainwashed by one harlet Baklundish girl, then what peril the Imperium was in! See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 184
1554 SD
   The lead pyramid pulled on Gavron's neck.
   He had never gotten used to the necklace. The pyramid represented the Dead gods. Well, if they were dead, then why worship them?
   Lord Arik had insisted. The Dead gods were the official religion of the Empire of Vecna.
   Every soldier. Every Ur Flan. Every Freeman wore the pyramid. Temples were everywhere. Not that it was a demanding religion. Apart from the weight of the lead, following the Dead gods was easy enough. Five to ten minutes in the temple on most days, and an hour on Thursday.
   Gavron noticed that most people didn't really believe at all, that  they were just giving lip service.
   Not all of them. There were some who embraced the Dead gods with a fervour that made Gavron shiver. He noted that they tended to be the ones who took sadistic delight in the suffering of the slaves, or those captives of the resistance.
   Now they wore black cloaks and hoods, and called themselves Black Monks.
   Weren't the Black Monks an alien culture from far away Oeridia?
   As Vecna's empire expanded, it seemed to become infected with foreign ideas. 
   Did Vecna resist?
   What did his Eye see?
   What did his Hand feel?
   The fact that Gavron was forced to wear the pyramid necklace told him that at best, Vecna was indifferent to the spread of the Dead gods. And at worst?
   Perhaps Vecna was a Dead god himself.
   Gavron stretched out his arms and shook his thoughts away. His Lord was gesturing to him.
   They were high up in the northeast Blemu Hills, Gavron, three fellow Ur Flan, some fighters in ring mail and Lord Arik himself.
    The hills were carpeted with flowers. The locals said that these hills were connected to the fantastical land of Fey, and that half elf bards hid special magic in the hills,  secretly plotting against the empire.
   Lord Arik was atop an overhang and there he stood, calling Gavron over.
   Arik wore the pyramid necklace, of course, but Gavron wasn't looking at that.
   Lord Arik's Ruby eye was dim, but his face glowed with the blue of his Sapphire eye.
   "Look," he murmured, "from here we can see the sea."
   The overhang was a natural lookout, and indeed, on the horizon was a thin band of blue green.
   The breeze was quite strong, and Gavron pulled his cloak tightly around him. Arik was cloak less, his tunic partially unbuttoned and showing the gleaming metal of his chest.
   "Yes, I see the sea too," answered Gavron.
   "If only this hill was a little higher...do you think we would see Mystara?"
   "Perhaps the Silver Mountains...?"
   "Yes. Yes. The Silver Mountains. Beyond which is my land, Silver Land!"
   Gavron gently corrected him, "Vecna's Silver Land, surely."
   "Of course!" snapped Arik, "that goes without saying. I meant...who administers it now? Why did the Emperor pull me away?"
   "Do you question the Emperor?"
   Arik rounded on Gavron, suddenly animated, his Sapphire eye flickering and his Ruby eye flashing.
   "Why are you being so difficult today, Gavron? I am trying to tell you what I feel.. can't you understand what I feel? That I can have my heart set upon a certain place? Here I am, doing Vecna's bidding, and I am grateful! But I feel an empty cavity within my chest."
   Gavron looked upon his Lord with steady eyes.
   "My Lord, your emotions are strong today."
   Faithful Gavron mumbled some words, then laid his hand on Arik's shoulder. The Sapphire eye shouldered then dimmed. The Ruby Eye spluttered, then blazed.
   "Ah, good Gavron," said Arik, "how you comfort me. Come! Time to round up those bards." See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 185
1557 SD
   Jiace liked welding a sword. He flashed it now, admiring the gleam of the blade.
   Jace was encumbered with heavy red leather, fortified with broad bands of yellow bronze. A heavy bronze helm sat on his head, and his leggings were studded with iron bolts. His boots were reinforced with spikes.
   He didn't carry a shield, but many of his mates did, because Jace liked to wield his sword two-handed. Jace's sword was long and curved and broad.
   He and his Suel warriors had crossed the mountains to the west with ease, because the passes were well known and dotted with villages. Funny to think that the Suel ancestors used to find the mountains a barrier. They obviously hadn't looked hard enough.
   Perhaps that was why the Suel Imperium was   young; the old ghosts of the past were stupider and slower. Jace had seen some of the old art of the Suel kingdoms. He could paint better than them, and he wasn't even very good.
   The lands beyond the mountains were forested in tall trees coated in mist.
   It was always raining, but the drops were very light and cooled the skin of his face when he looked up.
   Amongst the trees were wide patches of open land populated by gigantic rhinos, elephants and huge spotted lions. The trees on either side of the fields were short and twisted.
   One of the younger soldiers had become very excited:
   "Fie, Zindia!" he boomed, and some of the others took up the chant.
   It was lucky that the Suel planned no ambush, because that was out of the question now!
   And now they were here, emerging out of the trees. Dressed in either colourful robes or loincloths, the Zindians, or the Baklundish, or whatever the Syrul they were.
   They came out firing arrows.
   Several Suel fell, but not many, for their armour was strong and the arrows were small.
   The Suel advanced in a rush.
   Jace remembered the feel of the crunch of bone against his sword. This was his first battle against fellow humans. It felt more satisfying than caving in the head of an orc.
   "Fie, Zindia!"
   Now he was yelling too.
                                   ******
   The campaign against Zindia went on for several weeks. Morale was high and the anger that the Suel had for the Baklundish was healthy.
   The Baklundish were corrupting the souls of the Suel. How could Suel ascend to the Happy Place if their souls followed the alien Star Man instead? On the way to the mountains, Jace had seen the Crix Province. Fanatical Suel dressed like Baklundish, dancing in the dark, seemingly unaware of their corruption.
   This was a good expedition, a holy campaign to save the Imperium. 
   Tonight however, Jace noticed something strange. Some of the younger men hadn't returned to camp. He had seen some of them that afternoon, collecting firewood (damp as the wood was), and this part of Zindia was conquered and free of Baklundish.
   One or two meeting some kind of foul end was possible, he supposed, but these lads were good and well seasoned  now, and they were boisterous. A gang, fifteen strong. The camp was too quiet.
   The commanding officer was puzzled too..He ordered Jace and some others to go look for them. It was already dark, so the brave soldiers brandished torches as they entered the forest.
   There, down that slope.
   The young men were here, in the dark, amongst a small meadow, sitting in.a circle. They wore their Suel armour but their hair was tied with colourful ribbons.
   In the middle of the circle was a Baklundish woman. She raised her arms and... No, it wasn't possible...
   The cross-legged Suel levitated off the ground until they hung five feet in the air.
   The Baklundish woman was chanting some kind of foreign muck, words that Jace was glad that he didn't understand. Yet, he listened anyway.
   And now the Suel rotated in the air.
   "Star Man," they cried, in Suel.
   And Jace and the other searchers ran towards the circle, crying out for the Star Man too,  though they had no idea who he was. See less
