posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 186
1558 SD
   Empress Wee Jas felt queasy. Three provinces had succumbed to the new religion. Three!
   The Suel Palace was constricting. The beautiful marble hall was gone. The third level was sealed. Syrul was angry.
   Her headaches were increasing. Syrul's displeasure, she presumed.
   The Suel soldiers were too weak. Not in terms of arms, but in mental toughness. Whole battalions had succumbed to the Baklundish witches.
   If the Zindian religion continued to spread... The Palace might disappear altogether, and the sacred line of the Suel Imperium would be over.
   Across the Hellfurnaces was another empire, Vecna. Wee Jas had planted spies there, and their reports were damning. Such a young empire, and already strong. Vecna held his empire in a tight grip. Dissent was crushed and everything there was functional and organised. The slaves were disciplined, the overseers were diligent. 
   Vecna cultivated a strong atmosphere of fear.
   And it worked.
   Humanoid soldiers marched side by side with Flan and Ur Flan. 
   Vecna's Empire worked.
   Wee Jas was envious. She considered herself a stern but fair ruler, and she had stabilised the Imperium, but the unexpected arrival of the Star Man cult was ruining everything.
   What if she could borrow some of Vecna's power? The Imperium was rich, how much would it cost to buy some Vecna mercenaries? Ruthless Vecna mercenaries, preferably half orcs or kodge?  The Baklundish dancers wouldn't move such soldiers at all. 
   Unfortunately, Wee Jas had been less than courteous when the Vecna delegation last came to visit. Perhaps Vecna would meet kind with kind.
   Wee Jas thought over it, and finally decided to send a grand delegation of her own to the Luch Lord. One hundred resplendent Suel in white, red and gold., bearing gifts unique to her land. And some Suel magi, trained by the Ur Flan. That would show a continuum of their cultures, and hopefully show good willl.
   And if Emperor Vecna brought up his own awkward visit to the Suel Imperium? Well, Wee Jas had listened after all. She had kept to their borders, and she hadn't invaded the Sheldomar had she? 
   Lord Vecna, I give you my hand in friendship.
                             ******
   The Suel delegation had made a big impression in the lands of Vecna. Brightly coloured Suel soldiers in heavy armour brought gifts of gems and art to every town they crossed as they made their way to the Cairn hills, where Vecna's new tower had been built.
   There had been tense moments when black ring mailed warriors had been suspicious, but the Empress documentation eventually satisfied them. 
   Finally the reached the gates of a squat, grey city. The Suel were told to wait.
  Then, a squad of Vecna soldiers came to the gate and had it opened.
   Gavron greeted the delegation, his cloak furred and grey. Gavron had been part of the Vecna visit to the Imperium. He recognised one of the magi.
   "Welcome to Spar," he said, "here you can rest and refresh. The Emperor Vecna himself will see you in two days." See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 188
   The Suel delegation had taken the news much better than Gavron had expected.
   When they heard that they would not be met by Emperor Vecna after all, Gavron saw some consternation on Suel faces, but after some hasty discussion, the head of the delegation, a Suel magi that Gavron had first met in Fleeth, bowed his red coned hatted head and announced that the Suel would be grateful to talk with anyone great Vecna chose to represent his empire.
   Interesting. It seemed that the Suel were under instructions to remain courteous, harmonious and constructive no matter the setbacks. The Empress Wee Jas must be desperate for something.
                              *****
   Gavron had passed this information on to the secretary in the hopes that somebody other than Lord Acererak could be arranged, as it was likely that friendly relations between Vecna and Suel could be established.
   The secretary promised to act 
                               ******
   Gavron led the delegation into a grand hall.
   It wasn't really very Grand. It was a squat, stone building but it was very wide and contained long wooden seats amongst several hardwood tables. Nothing in the Empire was flashy or ornate. Vecna liked simplicity.
   Slaves were attentive to the Suel delegates needs, and food and refreshments were plentiful, if rather bland compared with the equivalent in the Imperium.
   Gavron looked at the double doors at the far end of the hall. Beyond was the Royal Box, and whoever was behind the doors would be readying themselves.
   Gavron hoped it wouldn't be Acererak.
   Acererak was a complete unknown. A legend. A myth. It was a shock to discover that he still existed. One thing was likely, Lord Acererak would be a poor ambassador.
   He still held some hope that Vecna would come through the doors. Vecna was rational. He was balanced. He was unnerving to be sure, and extremely dangerous to cross, but his pragmatism would reign him in. So, hopefully it would be Vecna.
   Gavron looked around at the Suel. They were subdued, speaking in low tones for the most part, though there were a few at the back being raucous. 
   Perhaps it would be one of the younger lords. Gavron knew a few of them. Nasty pieces of work for the most part, but more bark than bite. And a couple of them were decent enough.
   Yes. One of the young lords would do.
   The double doors shuddered and opened.
   It was Lord Acererak.
                           *****
   Lord Acererak was no longer an athletic old man with toned muscles and a mane of long white hair.
   His body was thin, twisted, jerky and spindly.
   His expensive clothes hung off him as if he was a coat hanger. He wore a number of brooches and amulets, presumably as decoration, but they appeared oversized compared with his shrunken width.
   Acererak's face was squashed in and distorted, the jaw evidently dislocated, and most of his teeth were long and loose, for his gums were virtually gone, and what was left of his lips was black fungus.
   Two milk white eyes sat scrunched within his spore ridden head, cloudy and with no irises.
   If he was in pain, he showed no signs.
   Lord Acererak jerked his way to a table, then stood over it, leering out at the Suel, all decked out in red, yellow and gold.
   Gavron groaned silently. This was worse than he had imagined. Lord Acererak looked like he had just dug himself out from his grave.
   Lord Acererak stared at the delegation, coldly, dispassionately. He licked his black lips with a grey tongue. 
   Then, it was as if he had suddenly noticed Gavron. The Lich inclined his head, as if he wanted Gavron to speak.
   "Suel delegation," stammered Gavron, but he quickly straightened himself, "I have the pleasure of introducing you to one of our most senior advisors of Emperor Vecna himself. May I present to you, Lord Acererak."
   Acererak continued to look and stare.
   Gavron began to doubt whether Lord Acererak was able to speak at all. Perhaps he was dumb and mute. And those milk eyes. Did the lord just pretend to glare? Was he blind too?
   Then, with the whispering tones of dead and dry leaves, words erupted from Acererak's mouth.
   "Filth. Filthy, dirty beasts."
   Everyone became deathly silent.
   Lord Acererak tore off a green brooch then threw it onto the table. The brooch exploded into acrid mist.
   The Suel began gasping and choking, and so was Gavron. 
   Once again, the Lich noticed him. Acererak tossed him a topaz amulet. Gavron grabbed it, then he was suddenly hovering against the ceiling, the corrosive gas floating below his dangling feet.
   The gas spread quickly, and the few Suel and slaves that made it to the front door found it sealed and locked. 
   Holding onto the amulet, the only thing keeping him clear of the gas, Gavron watched Acererak stagger around, prodding convulsing figures with whispering cries of "filth."
   "My Lord,"  Gavron called down to him, "my Lord."
   Had the Lich detected the horror and disgust in Gavron's voice?  He looked up, his head a visage of mouldering decay. Then his face contorted into a grimacing smile.
   "Meat packet of Vecna. Watch the cleanse."
   Acererak grabbed a Suel, still shuddering, then banged him against the wall until he was dead. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 189
   The Empress looked out the window at the ranks of red, white and gold standing to attention in the plaza.
   She frowned. She didn't like what she saw.
   "Stairs," Wee Jas commanded.
   The corridor folded into spiral stone steps that Wee Jas moved down with quick determination, as if the stairs might collapse at any moment.
   Syrul was still being recalcitrant.
   This time though, the Palace remained stable and the stairs took her to the foyer. 
   Four armoured Suel stood to attention as Empress Wee Jas approached. Beside them was a tall, pale skinned magi in a long conical red hat. He was her favourite advisor, Mub.
   "Don't go out," said Mub gently.
   Wee Jas flicked her dark hair.
   "Why not. I can see that the delegation is back, and they are waiting for me."
   "The soldiers in the plaza?"
   "Yes. I saw them from my window."
   Mub looked earnest as he said, "They are not the same. They are altered..."
   Wee Jas glared at him.
   "Do you think that I can't see that for myself? But it is them. They have returned, and I must receive them."
                            ******
   Magi were positioned around the plaza with orders to blast the delegation if they made a hostile move. Wee Jas was a powerful magician herself, and she held onto a wand of light concealed beneath her blue, violet and grey robe.
   She left the Palace and strode out onto the marble plaza.
   The delegation stood to attention. As she approached they slowly drew white swords. Wee Jas gripped her wand, ready to release lightning, but the swords were raised in salute, not attack. 
   They were hailing their empress.
   Wee Jas now looked at the colourful soldiers with compassion rather than dread.
   What horror had befallen her noble ambassadors?
   Still they stood, rigid, sword upraised, waiting for their ruler to attend to them.
   They were all intact, though some had torn clothes or broken armour. 
   Except none of them had heads.
   They were headless zombies that had returned to their beloved Imperium.
   The Empress stepped closer. She could smell the rot.
   Now she noticed that each zombie held a leather bag in their other hand. 
   As one, the zombies resheathed their swords then lifted their bags.
   The bags were unfastened.
   Their heads tumbled out.
   The heads rolled across the plaza, eyes bulging, mouths contorted into unnatural shapes.
   Wee Jas became Incendiary.
   Barbarians.
   Savages.
   Vecna was a monster!
   How dare he do such evil!
   No matter the cost, he would pay.
   A chill descended upon the plaza.
   The heads were all looking at her.
   "We have a mess...age....From....Vecna."
   She could hear their words, but she couldn't tell whether they were speaking out loud or only in her skull. Suddenly uncertain, she glanced back at her guards and the positioned magi. 
   Their faces were white, their eyes were wide.
   They had heard the heads speak too.
   "Stay behind the mount..ains...," continued the detached and dead heads, "Do not come again." See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 190
   Lord Arik didn't want to see him
   Gavron now knew that he was in danger.
   He had been too outspoken, but after what he had seen... 
...surely the atrocities he had witnessed were not acceptable to the Emperor. Lord Acererak made him watch as the Lich went to each Suel delegate and dashed their brains in.
   Then...then...
   The kodge entered, their axe heads charcoal grey. Soon their orange fur was matted with blood.
   Acererak made Gavron watch it all.
   And then, after the beheadings, the Lich animated the corpses.
   Only after the zombies marched out of the hall did Lord Acererak gaze up once more, his milky eyes looking into Gavron's soul.
   "Meat packet," he whispered with the timbre of crushed leaves, and the spell that dangled Gavron in the air was broken.
   The fall also broke two of his teeth.
   Then Acererak stepped over his stricken body, leaving Gavron alone on the blood splattered floor.
                               ******
   He told the others in the barracks. He had nothing to hide. It wasn't exactly a secret, what he saw. He had been allowed to watch. Forced to watch.
   The Ur Flan and the soldiers had been non committal. They had shrugged, some expressing surprise at the return of long lost Acererak. 
   But none had shown anger, or fear, or any emotional reaction.
   Whatever they felt, they kept it close to their chests.
   Gavron hadn't done that. He told them that what happened was wrong. That this was not what the Emperor stood for.
   And then the lords would no longer see him.
                             *****
   Next, Gavron tried to see the secretary.
   A burly guard in black ring mail led him into a small room.
   Gavron was made to wait until another guard came in.
   But it wasn't a guard.
   He was a Black Monk. A leader of the Dead religion.
                            *****
   It could have been worse. Gavron wasn't tortured, but he was interrogated.
   Why do you question the Empire?
   The Lords are gods, not to be rebuked.
   What plots are you involved in?
   Who are your associates?
   Do you plan to assassinate the Emperor?
   How do you plan to assassinate the Emperor?
   And then, after many hours, the Black Monk let him go.
   Gavron was warned that he would be watched, and that he must not return to the barracks. And, likely he would be arrested again and charged.
   "Get your affairs in order," warned the Black Monk, "it is only the intervention of Lord Arik that sees you still alive. Perhaps you will prove that his trust in you is warranted. You will know in a week."
                               *****
   Gavron spent the next few days feeling miserable, wondering what would happen to his family. He had a wife and three little children. He asked them to promise him that they would denounce him when he was executed, and they would do whatever was asked of them. He knew that Lord Arik would do what he could for them if they showed loyalty to the Empire.    
   Gavron considered taking his own life. Better to end on his own terms, he thought, than suffer torture for years. But what would happen to his family then? Probably the Black Monk, or even Lord Acererak would seek revenge for his evasion of their justice.
                              *****
   Four days later Gavron was called to attend the Judgement office.
   Gavron kissed his family goodbye, then packed a small bag and went.
   He was taken into a small, dark room. A very dark room, for it was pitch black.
   Gavron was tied to a chair, then he was left alone.
   Gavron stared into the black void. 
   A creak. Perhaps a rusty door opened in the darkness.
   The darkness was pierced with light.
   Orange and yellow light.
   The orange and yellow of a cat's eye.
   Vecna!
   Vecna spoke, and his voice was soft as silk;
   "Gavron. You were never made a Lord. Why not?"
   Gavron felt that he had to answer Vecna. He still felt loyal somehow. Perhaps the fact that Vecna himself was here was a good thing. 
   "Dear Emperor, you never made me one."
   "True. But I planned to. I heard only good things about you. Lord Arik said that you were indispensable."
   "I love the Empire," said Gavron.
   "Yet, you never put your hand up. Why?"
   "I was satisfied with my position, dear Emperor. I am satisfied with my position," he added hastily.
    "And now you are here, in a black room. In a predicament. What brought you here?"
   "I was in charge of the Suel delegation, dear Emperor. I saw an opportunity to increase the happiness of the realm. Lord Acererak... surely he overstepped..."
   Vecna expunged a gasp. Gavron stopped.
   "Gavron. What right do you have to decide what is happiness? What right do you have to reject honest instruction given you by your superior? You have no ambition. You don't understand power. You are a corruption Gavron."
   The room turned bitterly cold. Gavron half imagined Vecna reaching for him with his grey hand.
   He flinched. This was the end.
   "Despite this, Gavron. Despite your lack of understanding. Despite your betrayal. I show mercy to you."
   "Mercy, dear Emperor..."
   "Your family is already dead. See, I didn't make you watch. I understand that you are squeamish about these things,"
   Gavron roared and screamed.
   "Kill me, Vecna! Kill me!"
   "Kill you? No. Gavron. I release you from my service. You may go where you will. Make sure you tell of my beneficence. Make sure that everyone you meet knows of my mercy." See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 191
1560 SD
   Wee Jas had retreated into the arms of Win-Daled.
   The Suel Lich was the First Queen, and she looked like a silver haired man.
   She understood her better than anyone.
   Win-Daled knew despair.
   Fire giants had emerged from the Hellfurnaces, and whether they were paid by Vecna or not, they had taken advantage of the disorder, and their barrel -like bodies fastened in splint mail roamed the farms and villages near the capital.
   But the west was worse.
   The Zindian religion continued spreading, and the Suel Imperium was about to fracture.
   She could feel it.
   Win-Daled soothed her. She understood.
                            *****
    The door screamed open and with a burst of eldritch fire, Syrul appeared in the doorway.
   Her grey hair was tied into a severe bun and her face looked tired, but her grey eyes were filled with rage.
   "Wee Jas. You are failing me!"
   Wee Jas pulled herself away from Win-Daled and reached for her clothes.
   "Yes, Empress, get dressed. Die with some dignity."
   Wee Jas stepped into her dress. Was Syrul going to kill her? The goddess had shown her displeasure more and more. 
   Well, it was no disgrace to die to a god.
   "Good," said Syrul, once Wee Jas was ready, "now return to the throne room. Face those who wish to assassinate you."
   "There are assassins in the throne room?" asked the Suel Lich., "I will remove them."
   "No, First Queen," said Syrul, "your time is long over. The Empress must face them herself. Three Houses have banded together to take her down."
   "And you have let them in," said Wee Jas, "you have betrayed me."
   Syrul glared at the Empress, "you are the Empress, but I am the Suel Imperium itself. You, Wee Jas have betrayed me. What hopes I had for you. Finally a competent ruler....well you have ended up being as bad as all the rest."
   "So now you just expect me to walk into the throne room and be cut down?"
   "Yes."
   Wee Jas turned to Win-Daled, still in the bed.
   "Stay there," said Wee Jas, "I shan't be long."
                              ******
   Legends still tell the tale of Wee Jas and the duel of the three Magi. Did Syrul know that warning Wee Jas of her impending doom gave the Empress a fighting chance?  Or was telling her of her imminent demise a final chance to gloat before there was a new emperor?
   Wee Jas was trained by the Ur Flan of Glantri. She knew secrets not even throught of in the West.
   The throne room was lit with lights. All those across the city could see the flashes of blue and green that shot out across the sky.
   The lights transfixed the clouds, turning them inside out.
   The clouds fell back to Oerth, not as rain but as diamonds that bounced of roofs and scattered across the streets, sparkling with beauty.
   Did Syrul intervene, and if she did, who's side was she on? The tales do not agree.
   Ultimately, it was Empress Wee Jas who remained standing amongst the twisted wreckage. She handed her crown to her faithful Mub, then she left the ruins of the Sacred Palace to follow a new path. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 192
   Wee Jas wandered the outer provinces of the Suel Imperium.
   She had changed her appearance, because she was a striking woman with dark hair and extremely recognisable. Now she was considerably shorter with light hair , although she was still conventionally beautiful.
   Wee Jas wanted to understand the appeal of the Star Man. Most Suel had not succumbed magically to the Zindian religion, so why had they turned away from their culture to embrace this strange Baklundish one?
   "The sky is our protector," she heard.
   "The Stars watch over us, but they do not judge."
   "The world feels bigger now, and full of hope."
   Wee Jas went to the new temples, but she remained unimpressed. The Star Man didn't come down for her. The Zindian cult remained a nonsense.
   She heard that Emperor Mub was working hard to regain the territory lost to the fire giants, but out here in the west it seemed a distant problem affecting a distant people.
   The Suel Imperium really was fracturing.
   The Suel here dressed like Baklundish. Already they talked about the old ignorant times with disbelief. Had they really been so stuffy and uptight? Were they only interested in material wealth, of status and pride and cruelty?
   Thank the gods for the Star Man.
   The sky was enough. See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 193
1561 SD
   Wee Jas went into Zindia.
   Where were the Baklundish?
   Most of them were gone. There were a few wandering about, along with some Jann and the old Pyanor, but the priestess Wee Jas had encountered a few years ago had left too.
                            ******
   The rakasta yowled. She had been hunting on the rocks and was annoyed at the interruption. She turned her white furred body around, staring at Wee Jas with yellow and black eyes.
   "Sorry, I didn't mean to trip," apologised Wee Jas to the cat person.
   The cat person, the rakasta, strode up to Wee Jas on two muscular hind legs, tail twitching. Her hands reached out, claws extended. Wee Jas apologised again, ducking away as she did so. The rakasta was over five feet tall and her teeth were sharp. Wee Jas could see muscles rippling beneath the fur.
 The rakasta hissed out a string of incomprehensible words.
   Wee Jas waved her hand. Suddenly the words made sense. 
   They were not very nice.
                            *******
   They were an odd pair, the white cat woman and the Suel, yet Wee Jas was glad to have befriended the rakasta. She knew Zindia as well as anyone, even if she was more focussed on the best hunting spots than the fastest way from A to B.
   They slept in rakasta villages, crossed orc and gnoll lands unmolested, for the rakasta were respected and feared, and hunted in both forest and plain.
   The rakasta was called Rhhha, and she was a loner by nature, but she had taken a shine to Wee Jas, perhaps because Wee Jas was the first human who spoke the rakasta language. She didn't seem to realise that it was because Wee Jas had cast a spell, and not actually learned the 'spitting language.' 
  Wee Jas left Rhhha to hunt alone when she wished, and always prepared a good fire to cook the catch when Rhhha returned.
   Rhaaa knew nothing about the Baklundish priestess or the Star Man, and didn't want to, because humans always wasted their time on abstract things, but she went along with Wee Jas when the Suel woman made enquiries with the few Baklundish they met.
                                  ******
   The outskirts of Zindia were framed with mountains, a deep purple lit by a dipping sun. The old Baklundish man, eyes brilliant green, pointed his staff towards them.
   "She went that way," he said.
                                  *******
     Rhaaa refused to go any further.. Zindia was her hunting ground. How was she expected to find prey on unfamiliar territory? She didn't say goodbye, she just turned away.
   Wee Jas looked up at the forbidding mountain wall. Time to use some magic. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 194
   "Wee Jas, come forward."
   Wee Jas was just one amongst the congregation sitting cross legged in the clearing. How had the priestess detected her?
   Wee Jas climbed to her feet then made her way to the Baklundish priestess. The priestess smiled warmly.
   "This is Wee Jas, " the priestess announced to the congregation, "she has come a long way to find me, yet, she believes not in the Star Man,." Now she turned to Wee Jas and her expression hardened, "you don't believe, do you?"
   They were in one of the more fertile regions surrounding the desert. Nearby was a narrow stream, and scattered about were shrubs and low, sprawling trees, pale grey in the moonlight. Wee Jas had crossed a large area of  Western Oerik searching for the priestess. She had joined the congregation in order to observe the Baklundish woman. Wee Jas wanted to understand the power that the priestess wielded.
   Wee Jas had lost her throne because of her.
   No. Wee Jas didn't believe in a Star Man. The only god was Syrul. She wasn't particularly nice, but she was real. 
   "Look up, Wee Jas..see the stars?"
   The stars again. Lights like little eyes looking down at her?
   They were lights. That's all. There is no Star Man. The Baklundish witch was a sorcerer beguiling the world.
   The priestess sent Wee Jas back.
   "Beautiful friends," she said, "do not hinder her. Let her watch, or go, at her pleasure. If the Star Man does not touch her heart, then that is between her and the Star Man. Let us enjoy our own blessings."
                               *****
   When Wee Jas woke up in her tent, the priestess was there.
   Wee Jas jumped.
   "It is day now," said the priestess, " the Star Man is asleep. My name is Johla. Would you talk with me? Sorcerer to sorcerer?" See less

Part 195
1564 SD
   "I told you so, didn't I?"
   Nub put down his empty tankard with an excessive thump. He looked over at Grinn whose eyes were bulging out of his craggy skull. Gods, Grinn an ugly goblin. He looked like he had been weaned on curdled milk. Not that Nub was a good looker, but at least his lumps weren't green.
   "What are we to do then?" moaned Grinn, nursing his own tankard as if every drop was worth its weight in gold.
   Nub gestured around the tavern. It was a homely place, part stone and part wood, jutting out of the mountain like a leering head.
   "Well, we won't be able to afford to go here anymore. I suppose the Skewered Man will close down."
   Grinn pulled a gold coin out of his pocket.
   "Nub, this is my last one. Suppose we don't get paid tomorrow?"
   Gods, Grinn was as stupid as he was ugly. If Nub could find somebody else to talk to he wouldn't waste his time with the runt.
   "Grinn, you ape! I told you. We ain't gonna get paid!  The money's run out. Vecna has shut us out!"
   "But why, Nub?"
   Nub called for a refill, then he turned back to Grinn, whose befuddled earnestness made Nub want to strike him.
   "Why? You dense ape. Vecna don't need us no more. He got everything he wants. He's got his standing army, and he's got his Ur Flan ain't he? Why pay us for nothing?"
   The goblin wench gave a dirty look as she deposited down a fresh ale.
   "You better shut it, Nub!" she hissed, "you are talking gob! There's just a delay. You'll get yer wage."
   Nub's blue face burned violet. He always struggled to contain himself when a girl gave him any attention.
   He winked frantically, trying to be suave and rakish, "Ah, miss," he stammered, "what delay? Vecna runs everything like jelly."
   "You bet he does," she returned, "and he won't take kindly to your talk will he? The delay is because of that ruckus with Lord Arik. Vecna will fix him up good and proper, and then the shipment will come."
   A ruckus with Lord Arik? Nub hadn't heard anything about it.
   "Oh, that" said Nub, "old news."
   "Yeah? You're full of elf dung. You and your ugly friend ain't gonna give this place a bad name, got it? Say one more damned thing and I'll call Crooked to come out and eat you. Drink up then get out!" See less

Part 196
   Lord Arik had actually knocked Vecna over.
   It hadn't taken much either. Just a push. Arik's temper had gotten the better of him. Again. He remembered his Ruby eye blazing with fury, his Sapphire eye strobing alongside. 
   Vecna wasn't letting Arik return to Silver Land.
   "Why not, Vecna? That place calls to me. It cries out night and day!"
   "Calm yourself, Lord Arik. You are required here. Lord Kint will administer Silver Land. It is a far away nub of my empire. Why you should wish to be there I cannot understand."
   Arik couldn't explain it, because he couldn't understand it himself. Mystara wanted him. He didn't know why.
   But Arik knew what he felt. 
   Enraged, he rushed the Emperor. Vecna's head turned away from the burning red fire, and then Arik pushed Vecna over.
   Vecna was astonishingly light, and he toppled over like a mannequin.
   Vecna crashed to the floor with a thud.
   Arik's Ruby eye shut down and his Sapphire eye glowed coldly.
   He was done for!
   Vecna might be sprawled on the ground, but he was already beginning to right himself, his waist bending unnaturally, his spine twisting, his shoulders returning to position.
   Vecna would destroy him now.
   Arik tried to run away, but the fear he felt caused him to stumble and fall into the wall. 
   Vecna was up, hand outstretched...
   The blast of black smoke burned through Arik's body. A lesser mortal would have had their insides vaporized, but Arik was part machine, a half-golem. He felt the tar shoot through him, turning his metal parts cherry red. But only for a moment. The searing sensation was soon gone. 
   Vecna was staring at Arik, more puzzled than angry. His great leopard eye blinked with astonishment. No one before had ever survived the Burning Death.
   Arik stared back, fear, wonder and other emotions he couldn't identify surging through him like an after effect of the black smoke.
   Vecna bowed.
   "Well, Lord Arik, you have bested me today. You had better go now."
   Arik backed away, bowing too.
   "I suggest," said Vecna in a low whisper, "that you get your army together quite quickly. I am sure to gather mine." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 197
   Thank the gods his pirates had received the message.
   Arik's loyal buccaneer fleet was blockading the Vecna fleet. How he wished to join them!
   He was trying to get to the docks, but Vecna had been too quick. Hordes of Flan, kodge, goblins and bugbears and ogres cut him off time and time again. Lord Arik had been forced to retreat into the Rakers, that large twisty mountain range in the north east.
   He was only about seventy miles from Grendep bay, the body of water that flowed directly into the Solnor sea, but it might as well be a thousand. The Rakers were filled with treacherous paths that wound nowhere. The caves were inhabited by hostile troglodytes or monsters, and the reclusive mountain dwarves were no friend of any part of the Empire.
   Arik had reached a narrow valley that had been occupied by a family of carnivorous lamias. Now he and his troops had seized it for themselves. It was idyllic compared with what he had seen of the Rakers so far. The valley was one of a series that zigzagged through this part of the chain. Arik hoped that navigating through them would lead him out to the coast. He decided to recuperate here a couple of days and gather fresh provisions, because the game was good here too. He sent out a few scouts then forgot all about them.
   Arik was going to try and get some sleep.
                            *******
   "Wargs and goblins! They are coming!"
   Damn! The scouts brought back the worst news. Warg riders were fast and terrifying. And there they were, his superior vision making out wolfish shapes coming down a distant ridge.
   Archers. Where were his archers?
   A few ragged Flan with short bows and only a clutch of arrows between them.
   "We were in the process of making more..."
   Arik struck the fletcher down in a blast of red fire. Never mind. Now, how many war wizards left?
   Three.
   Three? Not many, but enough. Arik himself would lead from the front. He figured he could take out a dozen wargs and goblin riders on his own.
                               *****
   The eldritch blasts of red, blue and green obliterated the first wave of warg riders, but the second wave seperated and circled the valley, stretching Arik's ability to defend. The wargs snapped and growled, the goblins hurling small spears, keeping Arik's men at bay. The war wizards and archers didn't know who to focus on. 
   Wargs would charge forward then feint back. One war wizard was suckered in, his flaming blast striking too late, for the warg riders had leapt away just in time. Before the Ur Flan could recover he fell, a spear skewering his throat.
   "Fall back to the centre." cried Arik. Hopefully this would draw the attackers in, then he would unleash hell.
   The wargs and goblins did move forward, the giant wolves black, brown and red, the goblins atop like horrible distortions of nature. There were many more than Arik had expected. They kept coming into the valley, ten or fifteen at a time. Some had spears, some had swords.
   Arik readied himself for a last stand. He swore to bring down a hundred.
   A horn blast, but it was the horn blast of a demon, low, dissonent and jarring.
   One of the scouts was hidden within the rocks around a natural rise. He called out a terrible name:
   "These are the wargs of the secretary. Secretary Spingle is here!"
   Arik's Ruby eye flashed, disintegrating four wargs instantly. He lumbered forward, bodily taking on the gathering hordes. Blades broke on his shoulder and neck and chest as he waded forward.
   "Secretary!" he boomed, "Puppet of Vecna! Is our Emperor so afraid of me that he sends you himself?"
   Another horn blast, then coming down a crooked path on a huge two headed death dog, was the secretary.
   Secretary Spingle had changed.with age. His skin was like thick leather, brown and orange, his one arm long and thin as a rotten tree branch. He had grown as well, horizontal and vertical both, so he looked like a distorted reptile. His long fingers were wrapped around a thick black rod and his eyes were bloodshot and uneven.
   Lord Arik met his gaze with his own gemstone eyes blazing red and blue. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 198
  Secretary Spingle urged his death dog forward, the beasts two heads filled with yellow sabre teeth. He swung out with his rod, displacing the air with thunder.
  Lord Arik's fire blast deflected away, detonating a patch of shrubbery fifty feet away with a sonic boom.
   The death dog leapt, but powerful as the monster was, Arik was stronger. His broad metallic body stayed planted on the ground, his legs like anchors. The death dog draped itself awkwardly about Arik's shoulders, surprised that its momentum hadn't subdued its prey.
   Spindle himself over balanced, and with only one arm, he fell hard, shaking the ground.
   The death dog's heads tried to find something to latch onto, but only snapped air. Three nearby warg riders spun around.. Their master was in trouble! They barreled into Arik's legs as the half golem grabbed at the death dog's tail, it's bushy mass as sharp as quills.
   Now Lord Arik did tumble over, the sideways impact taking him by surprise. Goblin swords slashed at his face, drawing blood. The death dog was free again, now it turned, snarling in stereo. 
   Secretary Spingle had returned to his feet too, his side torn, the already congealing blood the consistency of sap. He had lost the rod and was half looking for it while fixing a beady eye on Arik.
   Arik knew he was in a very bad position. He couldn't focus his eyes, the Ruby and Sapphire glow rising and falling with each breath. He found getting back to his feet labourous, particularly with wargs and goblins all about him, slashing and thrusting with their weapons. The death dog had seized an arm and was using its strength to keep him down.
   Horn blasts.
   Not demonic bass notes of dissonance, but warm, bright and stern. 
   From another rise burst forth a volley of arrows, sending the warg riders howling, spinning around to try and find the source. Two arrows struck the death dog who yelped with his free head, but still held onto Arik's arm.
   Another horn blast. 
   Figures were making their way into the valley, large, broad fox- headed shapes, kodge. Their comrades covered them with arrow fire.
   Spingle cursed. Rebels! Where was his damned rod?
   Arrows plunged into wolf and goblin alike. Now they panicked. They were shock troops, they did not like it when the tables were turned. Besides, one kodge was as strong as a warg, and they were armed with axes, their snouts twisted into smiling grimaces.
   With wargs and fallen goblins milling about, the death dog still struggling against Arik, arrows thudding everywhere, the secretary took the demon horn from his belt and blew an ugly rasp.
   It was time to go.
   The death dog let Arik's arm go, for it wished to return to its departing master. Arik gave it a parting stare, his fire blast turning the beast into ash.
   The first kodge thundered past the bubbling stream, then they slowed as they approached Arik.
   Arik was back in his feet.He was bloody and bruised and dented, but he was still extremely dangerous. He didn't know how many kodge there were, or how many arrows they had ranged against him, but he knew that there would be a lot less than now after this battle was ended.
   Actually, the arrows weren't raining down anymore.
   The kodge halted thirty feet away. One spoke, his Flan almost perfect;
   "Lord Arik. We come from Gavron." See less

A History of Oerik

Golden Age 
Part 199
   The cavern still stunk of troll. Arik wrinkled his nose as he was led through the dank miasma towards stone steps leading downwards.
   Here the air was less flavoured, but  lingering with faint musk. The surrounding walls were bathed in blue light, for Arik's Sapphire eye was  dominant.  The passageway opened into another cavern, wet with slime, but Arik was directed to raised stone platforms accessed by ladders.
   Arik was clumsy on the ladder, and he feared that his weight would break it, but despite the strain it held, and reaching the top, he found himself bathed in the orange and yellow of torchlight.
   Gavron was there, wrapped in furs. So were a number of kodge and Ur Flan. They had set up bunks, seats and hammocks, and some were sleeping or playing dice.
  Gavron..Arik hadn't seen him since the Suel delegation massacre. His blue eye gazed into Gavron's eyes, trying to read him.
   Gavron looked tired, worn but his eyes were filled with determination. 
   "Dear Gavron, you have made yourself a leader at last."
   Gavron smiled.
   "Lord Arik, I am no leader. We work together. I heard that you had a falling out with Vecna. Perhaps you can join us?"
   "Join you?" boomed Arik, "and hide like a rat within the mountains? No, Gavron, I head to Mystara, to the Silver Land. Let me go!"
   Gavron held out his hands placatingly, "Lord Arik, we only want to help. If you want to get to the docks, we know the way. Whatever you do that hurts Vecna will only help us."
   "The docks? How far away?"
   "Four days journey. But my guides know the mountains far better than you. Without them you probably won't ever reach the coast."
                             ******
   The motley mix of dwur, Flan, Ur Flan, kodge, orcs and gnomes led Arik the half golem through a network of underground tunnels and outdoor valleys. After four grueling days, Arik's knees squeaking with every step, the party reached the edge of a cliff. They looked down upon the green sea.
   There! There was a ship. A merchant caravel. It was moored only a mile from the beach.
   "Come with me," called Gavron, who had joined the group, "I know the way down from here. That's one of our ships. They'll sail you to Mystara."
   Dark shadows flashed across the sky.
   Dragonels. The huge pterosaur-drakes, ridden by Ur Flan, soared out towards the ship.
   Arik could feel the explosions from the cliffside.
   The ship was on fire. The dragonels circled about, then came for them!
   Arik wondered how they knew that he was coming.
   Foolish question. 
   Vecna's Eye. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 200
1566 SD
   Wee Jas stared out into the Universe.
   The Universe. 
   That Eternal Mystery. A great stretched out State,
   Black and Airless and Remote,
   Alien yet full of Wonders.
   Behold, the Stars!
   Little lights twinkling in the dark, yet they conceal layers,
   Behind each star sit other stars, on and on, stars and worlds and comets and fire.
   Are they just Lights?
   "Don't just see them," said High Priestess Johla, "it means little to just see them."
   Wee Jas did not understand.
   Still she did not Understand.
   "What more can I do?" murmured Johla, "you have opened yourself up to me. You have been attentive and Talented. Your Magic is undoubted."
   "Yes, yes!" cried Wee Jas, "I touch the sky and I feel the threads holding it up. I know what matter is. I know what the soul is."
   "But the Stars," urged Johla, "what of the Stars?"
   Wee Jas shook her hair, cosmic dust spilling from her hair.
   "The Stars... They are just stars...."
                           *******
   Wee Jas retired to her tent. The sun was up, and daytime was sleep time. She was frustrated and annoyed with herself. She had become something else than the sorcerer empress, but whatever it was that she now was, it wasn't quite enough.
   What held her back? Was it some kind of scepticism? Was it stubborness? Was Wee Jas too proud to fully commit to Johla's teaching?
   Johla floated the dimensions, serene and fearless, blessing people with the gift of the Star Man.
   The Star Man was the missing piece.
   Wee Jas knew that he wasn't real. Nothing that she tried changed that fact. 
   Wee Jas was so close to being Complete.
   Believe in one Fiction more. Imagine that He is real. 
   And how can you know that he is not?
                              ******
  Wee Jas could control her dreams. She had dreamed of lovers and banquets, and stillness and chaos. Her dreams had taken her into the past, and she had seen the Dragon Times.
   Her dreams had taken her into the future too, but there everything shimmered like reflections in a pool.
   Now she dreamed of the Star Man.
   And there he was, in a dark triangular room.
   He was as shadowed as the dark side of the moon and his eyes blazed white. His black  cloak glittered with stars.
   Wee Jas was in the room too, looking through a long metal tube.
   Through the tube she could see a star.
   But it wasn't twinkling light.
   The Star was an Inferno.
   "Hello," Wee Jas, " said the Star Man.
   Wee Jas turned away from the tube.
   "Hello," she returned.
   "You don't believe in me?" asked the Star Man.
   "No. Not really."
   "You still don't believe in me, even though I am right here?"
   "No," said Wee Jas sadly, "because I am dreaming of you. But you can try and convince me. I would like you to convince me."
   The Star Man shook his head, "I haven't the power. You are right that I am dreamstuff. I mean, this particular manifestation of me. Yet, I can say with certainty that I exist."
   "Why do you say that with certainty?"
   "Because I was born a mortal. Because I raised myself up through necessity. Because I know my name. I am Celestian." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2;
Golden Age 
Part 201
   "I don't need the Star Man," announced Wee Jas, "but I do need Faith."
   Johla gazed up at Wee Jas.
   She was luminous.
   "You are powerful, Wee Jas, " said Johla, "but you are not a god. The Star Man lends his cosmic dust to His believers. Just close your eyes. Believe."
   Wee Jas glowed.
   "I have tried. Many times. I have even met the Star Man."
   "Ah," whispered Johla, "then you must be close..."
   "No. He is the Star Man, but he is still just a man. If I am to transcend fully I need Faith."
   Wee Jas gently touched Johla's naked, brown arm.
   "And I know where to find it."
                             *****
   Long ago, a wise priest, perhaps the wisest priest that ever lived, ventured west to the Empire of Lynn.
   He sought liberation of the spirit and the truth of all things.
   There, in Lynn he encountered Tiamat, the dragon goddess of death. 
   Tiamat was as evil as the priest was good. Long they fought, and the people of Lynn trembled, for they had never seen such power unleashed upon the Oerth.
   The priest finally smote Tiamat down, plunging her back into the abyss.
   The Lynn people wept, for they were overcome with his goodness. He had saved them all!
   But the priest did not get up.
   He was grievously wounded, for the blood of Tiamat had burned his flesh.
   Yet, he smiled, and he blessed the good people of Lynn.
   "I go up to the Heavenly place," he said," but I lend you my wisdom. When I die, remove my teeth. They contain my Faith in all things."
   And so, the priest went up to the Heavenly place, and the Lynn Holy woman gently removed his teeth and placed them into a small leather bag.
   "Behold," she said, "here is the final blessing of high priest Dahlver- Nar.  I hold in my hand, Faith itself." See less

Golden Age 
Part 202
   The Suel Palace had rebuilt itself.
   It appeared as twisted blocks of  wood, metal and stone, intertwined into a serpentine and tentacled mass. The plaza before the Palace was pitted and corrupted, the little gardens were gone. 
   Wee Jas alighted onto the plaza. She wore the billowing robes of the Baklundish and her hair flowed with glitter. She wore silver earrings, each one encrusted with a tooth.
   Her skin was white as porcelain, contrasting with the lead grey of the Palace.  Wee Jas walked around the vast structure, her feet light as a dancer, and found that there was no entrance. No door or window. The Suel Palace was sealed.
   Wee Jas went inside anyway.
   The interior of the Palace was almost completely absent of light, except for a deep red glow as if from an unnatural sepulchre. Wee Jas blinked twice, then the light was bright blue and sunny.  Wee Jas was inside a bare, stone, completely empty room.
   "Where are you, Syrul?" Wee Jas demanded.
   Syrul oozed out of the wall like Quicksilver, collecting into the floor and rebuilding itself into a plain looking, middle aged woman in a severe robe. She met Wee Jas's defiant expression with a scowl.
   "You are not welcome here, Wee Jas," hissed Syrul, " you are deposed. You are no longer the Empress of the Imperium."
   Wee Jas tapped Syrul lightly in the face. Syrul glared at Wee Jas in shock. She dared to strike a goddess...?
   "Of course I am no longer the Empress. I left on my own accord. But I have returned now."
   Syrul considered blasting Wee Jas down with lightning and poison and fire, but there was a stillness in Wee Jas that checked her. Syrul still felt the sting of the slap.
   "Well," said Syrul, "I can see that you have. What do you want?"
   Wee Jas looked radiant.
   "Why," said Wee Jas, "I want your job. I wish to become the Imperium instead of you."
   Syrul blinked in astonishment.
   This would not stand. In fury she threw her arms about as if she was conducting the final bars of a great symphony, and she screeched the language of the underworld.
   Gargoyles came down from the ceiling, black obsidian scaly horrors with glowing eyes, bat wings and twisted horns growing out of their foreheads. They sprung and leaped and glided around the room, slashing at Wee Jas with long talons.
   Wee Jas sighed.
   The gargoyles whimpered.
   The room rained black dust.
   Syrul coughed gargoyle dust out of her throat. Her eyes were wide with fear.
   "Wee Jas...what have you become?"
   "Syrul...in your own way, you have served the Imperium well. But it is time to lift the shadows. I have seen the beauty of the universe. I have felt the pain of eternity. I have conquered the stars."
   Syrul felt herself being lifted up by invisible hands.
   "Syrul, the Imperium is now mine. It is now me." She turned around the empty space, Friends, I restore you!"
   The bare walls transfigured into an opulent lounge room with long couches, deep, velvet chairs and round wooden tables. Double doors appeared, and coming through them were Win-Daled the Suel lich and the ghost of Dalt.
   Once Wee Jas had been frustrated that she had never encountered the famous ghost of her former throne room, but now she could see him, handsome, but pensive, finely clothed but translucently pale. 
   Win-Daled had a roguish smile on her face as she strode up to Wee Jas, but Dalt floated towards her with seeming reluctance.
   Syrul could no longer contain herself. She screeched a curse and the opulence was  choking ochreous poison, living, flowing venom that smoked death.
   "No," said Wee Jas, and the venom turned into salt.
   The sorcerer let the invisible hands bring Syrul down.
   Wee Jas looked down upon the confused and stricken Syrul with beneficence.
   "Syrul, I have bested you, can you not see that? The Imperium is you no longer. I send you into the cellar."
   And Syrul was gone.
   Wee Jas restored the lounge room.
   She smiled at the two dead things, one her lover and one that she was sure to soon be her friend.
   "Well," she said, "how is Emperor Mub?" See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 203
1570 SD
   Gavron was worried about Arik. Arik's Sapphire eye burned almost constantly, his Ruby eye emitting only the faintest of light. 
   The fact that Arik was never in a rage wasn't the problem. It was the fact that he was deeply unhappy.
   Gavron and Arik lived in the underground, deep within lead lined chambers protecting them from Vecna's Eye.  Gavron had remarried, and he and his wife looked after their toddler, Eggert. It wasn't a great place to bring up a child, but what place was these days?  Flan shared the caves with kodge, half orcs, dwur, halflings and orcs. 
   Fights broke out. Old hatreds resurfaced, and Gavron, Arik and the other leaders worked hard to bring tensions down. They were all here for a reason after all.
   All were against Vecna.
   Yes, mused Gavron, they were all against Vecna, but what could they do? The surface was his. Towns and villages populated by his spies or the Black Monks, squads of goblins and worse, the Flanaess divided into administrative districts ruled by liches or powerful Ur Flan.
   Dragonels circled the skies.
    Vecna's Hand held it all.
                  ******
   Gavron went to check on Arik. Arik hadn't come to council, and Gavron was worried that Arik's melancholy was consuming him.  Arik was in his quarters oiling his knees. He looked up when Gavron approached, his face lit with pale blue light.
   "Ah, my Gavron. What can I do for you?"
   "No, dear Arik, what can I do for you? You missed council."
   "Ah, yes, well, what's the point of council? We never do anything. Do you know why, my Gavron? Because we can't do anything."
   His Ruby eye began to glint.
   "Do you remember when we were part of it, Gavron? Part of the Empire? I remember that feeling when we were part of the inner circle. Beautiful times. Just beautiful."
   Gavron frowned.
   "You think so, Lord Arik? I recall feeling sick inside mostly. I liked the order, and I liked the cooperation... but the Emperor, Emperor Vecna...he is a monster."
   Arik laughed bitterly, "As am I. As are you. I am some kind of golem, you are an enchanter, we are guarded by bloodthirsty fox men, ragged orcs wander about our lair hitting halflings with clubs. ... We live in a Golden Age for monsters, my Gavron. A Golden Age."
   Gavron felt his face flush. His hand made a fist. Overcome with anger and sadness both, he turned away from his old friend. Let Arik rot! See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 204
   This time, Arik went to see Gavron.
   Gavron was in his quarters, playing with little Eggert. His eyes flashed when Arik's blue shadowed light approached.
   "Gavron, I have come to make amends. I didn't mean to upset you yesterday."
   Gavron gave a tiny nod. Arik took that as a sign that he could come closer. Arik held a crystal in his hand.
   "I brought a gift for your baby," said Arik, handing the crystal to Eggert, who latched onto it with tiny fingers.
   "See, it's a crystal in the shape of a star. It's quite natural. I found it a little while ago. In that dead end passage."
   "Thank you," said Gavron.
   Eggert dropped the star onto the floor, then began to push it around. Arik was bemused, "I thought that small children liked to put things into their mouths. I thought Eggert would chew on it."
   Gavron shook his head, "not Eggert. I have to teach him to eat all the time."
   Arik and Gavron stood silent for some time, watching the boy. Eventually, Arik spoke;
   "I still want to return to Mystara," he murmured softly.
   "I know."
   Gavron invited Arik to the guest room. They can talk privately if he wished. Gavron's wife took Eggert away.
   "I have very strange dreams," said Arik, sipping a sharp brandy after he and Gavron had retired into the guest room.
   "Yes?"
   "My Gavron, you are going to think me even more absurd... I sometimes dream that I am riding a dragon. A white dtagon."
   "It's not that strange. Have you ever seen a  white dragon?"
   "I have actually, in the Corusks."
   Gavron knotted his brow, trying to remember whether he had seen one himself. Perhaps once, when he travelled for the Empire.
   "Well," he said, quaffing his own brandy, "that can't be the end of the dream. What happened next?"
   "I was atop a huge white dragon," continued Arik, and his Ruby eye began to glint, "I was me, but I also wasn't me. My skin was bone white, like a Suel, and I grew a long blonde beard. I was donned in heavy metal armour, and I swung a two-handed sword. I flew my dragon over great glaciers searching for something. Something important."
   "Getting interested now. What were you looking for?"
   "Gavron...my Gavron, I was looking for my own eye...my Ruby eye."
   "You were one eyed then?"
   Arik shook his head, "no. No. I had two eyes. Ordinary eyes. I was a Suel Warlord I think, yet I still felt like me. I told you that it was strange. Anyway, I scanned the glacier as I flew, and there... Half buried in the ice, I found it."
   Gavron leaned forward, " you found your Ruby eye?"
   Arik's face was clouded in red and blue.
   "Not just the eye, " said Arik, "I found my whole head." See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 205
   It had been a cool Summer, and some of the birds hadn't returned this year. 
   Gavron was wrapped up in a black cloak with a deep hood, making him look like a Black Monk. Gavron periodically went up to the surface to trade with the merchant caravans, and to gather information from his spies. 
   He didn't feel Vecna's gaze upon his back.
   Vecna wasn't interested in him, Gavron knew that. The Emperor had punished Gavron already when he had murdered Gavron's first family. Now Gavron was a walking warning, allowed to roam at will, as long as Vecna never spied his new family.
   Little Eggert and Gavron's wife stayed hidden under the Rakers.
   Gavron found the dead temple dilapidated, inhabited by a small group of indifferent worshippers. The local Black Monk had died a few years ago and he had yet to be replaced. The thickset Flan with their pyramid necklaces were actually friends of the rebels, forgotten by Vecna, if he had even ever bothered to know of their existence in the first place.
   Gavron conducted the service, including only the required catechisms. If any of the spies were double agents it would look like Gavron was an itinerant preacher in the way to somewhere more important.
   Deep in the night, Gavron met with his most trusted Flan, a loyal rebel who had been helpful in establishing an illicit trading network. Could they get Arik out of Oerik? 
   No. Dragonel riders patrolled the coast, and the pirate ships were mostly loyal to Vecna.
   What about South? Cross the Gearnat sea, enter the Azure sea, then sail into the Solnor sea from northern Hepmonaland?
   No. Sahuagin infest the Tilva Strait at the edge of Hepmonaland, and the Azure sea is filled with Vecna pirates too, all the way to Oeridia below the Suel Imperium.  And Arik is a marked man. If the former Lord were to poke his head out of his cave Vecna's Eye would see him.
   Gavron refused to give up. Any other way to Mystara?
   Always magic, of course, but Vecna's Hand would feel magic's touch. Teleporting to Mystara would alert his invisible stalkers.
   What about masking the magic?
   He didn't know of any way to do that...then he remembered a story he had once heard. Perhaps the great artifact to the west.
   An artifact?
   Huge rings of stone, near an enchanted lake. Created by a lost civilization and studied by the Baklundish. The story says that the stones are mirrors and portals to other worlds and places. 
   Gavron smiled. Yes. The stone circles called Tovag Baghru. He'd been there. They were real. The magic of Tovag Baghru was surely beyond the control of Vecna and his minions. Arik could use the stones to reach Silver Land in Mystara, or at least use the power of Tovag Baghru to find out why he seemed linked with the eastern continent.
   But there was still the problem of getting Lord Arik there. Tovag Baghru was over the Crystalmists, and the Crystalmists were right on the other side of the Empire. Gavron agreed that crossing the seas was too perilous, but surely the roads overland would be equally so. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 206
   "My Gavron, and do you really think that this will work?"
   Gavron shrugged, "well, lord Arik, it will work all right, but a thousand things could go wrong afterwards."
   Arik and Gavron were discussing Gavron's plan. Arik was intrigued, but highly concerned.
   "And what shall I do, if something goes wrong, Gavron? Stay as rigid as a statue?"
   Gavron laughed, "yes, because you will be a statue. Look, there is no safe way forward, unless we stay here, under the Rakers."
   Arik's Ruby eye flashed with annoyance, "no. No. I don't wish to stay here forever. But what happens if we do reach the magical stones? If I am a statue..."
   Gavron leaned forward on his stool, "the theory is that once we cross the Crystalmists, leave the Empire, Vecna won't be able to see you. Then you will be revived."
   "...and the stones take me into Mystara?"
   "Maybe, or at least give us an answer why Silver Land has such a pull on you."
   The Sapphire eye glowed faintly, "and you are sure that you can turn me completely to stone?"
   Gavron shrugged.
   "Don't ask me," he said, "ask the cockatrice."
                                 ******
      The statue was placed carefully into the crate. The caravan was enormous, the biggest merchant train in the Flanaess. Hundreds of merchants, soldiers, Ur Flan and priests with at least a score of oxen were about to cross the Empire. The caravan carried gold, gems, silver, weapons, food, cloth and who knew what else. Gavron was once more disguised as a Black Monk. Just another member of the caravan.
   Gavron sincerely hoped that his plan would work. Turning lord Arik into a statue should protect the half golem from Vecna's gaze. After all, a statue had no thoughts to detect. If that proved true, then the merchant train would take  Arik and Gavron all the way to the frost giant kingdoms of the Crystalmists.
                             *****
   The journey was slow going. Very safe, because which norker or bandit band would dare take on a caravan this size, armed to the teeth and under the protection of the Empire, but very slow, because oxen liked to plod. Gavron wasn't completely alone, because a couple of the merchants and a few of the guards were his spies, but he kept to himself most of the time. Gavron played the part of a Black Monk, intimidating, pious and completely uninteresting.
   The road followed the river. Wooden platforms became simple barges, and from time to time  a few merchants would peel off the caravan to take their goods over the water. The train was heading to the Rift Canyon. The Emperor was trying to establish settlements there, attempting to tame that wild broken land. The train was bringing in some much needed supplies.
                               *****
   The road narrowed into a gravely track. Here the caravan must needs to break up and divide, the oxen left with guards and the bulk, the Rift Canyon destined merchants carrying their wares with the help of half ogres. Gavron was inclined to stay with those remaining, and near the statue, but the dead priests and the other Black Monks were eager to find new followers and punish back sliders, so Gavron would become conspicuous if he didn't descend into the Rift.
   It was possible to wind down and down into the Rift Canyon if you studied your footing and walked single file. It was arduous and surprisingly warm. Steam shot out from vents, and occasional pools of still water smoked. 
   On a plateau, about three thousand feet down, was a stockade, a small trading station. Gavron could stretch again, and his vertigo settled. The priests made a beeline for the tiny dead temple and Gavron followed them.
                               *****
   Gavron was asleep in the main cave when one of his merchant spies roused him.
   "A problem," said the merchant, "I have been ordered to the Isles of Woe."
   "So? The lake is on the way."
   "I have to cross the lake. I have to bring the crate with the statue."
   "Why?"
   "One of the damned Rift Canyon merchants found out that that particular crate was empty but for the statue. I told you we should have filled it up."
   "And if we'd done that, how were we ever going to get him out without help?"
   "Well, the merchant commandeered the space for the Empire. He filled it up with weapons."
   "Weapons? Why?"
   "Don't know. They are to go to the Isles of Woe. We are going to have to cross the Lake of Unknown Depths and bring Arik to the prison islands." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 207
   While Gavron was descending down into the Rift Canyon, Vecna officials in black leather emblazoned with a leopard eye hiked up a tertiary path to the awaiting bulk of the merchant caravan.
   There were seven of them, accompanied by heavily armoured kodge. The officials systematically went through the wagons and crates, taking notes as they went.
   One official came across a group of three mountain dwur from the Rakers. The official bristled when he saw them.
   "Dwarves," he exclaimed, "why are you with the caravan?"
   The dwur explained that they were merchants bringing wares to the Crystalmists.
   "I can hardly understand you," complained the official, "your dwarf accent is too thick. Are you even speaking Flan? Do you know the common speech?"
   One of the dwur became flustered.
   The official nodded to a kodge. The kodge smiled sadistically, his snout curving upward, showing gleaming teeth. He drew a jagged sword, stepping forward.
                             *****
   Gavron returned to the caravan to find his dwur guides gone. They were going to help him negotiate the Crystalmists once he left the train. And behind Gavron came Rift merchants with the weapon consignment.  Gavron couldn't do anything without blowing his cover. The weapons were placed on top of the wrapped up statue of Arik, and Gavron noticed that they were crude, simple axes and swords, rudely made of pure iron. 
                               *****
   The merchant train went Southwest, then after a slow going week, a couple of barges were dropped into the Nyr Dyv, and Gavron accompanied the crates and merchants rowing towards the Isles of Woe. The Nyr Dyv, the Lake of Unknown Depths, was an impossibly deep blue lake created by the same magical calamity that had befallen the Rift Canyon. They weren't the only waterborne craft plying the dark water, for sailing boats, row boats and barges were commonly travelling across. If it wasn't for the occasional sea serpent or reptilian horror that emerged from the secret depths, the Nyr Dyv would be a beautiful place.
   Somewhere near the centre of the lake were two ugly islands, the Isles of Woe. The largest was where they were heading. Gavron hadn't been to the prison islands before, and he felt pale when they closed upon stark iron walls jutting up from a stony beach.
   The barges slid onto the beach, the crates unfastened and then taken through the great iron gates into Vecna's prison. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 208
   Behind the iron walls, pitted with rust, lay Vecna's prison.
   Squat, square blocks of stone, broken only by one iron door and a few tiny barred windows, sat upon either side of pebbled roads in long rows of despair. Who knew how many prisoners were housed in each block? Probably hundreds. Whole towns had disappeared over the decades of the Empire, the unlucky taken into the Isles of Woe.
   Gavron, a few merchants, a couple of priests, two oxen and the crate carrying the statue of Arik wound their way through the streets, squads of goblins and Flan soldiers checking their credentials every half mile. Black smoke issued from black chimneys, chained convict trains dug trenches or erected new prisons. Here and there were stalls selling drinks, food, clothes or armour to the guards or the goblins.
   Where was the final destination? Gavron saw that ahead, and slowly growing in size as they approached, was an iron and stone fortress. Another prison? As they reached the final hundred yards Gavron saw a yawning open portcullis with a number of well dressed people going in. On either side of the archway were a handful of Ur Flan and half ogres taking coins from those entering the fortress.
   What was going on?
   The merchant from the Rift Canyon suddenly clapped his calloused hands together with a loud slap. There was to be an Entertainment today!
   "Entertainment?" asked Gavron, as they approached an officious middle aged Ur Flan in  bear furs.
   The merchant stared at Gavron, a little nonplussed. 
   "Aren't you a Black Monk?"
   Gavron answered carefully, "I have not passed this way for many years. My flock is a little isolated from the larger world."
   "Oh, then you are going to be in for a real treat. The Entertainment..."
   He was cut off by the Ur Flan, "I know that voice." He pointed to the Black Monk, "Gavron, that's you in there, isn't it?"
   Gavron groaned inwardly. He had assumed that his Black Monk disguise was impervious. He hadn't thought that anyone would recognise his voice. Ah, but now he recognised the Ur Flan in turn. They had studied together when they were young. They had even been friends.
   Well, the quest was probably over now. Likely he was about to see inside one of the squat prisons.
   "You know each other?" The Rift Canyon merchants asked, "I wouldn't have thought an Ur Flan and a Black Monk shared the same circles."
   The Ur Flan pulled Gavron's hood back.
   "That's because Gavron is an Ur Flan like me,  he laughed, "Passing himself off as a Death priest indeed. You have always been as impious as they come."
   Gavron shook his head. One of the half ogres was looking at him now, his eyes slowly narrowing.
   "Oh, relax Gavron. I know all about you. I know about your falling out with the Emperor. There's nothing at all to worry about. You are a free man, Vecna's Mercy is renowned. In fact, I consider you to be my own personal guest of honour. This evening, you will sit at the Entertainment with me." 
                               *****
   The fortress was huge but open, consisting of wide halls lit with great fires, surrounded by people talking excitedly as they ate and drank. The merchants took the crate down into the dungeon with the help of half ogres. The weapon consignment was apparently needed there. Gavron didn't like being split up from Arik, but showing an interest in the crate would endanger his stone friend.
   He had gone with the Ur Flan into a smaller chamber three levels above the entrance. Here he could see that the central area of the fortress was open to the air, the open area a vast sand pit surrounded by metal rails. 
   "Prime position for us," said the Ur Flan, pointing down at the pit, "not like in the stalls."
   Around the pit were a series of wooden stickades making compartments.
   "That's where the guards and the commoners will watch. They have to crowd together in those little boxes. They get up nice and close to the action, but no overview."
   "And what is the entertainment exactly?"
   "Bloodsports. Prisoners against monsters. Monsters against monsters. Prisoners against prisoners."
   Gladiatorial competition? Is that all that the Entertainment was? Gavron had attended similar events throughout the Empire.
   "Not like these ones," said the Ur Flan, "you'll see. The Isle of Woe is a special place. The Entertainment is directed by non other than Lord Acererak himself." See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 209
   Below the arena, in the dungeon, kobolds pulled iron weapons out of a crate. They were scaly little creatures with dog-like snouts, rat tails and tiny blunt horns. They were supervised by a couple of enormous long eared bugbears. The kobolds jumped into the crate, coming out with weapons as big as they were, but crude, and roughly made. Other kobolds then took the axes and swords away, presumably for the gladiatorial games about to get underway.
   One of the kobolds noticed that below the weapons was a layer of cloth. Once all the weapons were removed he sneaked back to the crate and began to unwrap the cloth.
   Below the cloth, at the bottom of the crate was a large stone object...
                             *****
   Lord Acererak!
   Gavron hated that old lich. Acererak was a sadistic horror, a depraved undead monster. Gavron had encountered him before, and Acererak was why Gavron had become a rebel.
   Horn blasts.
   Gavron's old Ur Flan friend poked him in the ribs. The games were about to begin 
   Two squads of orcs entered the pit from opposite ends. They wore ring mail and were armed with spikes clubs. Within moments the orcs launched full frontal attacks.
   "The orcs have all divided into rival clans," explained the Ur Flan, "and they hate each other. Their hatred gets in the way of the smooth running of the Empire. Vecna is purging them from the Flanaess."
   Gavron nodded. More than a few orcs had joined the rebels, and their amniosity towards each other was a headache for him too.
  The orcs slaughtered each other, brutally and crudely. The caged spectators oohed and ahhed. Gavron wasn't the least bit impressed.
   "Oh, this is just the curtain raiser," said the Ur Flan, simple slaughter for the simpletons. Let's see what comes out next."
   What came out next were two dwarves, their  clothes ragged, their hands empty of weapons.
   Gavron recognised them from the merchant train. They had become prisoners!
   A steel gate rose up and a weird, hooting whistling screech echoed forth.
   Emerging into the arena was an eight foot tall bear shaped beast, covered in black fur and pale grey feathers. It leaped about upon its hind legs, it's front paws raking the air with jagged claws. It's head was squat and square with tiny, red eyes, and instead of a snout there protruded a grey, horned beak.
   "It's an owl bear!" cried the Ur Flan, full of enthusiasm, "a new creation of Vecna."
   The owl bear rushed the dwarves, who were slow to react due to their terror. The owl bear hooked a dwarf, then threw him into the air, catching him in its beak with a wet crunch. The second dwarf regained his senses, and found a discarded club from the orc fight. He drew it up, facing the enraged monster which now had blood dripping down its downy front.
   The dwarf fought like a dancer, his balance always centred, his movements efficient and effective. Gavron thought that the dwarf might have once been an elite soldier from the Sulhauats, a Hack master.
   Despite the owl bear weighing two tons, and despite it being faster and far larger than the diminutive dwur, it was the unarmoured, club wielding dwarf who won. The dwur climbed up onto the prone hulking back of the fallen beast, then turned and faced the upper row of spectators. He spied the dispassionate face of Lord Acererak and scowled.
   The dwur let forth a stream of expletives, vowing complete destruction.
   Acererak stared back, his eyes pale and indifferent. His expression on his skull -like face did not change, but he lurched up, all skin and bone, then clicked two gnarled fingers.
   The dwur rose up, off the sand, floating in the air 
   Lord Acererak snapped his fingers again. Gavron saw the poor dwarf writhe, squealing like a baby pig.
   The dwarf twisted about, every bone of his body cracking and snapping.
   Acererak released the dwur from his thrall, and the broken dwarf fell down to the sand, crumpled and lifeless.
   Acererak sank back into his seat.
   The crowd went wild.
   "See," yelled the Ur Flan over the noise, "this is what I was talking about. Acererak gets hands on. What a show!"
   Gavron was speechless. See less
