posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 210
   The kobold gathered some friends and soon they were dragging the stone statue towards the servant quarters.
   "What's going on?" boomed a deep voice.
   A bugbear overseer had caught them!
   "Let me look at that...it's a statue of Emperor Vecna, I am sure of it. Look at the eyes. What were you trying to do, scum, steal it for yourselves? Take it into my room you rats."
                                *****
   Gavron wondered what horrors were scheduled next.
   A gate opened and a band of warriors marched out. They wore scale and were armed with gleaming weapons of various types. Their hair was brown and auburn, and they grew out their hair and beards.
   "Suel?" wondered Gavron.
   "No, barbarians from the north east of Mystara. I rounded up some myself earlier this year. They call themselves Oorviks."
   The warriors spread themselves around the arena, confident expressions on their faces. Gavron noticed that they were all extremely muscular too. Perhaps these were elite fighters like the Sulhaut dwarves.
   But what would they face?
   A portcullis shrieked. A shadow crossed over the sand.
   The monster was ungainly, unbalanced, long, sinewy arms stretched out almost unnaturally. The legs were bent at an awkward angle, but its stride was wide. It was entirely naked, green and warty. Its nose was long, almost a trunk, and the only hair was a dense, seaweed like mass on the top of its head. The head was box-like and carried an enormous jaw.
   Of course, Gavron knew what the monster was.
   It was a troll.
   "Oh, this will be good," enthused the Ur Flan.
   Did the Oorvik warriors have trolls where they came from? They were sizing up the nine foot troll as if they had its measure.
   Obviously, they didn't.
   The crowd in the wooden cages cheered as the Oorviks went to work, slicing off troll limbs, skewering it with deadly tridents and wrapping it in wiry nets. Within minutes the troll was massacred. The fighters, beading with sweat, bowed to Acererak.
   Oh no, thought Gavron.
   The pulpy mess that was once a troll began to twitch and writhe.
   The nets were torn asunder, arms and legs crawled across the sand, reknitting themselves to the torso.
   The head rolled about until it found its neck. 
   And at last the Oorviks sensed the danger.
   The troll was regenerating.
   It staggered back to its feet, raging in fury, reaching out at its foes with terrible claws.
   The warriors weapons could bring the troll down, but they couldn't stop it. 
   The Ur Flan was laughing. He could see that the eastern barbarians were tiring, and soon the blood and limbs scattered about the arena were not going to be troll.
   The Oorviks looked for an escape route. They threw themselves against the metal rails, but lightning cracked and threw them back.
   They cried out in an alien language. The people in the cages jeered.
   And then it was over. The troll had killed them all.
   "Why is this entertaining?" asked Gavron to his former friend, "it was no contest. Without fire they had no chance."
   The Ur Flan scoffed, "the way they were killed was the entertaining part."
   Gavron felt a gaze fall upon him.
   Lord Acererak's face had turned slightly in his direction, the eyes of the lich the colour of rancid milk.
   Had the lord noticed him?
   There were a couple more contests, less one sided, and Gavron fervently hoped that the tournament would soon be over.
   Lord Acererak was on his feet, gesticulating to a Black Monk.  The Black Monk went down into the fortress, emerging at last in the arena.
   "Friends," he intoned, looking out at the crowd, his voice magically enhanced, "I am afraid that your enthusiasm tonight was underwhelming. Lord Acererak worked extremely hard to deliver an extravaganza, and the poor entertainers spilt their own precious blood for your pleasure. Yet, our Lord noticed grimaces from some of you. Were the deaths not to your liking? Did they not meet your exacting expectations?"
  The Black Monk looked around at the wooden boxes. 
   "Three of the boxes will receive a special prize. Please, everyone remain seated until the prizes are given."
   Murmuring echoed around the arena. What was the prize?
   Acererak stood up once more.
   In his bony arms he held a large sack.
   He emptied the sack, and with a clatter, a pile of weapons fell out.
   Acererak raised a finger. The weapons shot up into the air, then soared across the arena.
   Gavron recognised the weapons. They were crude, basic iron swords and axes. The weapons from his crate. Is this what they had been brought for?  To fly around the arena?
   Then Acererak spoke, a broken, harsh croak.
   "Box four. Seven. Eight."
   The swords and axes glided into three of the boxes, the people inside suddenly shrieking in terror.
   This was the prize.
   Gavron closed his eyes and covered his ears, but he could hear the voice of Acererak over the screams.
   "Die, filthy beasts." See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 211
   A table full of luscious fruits, wine, mead and meats was laid out for the upper class spectators.  Gavron barely even looked at the food but his former friend set to hungrily.
   "You are an odd bird, aren't you Gavron?" said the Ur Flan peeling the skin off a spiky fruit, "you had more talent in your little finger than I ever had, you rose up the ranks like lightning, and yet you are a self proclaimed rebel. And now, safe and well in the heart of the Empire, you still refuse any enjoyment?"
   The Isles of Woe the heart of the Empire? Did the Ur Flan hear himself? The more Gavron looked around the more convinced he was that he had chosen the more difficult, but better path. His boy, Eggert deserved more than blood sports and oppression.
   The Ur Flan waited for Gavron to give an answer. When he didn't, he turned back to his fruit.
   "Do you think that Lord Acererak saw me?" asked Gavron.
   The Ur Flan looked up.
   "Of course he did," he answered, "Acererak isn't an old fool...you aren't exactly anonymous. You dress like a Black Monk but your body language is all you."
   "Then, I am in danger..."
   The Ur Flan slurped up the flesh of the fruit.
   "Gods...!" he snapped, "you worry about everything. No, you aren't in any danger. You aren't important enough. You received mercy, remember? I told you, enjoy all of this! You don't have to hide in a cave with lord Arik."
   Gavron was surprised, "you know that I associate with Arik?"
   "We know that you hang around the Rakers, and we know that Arik hides under there. It's pretty obvious you two associate together. Now, if danger is a concern for you, I would suggest leaving off Arik. Arik is a marked man. You don't want to end up as collateral."
   Gavron didn't want to be here any longer,  He had to get his crate back and leave the Isles of Woe.
   The Ur Flan promised to help Gavron retrieve it. After supper of course.
                                *****
   Lompy seethed. The problem with being a three foot kobold is that the mind was filled with hate and vengeance but the body could be knocked out by a halfling. 
   The Vecna idol had been taken from him. Stolen by the bugbears! Lompy wanted to suck on their bones! 
   Footfalls. Heavy footfalls. 
   If Lompy's mind hadn't been so filled with revenge fantasies he would have heard them sooner, and then he would have raised the alarm.
   It was too late now.
   Gavron, the Ur Flan and four half ogres stormed up to the entranceway of the kobold area.
   "Where is the crate?" asked the Ur Flan to the shaking kobold.
   "The weapons were delivered," answered Lompy.
   "Not the damned weapons, the crate," demanded Gavron.
   "I can give back the crate if you like," said Lompy.
                             *****
   The crate was empty.
    "There was a statue in here," growled Gavron, "where have you taken it?"
   "The bugbears," answered Lompy, "the bugbears stole the Vecna statue."
                                  ****
   Grok was happy because the shaman was happy.
   The shaman was never happy, but now he was.
   The Vecna idol was the most beautiful object that he had ever seen.
   Vecna looked down upon the bugbear faithful.
   Grok was glad that he had found it. The power of Vecna would make his tribe great.
   The shaman was grinning as he performed the blood ritual.
   And the shaman never grinned.
   The energy blast blew Grok into three pieces.
   The shaman stopped grinning. 
   A Black Monk, hands shrouded in fire, led an Ur Flan and several ogre men into the sacred place.
   "That is my statue!" roared the Black Monk.
   The shaman cursed. He should have known that stupid Grok had stolen the sacred gift from a Black Monk.
   "Don't kill me, master!" he begged, "it's not mine. Please, you can have it." See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 216
   Wild horses everywhere.
   The half ogres had heard about them, but had never seen them. And now the galloping beasts were running through the grassland. 
   Like centaurs, the half ogres thought, but instead of human upper bodies, their thick necks formed into monstrous heads with huge nostrils and black manes..
   The half ogres dropped the crate containing the statue, the statue they had dragged across the Crystalmists. They drew out grim morning stars.
   'Watch them run," said Gavron, "but don't be alarmed. These creatures eat the grass. The Wildmen sometimes jump onto their backs and ride them."
                            ******
   Several days later, the expedition found out that Gavron was right. 
   Baklundish in billowing robes were on the backs of the terrifying horses, and they fired arrows at the half ogres.
  With a look, Gavron blasted the arrows into splinters. He strode forward, his black cloak incongruous to the semi-arid terrain. 
   "We seek out the Seer of Tovag Baghru," he said, with steel.
                                ******
   Fishing villages were dotted all around Lake Underkakar. Little trading markets were also close to Tovag Baragu itself, or Tovag Baghru as it was now called. The grey stone slabs arranged into circles were impressive, looking alien and forbidding. 
   The party couldn't just enter. To enter Tovag Baghru without the blessing of the Seer would invite chaos and madness. They must enter the cave and await her summons. Gavron had only just begun down the steps when a small girl, perhaps nine years old with white pupiless eyes appeared at his side.
   "I see you," said the blind seer, "you are important. We must look at the stones together."
                                ******
   The vast stones were as smooth as mirrors.
   The half ogres put down the crate, opened it, then pulled out the statue 
   This strange statue of Vecna, with one eye of Ruby and one eye of Sapphire. None of the half ogres, hailing from the distant Griff mountains North of the Rakers, had ever met or seen Vecna, but something about this statue disturbed them. It was as if it had an aura mocking them, a spirit inside of it.
   A malicious ghost.
   Gavron went up to the statue, examing it carefully. No damage that he could see. Good. He was half amazed that the scheme had actually worked. Here they were, outside of Vecna's influence, surrounded by the magical stones of Tovag Baghru. Now, Gavron must return the statue of Arik to life and probably slay the half ogres.
   He pulled out a scroll, unfurled it, jogging his memory. He didn't want to get the spell wrong.
   "My Gavron."
   Gavron looked up, startled. Arik was smiling down at him.
   "But, how...?"
   The seer laughed, "The stones knew who he was! No one can deceive Tovag Baghru."
   Gavron frowned, then looked back at Arik. Arik looked a little confused, as did the half ogres, Gavron noted.
   Well, he was confused too.
   "How do you feel?" he asked Arik.
     Lord Arik thought a moment.
   "Like I just awoke from oblivion." And his Sapphire eye shone like a blue sun. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 217
   The half ogres, over seven feet tall and built like wrestlers, staggered back from the Vecna statue come to life.
   Was this Vecna?
   No. Gavron called him 'Arik.' 
   Arik? Could this be lord Arik, the Traitor?
   The half ogres turned to each other. One pulled out his morning star.
   Yes. Yes. They had been betrayed. Tricked! The false Gavron and the false Vecna would feel ogre might!
   Then the seer was beside them. The tiny human girl with clouded eyes.
   She smiled. "Look around you, see the stones? What do they show you?"
   The stone nearest the half ogres gleamed as bright as a sun.
   What they saw there...
   Tears ran down their faces. 
   "Can we touch the stone, miss?" asked one.
   The seer clapped with joy, "of course you can. Touch the stone! Feel it's warmth."
   The first half ogre pressed his palm to the stone. It went through.
   Oh!
   The seer nodded, "Yes. Your dreams are about to come true. Go into the stone. Live out your life in joy."
   One by one, the half ogres entered the mirrored stone. Then they were gone.
   Gavron frowned. He hadn't seen anything.
   "Did you see..."
   Arik nodded, and he looked a little shaken. He did see. His Ruby eye saw everything.
   "Then, what did they see...?"
   Arik shook his head. Some things had to remain private.
   The seer looked at the two of them with sightless eyes.
   Lord Arik," she said, "you have come all this way to discover yourself. You have been rebuilt in the Empire of Glantri, and you feel the pull of Mystara. Which stone do you choose?"
   Arik looked about. "That one " he pointed.
   "Gaze upon the mirror, lord Arik. What do you see?"
   Arik saw a blonde,bearded man riding a white dragon. The dragon looked old, with tarnished scales, and it's expression was of one resigned to its fate.
   Where had he seen that man before?
   The man turned, and he looked out of the mirrored stone, seemingly staring at Arik.
   The man's face crumpled into an angry visage.
   "Ariksbane!" he cried, "we have found him. It is the evil god himself!"
 The white dragon's head whirled around in rage. It gulped down air, then breathed...
   Arik's Ruby eye blazed fire.
   The frost breath struck the fire and was vaporised. 
   "Enough," said the seer, and the image of the man and the dragon vanished.
   Arik was shaking in anger. Somehow, he felt that he had just fought his nemesis, yet he had never seen the man before, except for once in a dream.
   "Lord Arik, you are in no danger now. The stone is closed."
   "Why did you show me this, this man?"
   The seer shrugged, " I showed you nothing. I am not the stones."
   Arik turned to Gavron, who was watching silently, "Gavron, we came here for nothing..."
   "No," said the seer, "you are simple. You are made up of Mystaran magic. Your eyes ache for the Silver Mountains, your metal body was forged in Glantri, you conquered the elves there, and you believe you own the right to rule them. You are no mystery lord Arik."
   Lord Arik was bathed in red light. He felt humiliated somehow, as if his soul had just been slighted.
   The seer stepped back from Arik, then she felt for Gavron with a probing hand.
   "Now you, my Gavron," she murmured, "you are far more interesting. What stone do you seek?" See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 218
   This dragonel was different.
   It was larger, and its scales were deep blue. Its wings were dark grey striped with blood red  fringes. And  the rider was wreathed in black, his face as pale as a skull.
   Could the rider be a Lich lord?
   Could he even be Vecna?
   The White Baron became afraid. 
   The dragonel didn't seem particularly bothered about her either. The other dragonels had balked and turned about when she appeared. 
   They were no match for the sparkling, gleaming white dragon of the lower Crystalmists, and they knew it 
   Watch them flee from her wrath.
   Watch them bathed in her frost 
   See them fall as ice.
   Not this dragonel.
   The White Baron had soared into view, spraying out a mist of liquid nitrogen, but the huge dragonel had lazily flapped its wings twice, then ducked down below the freezing vapour before riding up again behind her.
   Did she hear a rattling chuckle?
   The White Baron tried to spin around, but as she fought the air stream there was a crackle and she felt a hot stabbing pain radiating across her thigh.
   Her head swiveled, and as she rolled the gloating lich lord struck again; this time she saw the flash accompanying the crackle.
   He was throwing lightning bolts at her!
   The White Baron became very afraid. 
   She hated lightning! Lightning couldn't be hit back!
   And now she was too afraid to draw breath.
   The dragonel was after her, and the monster and its rider was a Storm.
   The White Baron needed help.
   Where was Gavron?
                               ******
   What stone should he choose?
   Gavron didn't like the way things were playing out. The seer, the young girl, looked up into his face with her useless eyes, smiling in anticipation. She was flushed, and she suppressed a giggle.
   Gavron looked at the forbidding stones around him. 
   "That one?" he asked.
   The seer frowned momentarily when she turned to the stone.Had she seen something there?
   "That one?" repeated the seer, "Yes. That one."
   Gavron went up to the smooth grey stone, twice as tall as himself. His merchant spies watched on. They had been silent since coming to Tovag Baghru, too afraid to draw any attention to themselves. Arik too, was quiet, his Ruby eye flickering, and now his Sapphire eye had begun to glow. 
   Gavron looked at the stone.
   Into the stone 
   His face turned white.
                              ******
   Deep within a temple built into the Yatil mountains was the imprisoned god, Tharizdun.
   His mind has become dull.
   His probing mists could no longer penetrate.
   He slept in his Black Cyst, worshipped by his adoring acolytes.
   He should be angry. Angry at himself for being lured into this cell of nothing.
   Angry at those that tricked him.
   Angry at his useless priests who kept him here.
   But he wasn't.
   Wasn't angry. Not really.
   A little perturbed, perhaps.
   After all, nothing was his goal.
   His goal was to be nothing.
   Tharizdun slumbered on.
    His misty visage sat within the Black Cyst like a heavy cloud.
   His extremities prickled. Coils of fog withdrew from the edges of his cell and Tharizdun suddenly felt cold. Somehow, he felt disturbed, though no one was here. Who was watching him?
   Tharizdun awoke.
   The Anger came. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 219
   Gavron gazed into the eyes of a man he had never met, yet he seemed to resemble...
... himself.
   Those eyes. The nose. The chin. The mouth...
   ...but how stern his expression, and he was taller and wider, a little chubby in fact, and his cheeks were almost muscular.
   The man looked back at Gavron through the stone mirror with disapproval.He wore a hat, black, round and broad, his tunic was brown and his leggings were the colour of straw. His boots were polished and black.
   "Do you know what you have done?" asked the man in a peculiar accent, "you have interfered with the nexus, you fool."
                            ******
   Tharizdun curled and coiled within the Black Cyst.
   There was a tall man suddenly beside him.
   A large, fat man wearing a broad black hat.
   "THIS IS MY REALM," said the mists of Tharizdun, "I WILL DISSOLVE YOU INTO NOTHINGNESS ITSELF."
   The middle aged man shook his red head. He produced a large, gnarly club.
   "Foul wretch of despair, it is I, Cuthbert of the cudgel who will end you once and for all!"
   Tharizdun snaked out a cloud of tentacles questing to wrap around and crush Cuthbert's chest. 
   Cuthbert did not flinch. He knew that the mist demon could not find any gap in his devout aura. His faith was unshakable, his goodness divine.
   A host of tentacles washed over Cuthbert, as harmless as a cloud of water vapour.
   Cuthbert's cudgel glowed with the holy fires of Heaven. It was time to smite this devil into oblivion, and to rid Oerth of the dark pestilence of this relic from the Dragon Age...
... But he was expunged from his task...
...and stared into the face of a fool.
                            *****
    Gavron went white.
   Somehow, he felt that he had interfered with the future.
   This man in the stone...Gavron suddenly he knew who he was.
   The Greatest of his Line.
   His Descendent.
   A Saint.
   "You recognise him," cried the seer, "yes, you do!"
   The image in the stone roared in rage, "Close the portal. Return me to my quest."
   Gavron looked to the seer. How was he to do it? The stone continued to project the image of the angry man, 
   This wasn't even his fault. It was the seer. 
   He closed his eyes.
   Opened them again.
   The angry man remained.
    "Release me!" he snarled.
   Gavron grabbed the seer, "you told me to look into the stone. Fix this!"
   The seer wriggled herself free from Gavron's grip, "there is nothing to fix," said the seer, "the stones choose what they choose."
   A gaseous cloud billowed up behind the man in the stone.
                              *****
   Tharizdun had struck at Cuthbert with a force that could break worlds.
   But he had sloughed off him like butter.
   And now the man was distracted, caught within two realities.
   Tharizdun felt Cuthbert's confusion.
   Tasted it on his tendrils.
   Tharizdun would strike again... 
                            ****
      Gavron ran to the stone and grabbed for his future descendent, but the stone was hard and rough, and his hands wouldn't pass through.
   The man fell, completely engulfed in violet and puce gas and cloud.
   The stone glowed purple.
                            *****  
   Arik picked up Gavron from the base of the stone. Weren't the stones portals to other times and places? What did it matter if they watched a man be absorbed into mist? Wasn't this a problem for the future? 
   Then he saw the seer.
   She was watching the glowing purple stone, and her white eyes were wide and her jaws were clenched.
                             ***** 
   Tharizdun turned Cuthbert's body to bleach.
   Where was the gap in reality?
   There.
   Could he reach through it?
   Yes!
                                 *****
   The seer began to mumble a prayer. She ran the words around her mouth, over and over, faster and faster.
   The stones are wise.
   The stones are wise.
   The stones are wise.
                           *****
   Had it been forgotten that the stones were made by Tharizdun?
   That the seer was his instrument?
   That Gavron was the key to Tharizdun's release at the moment of his own demise?
   Gavron the Ancestor. Cuthbert the Descendent.
   Time and Space collapsed within the Black Cyst.
   Tharizdun was free!
                         ******  
   Tentacles began to issue forth from out of the stone. Tentacles of aching cold. Slowly but surely they began to pull Tharizdun's enormous mass through...
   Red bolts flashed from Arik's Ruby eye, striking the tendrils, but they singed into smoke.
   Tharizdun would not be denied.
                        ******
   The White Baron hurtled across the sky.
   Where was Gavron?
   Gavron was an Ur Flan of the Empire.
   He would sort out the dragonel.
   The White Baron soared high above the stone circles called Tovag Baghru.
   That's right. Gavron wanted to visit the stones. Was he there?
   Yes! There he was, Gavron!
   The White Baron plunged down.
                                 *****
   The white dragon crashed into a stone, bouncing off and landing in the dirt. Her left flank was scorched and burned.
   "Gavron!" she cried, "a bad dragonel is coming."
   Tharizdun began to billow forth.
   Then, cautious but determined, the great dragonel rider came down from the sky. His sources were right, Gavron had smuggled the traitor Arik to the stones. The lich would finish the dragon, then Arik would die.
                         ******     
   Arik saw the dragonel, saw the lich. 
   The violet mist was roiling through the stone. He couldn't stop it.
   He blasted his red death at the dragonel 
                                  ****
   The lich laughed as he deflected the rays. Did Arik not think that he would be prepared for his Ruby eye?
  Below his dragonel, a strange mist was leaking out of one of the standing stones. What was the traitor Arik up to? He conjured a lightning bolt and hurled it at the half golem.
                          *******
   The bolt threw Arik backwards into the mist 
   The mist paused, then seeped over its new prey.
   Gavron ran to Arik, but the cold was too intense. He fell back, frost biting his lips.
                        *****
   The dragonel landed gently,  feet away from the struggling Arik. Interesting, thought the lich, whatever weapon Arik and the rebels had devised, it was now working against them. He dismounted, raising up a long, black sword. He would cut off Arik's head and return it to Vecna.
   Why did his hair prickle?
   The white dragon was staring at him.
   She began to breathe...
   The lich dived to the side.
   The White Baron's frost breath passed across him, and struck the violet stone.
                       *******  
   Tharizdun's bulk remained in the Black Cyst, only his extremities had touched a new world. Already he was bringing Death. He was the Cold of the Void. He was the Absence of Life.
   He felt the portal around him freeze. The stones were ghosts, and soon the Universe would be dead dust.
   A tremendous blow threw him back from the stone. 
   The stone had frozen solid.
   He could no longer get through.
   He had lost his prey.
   He was still in the Black Cyst.
   He could hear his idiot priests praying.
                       *******
   The stone had frozen solid, unable to take the cold on both sides.
   Arik climbed to his feet. He had been rebuilt well. He was still alive. He watched the fight around him as if it were a dream. Gavron struck down the lich with eldritch fire as the white dragon tore out the dragonel's throat.
   He held onto the stone to help his balance.
   The stone shattered into pieces of ice. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 2:
Golden Age 
Part 220
   The stones of Tovag Baghru were one stone less.
   The seer sat crumpled up beside the shattered shards of the broken stone.
   The Stones are Wise.
   The Stones are Wise.
   But why did this happen?
   Once upon a time, the seer was an ordinary Baklundish girl who could not see.
   The priests of Tovag Baghru rose her up.
   Now she could see Everything.
   She had been wrong.
                          ******
   Gavron limped from a sword slash. The White Baron had wounds on her thigh and her flank where the vicious hooks of the dragonel had prised off scales.
   The band had gathered together on the shore of the lake a few miles from cursed Tovag Baghru. The merchant rebels had gone into a village and brought back healing balms and fresh fish.
   The White Baron kept looking at Arik. She was puzzled. Where had he come from?
   "What do we do now?" asked Arik, his Sapphire eye glowing a dim blue.
   Gavron shook his head. He didn't know. He longed to return to his family under the Rakers, but how to go back with lord Arik? 
   Vecna would hunt Arik forever. The dragonel riders would not give up. 
   "Gavron. Come live with me in the lower Crystalmists," said the White Baron, "I will keep you safe within my secret lair."
   Gavron smiled. The vain white dragon had genuinely bonded with him. 
   "No," he said gently, "I must go back to my family." And he thought of little Eggert. That man in the stone... was Eggert his father? Grandfather? Even more distant...?
   "I want to go back to the lower Crystalmists."
   "White Baron," murmured Gavron, "you have done me a great service. Return to the lower Crystalmists with my blessing and await my reward."
   The White Baron licked her lips with a white tongue. What reward?
   "I will send you a wagon of gems from  the Rakers once I return."
                            *****
   Gavron, Arik and the two merchants watched the spectacularly white dragon fly off back to her home in the frigid mountains.
   "You must start your own journey home," said Arik, "and you must go without me."
   "What about you, lord Arik? What will you do?"
   Arik's metal arm squeaked as he rolled a shoulder, "I will make my way to Mystara. Fulfill my destiny."
   "How? We thought that Tovag Baghru would take you there, but we were wrong."
   Arik pointed below his feet.
   "I shall travel through the Underdark. The dwarves of the Rakers think that under Oerik is a honeycomb network  of tunnels and passages stretching across the continent."
   "Are they right?"
   "I don't know."
   Gavron thought for a moment, "I seem to remember stories about the Underdark when I was a child. Below the ordinary caves are great sinkholes that lead into caverns of fungi and light. And... weren't there tales about evil elves...Drow, who feast upon the wicked and worship a demon spider?"
   Arik laughed, but his Ruby eye flashed red, "children's stories! There are no Drow! In any case, my Gavron, I do intend on travelling through the Underdark, if it exists. And, if there are indeed Drow, I will live among them for a while, then, when we next meet, I will tell you all about them."
   And the sun came up through the clouds, and the water of the lake glowed with golden light.
                   The End of Book 2 See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3
Broken Empires 
Part 1
The Gladiator 
1619 SD
   Gruthert looked at the sad, old face  looking back at him in the mirror.
   The eyes were sunken, washed out.
   The skin was fat and puffy. One cheek was puffy, swollen and grey.
   The nose had been broken so many times that it didn't know whether to lean up, down or sideways.
   The jaw was imposing though, and the wooden teeth had been expertly crafted.
   The hair on the head was fuzzy, faintly red, and thin.
   Gruthert was looking at the face of a champion.
                             *****
   Gruthert had a couple of beautiful courtesans that helped to dress him. The perks of being a hero of the arena. They coddled him after every battle, even after those two fights where he had come off second best. Gruthert was sure that they loved him  They were dressing him now, washing and drying his coppery skin, placing polished bracers around his arms.
   Who was he fighting today? That ogre again? Gruthert smiled. He had shown mercy last time. It suited the narrative. Unexpected grace kept the fans on their toes. Probably best to take off his head this time, though. 
                               ******
   Gruthert took the wine. He fought better when he was glowing. How long did he have until the bout? Another thirty minutes. The curtain raiser was in full swing. He could hear it from here. Sandow and Cuthop were pretty entertaining and athletic, and they always despatched the orc horde with panache. 
   Those were the days! Easy battles, good versus evil. No complications. Gruthert had been too good, the strongest in his family. He was technically a slave like his dead father, Eggert, and his brothers and sisters. Gruthert had lived in the Isles of Woe for most of his life. His childhood had been horrible, but he had lasted. The only brother left.
   He was lucky that the Arena lord had seen something in that young, dour boy who was already developing a barrel chest. He hadn't been taken to Acererak's pit where his death was guaranteed. 
   Gruthert was made to be a Gladiator.
   Not a Sacrifice.
                               *****
   One courtesan affixed his white cape while the other dusted him down with white, numbing powder. Gruthert raised his right arm. His enormous spiked club was thrust into his meaty hand.
   Now he stood still as his mask was attached to his face. The leering gold and black mask that made him The Righteous Mauler.
   The battle in the arena was coming to an end. Most of the orcs had stopped squealing.
   In a few minutes it would be the Righteous Mauler that entered the sand.
   Oh, how the crowd would roar. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3
Broken Empires 
Part 2
Dark Desires 
1632 SD
   Bathed in pink and violet light emanating from gem-sized fungi embedded in the upper vault of the cavern, lord Arik and Lolth lay together, sprawled out and naked.
   Arik was more metal than man, silvery purple in the light, and Lolth was sleek and beautiful, her slate blue skin appearing pink and shadowed under the cavern roof. Both were asleep, Arik whirring with snores, Lolth breathing silently.
   Lolth woke up. Her drow eyes were bright violet,  and her slender  fingers reached out to pull away a strand of cobwebby white hair from off her face.
   She rested her chin on Arik's metal chest. Lolth was so glad that the half golem had entered her Underdark world. The male Drow were boring, unimaginative creatures, barely worth half a woman, yet Lolth felt no desire for the females, bright and strong as they were.
   This strange tin man! One eye was Ruby and the other Sapphire. What would happen if lovely Lolth plucked out his eyes?
   Would Arik still love her?
   Lolth gave Arik a gentle cuddle.
   He began to stir.
   A wicked idea came over Lolth then. She knew that Arik found her stunningly beautiful. Is that why he loved her back?
   As Arik's eyes began to flicker, Lolth transformed...
   Arik awoke to find himself squashed below an enormous, black, bulbous, thin-legged spider with a Drow head.
   "My Lolth," Arik murmured, looking at the demonic monster square in her distorted face, and his Sapphire eye burned blue with desire. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 3
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (1)
1659 SD
   The City of the Gods was real.
   Everyone knew it, but no one had ever actually seen it.
   Some said it was hidden within the Burneal forest.
   Others said it was sitting on a glacier in the Land of White. 
   Then, perhaps the City of the Gods was so far north that you could never reach it.
   Or that the City was alive.
   Capricious. 
   Always somewhere.
   But never where you were.
   All were in agreement though;
   The City of the Gods was real.
                             *****
   Snow Flower was in trouble.  What was she going to do?
   Three days ago she was walking on air. She had come to town with a real swagger, and why not?
   Snow Flower had robbed the bandit camp of their gold 
   They never saw her coming.
   They never saw her going.
   Her furry feet walked quieter than a whisper. And they were foreigners in a strange land.
   They didn't know Blackmoor.
   If they did, they wouldn't have posted just four guards.
   Snow Flower supposed that they had wandered unknowingly into the most dangerous land of the Empire. 
   If you wanted to survive in Blackmoor, you had to find at least one particular skill and excel at it.
   Snow Flower chose Stealth.
   Yes, Snow Flower was the master of Stealth.
   She was a little over three feet tall, a little big boned for a halfling, her skin faintly green from some distant goblin ancestry, but when she was working she had a way of melting into nothingness, neither seen nor heard.
   Snow Flower could only imagine the commotion in that camp when they all woke up in the morning. She imagined, because she was long gone by then.
   Yes, Snow Flower was floating on air, her magically capacious bags filled with precious gold.
   Now she could pay back Clever Speck.
   Snow Flower owed a lot of money to Clever Speck. 
   Clever Speck was the Shirrif of the town, a four foot tall halfling who walked about with a trained winter wolf twice his size. He had been very generous to Snow Flower, recognising her talents and rewarding her with loans and gifts.
   Loans and gifts she was expected to pay back.
   Blackmoor was a very dangerous place.
   It had taken time to master Stealth, and in that time she had had failures, and those failures saw her debts rise. 
   Clever Speck was running out of patience. He was tired of supporting thieves that didn't pay their way. He became threatening.
   Snow Flower left town, determined to score something valuable or die in the attempt.
   Guess what? She was back!
   Clever Speck wasn't home though. He had gone on some kind of expedition with a band of Ur Flan, and he wasn't expected back for a couple of weeks.
   That suited Snow Flower nicely. She could enjoy some of the gold, and still have more than enough, and this way she wouldn't have to hide any, because Clever Speck was surely going to take it all.
   Unfortunately, Blackmoor was a very dangerous place.
   Norebo, the gambling god, was not enamoured with Snow Flower.
  She wasn't sure how it happened, but within three days she had lost it all!
   Snow Flower was back with nothing, and the rumours were already circling.
   Clever Speck had abandoned the Ur Flan after some disagreement, and he was already on the way back.
   Travellers who had passed him on the road said that they had never seen him so angry.
   Snow Flower was in trouble.
   She had been lucky with the bandits and she was unlikely to be so lucky again. Most denizens of Blackmoor were tougher and smarter, and most didn't run around with large caches of gold.
   A gnome in the tavern, dressed in bright colours that went well with his bright red face, bought her a drink in commiseration.
  The hand that reached into his pocket to pull out the bronze piece had fingers decorated with bejewelled rings.
   "Don't even think about it," he snapped, "my rings will know if they have been stolen, and they bite."
   He spread out his hand so that Snow Flower could admire the gems.
   The workmanship was like nothing that she had seen before.
   "I am not surprised," said the gnome, "I bought them at the City of the Gods." See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 4
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (2)
   The gnome was planning to return to the City of the Gods. Did Snow Flower wish to accompany him?
   "But how do you get there?" asked Snow Flower, "how do you find the way?"
   The gnome looked at her sternly, "There is only one way, no other. You have to walk through the Burneal forest, and you must avoid the traps set by the guardian, for the City of the Gods is protected."
   "How did you find the path?"
   "Me?" said the gnome, "Why, I was born there."
                          *****
   Snow Flower couldn't help but think about the rings on the gnome's fingers. She had studied them while he held his soup. The gems were definitely real, and the metal was gold. The gnome was wearing nine. Snow Flower wasn't greedy. She didn't plan to steal them all.
   Three. Only three of the rings would be enough to scotch her debt.
   They had entered the dark green firs of the Burneal, and the trees towered over them like monuments crafted by giant fairies. Light snow covered the ground.
   Everything was green, brown or white.
   Or black. A few yards away, Snow Flower spotted a line of little black mushrooms.
   "I am glad that you noticed them," said the gnome brightly, "they are the first and most dangerous trap. You must not cross the path of the black mushrooms, or you will never reach the City of the Gods."
                            *****
   Yes.
   The gnome was asleep. 
   She had four hours before he awoke and resumed the watch. Then she could sleep.
   It was pitch black, for the gnome had warned against starting a fire.
  How many monsters did she wish to attract?
   Snow Flower was wasn't cold for she sat next to a pouch of warm air that the gnome had conjured. He knew a little magic, he had said.
   She was warm, but she still couldn't see.
   The forest was still, but strange cries erupted out of nowhere, and once she heard snarling and spitting somewhere in the dark that sounded like a fight between two giant cats.
   And sometimes yellow, blue or red eyes peered out from the blackness.
   Snow Flower was reconsidering her journey to the City of the Gods. She was only a day away from places that she knew well, and she felt uncomfortable in the forest.
   Only three rings.
   That was all she would steal. Then she would sneak away and return to town.
   The gnome was snoring gently. With clever fingers, Snow Flower reached out very slowly and very carefully...
   The rings seemed loose, as if they were too large for the fingers. Good. Then they would slip of easily.
   The first ring did not. She had coated the band with oil, so it should slide off quietly and quickly. 
   It didn't.
   The halfling thief pulled, gently but firmly. If the gnome woke up she planned to dart away so quickly that he would never even seen her.
   Ah! One ring gone.
   She faintly remembered a warning the gnome had made, that the rings would bite her.
   Well, that was a made up bit of nonsense.
   Now she had two rings in her pouch.
   Make that three.
   Great!  Time to make herself scarce.
    The gnome was still sleeping beside his own bag of warm air, breathing in the fragrance of pine, as Snow Flower stole into the shadows of the forest, and was gone. See less

posts.title: Golden Age
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Golden Age 
Part 5
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (3)
   Snow Flower slipped through the dark. Although she could only see shades of black, she moved swiftly and silently on her furry feet,  using her prenatural senses, and allowing her small size to push easily through the great trees. All in all, she was quite pleased with herself. Stealing the rings had been a good idea, and they would surely satisfy Clever Speck, at least for a while.
   Now, she must navigate herself and return south as quickly as possible.
   Then, a strange thought came over her. Was the gnome wearing a pyramid necklace?
   The symbol of the pyramid was common place in Blackmoor, and every Ur Flan or personage of some distinction wore the pyramid of the Dread gods, Nerull, Incabulos and Tharizdun. Clever Speck wore a pyramid necklace for instance.
   But Snow Flower had never seen a gnome wear one.
    Snow Flower made a wide circle around the sleeping gnome, and looked for the path back, but the moons were behind the clouds, and she couldn't find it.
   Behind her she heard a loud cry, starting high pitched, but ending with a roaring bass.
   The gnome had woken up.
   And he must have realised what Snow Flower had done.
   Snow Flower became desperate. The ground here was thick with thorny shrubs, and it slowed her down.
   Where was the damn path?
   A flash of light.
   The gnome had lit a torch.
   He was coming for her.
   The faint light actually helped her, the ground now lighter grey. She hopped about until her feet were clear of the thorns, then found herself on a bed of flowers. She looked around once again for the path. Can't see it. She must have circled too far.
   The light was moving, getting closer, and she could hear cursing in a deep, booming voice.
   "Where are you, little runt?" called the voice, "you cannot hide from me for long. I will smell you out."
   Then, she saw the shadow.
   Shadows in the dark are always longer and more distorted than the subject who cast them, but this shadow was enormous, far, far bigger than what could emanate from a small gnome.
   Snow Flower needed to see exactly what she was dealing with. She slipped inside a hollow log. If the gnome found her she would dash off through the other side.
   The light wavered about, he was searching, unsure of where she had gone, but after several minutes the light appeared again, quite close.
   And now she saw the gnome.
   He was lit yellow by the torchlight, but a gnome he was no longer.
   He was as tall as two tall Flan, and as broad as a hill giant.
   His hair was long and wild.
   His mouth was wide and filled with sharp teeth.
   Gods...! The gnome was a spriggan.
   The spriggan smelled the air.
   "Little halfling, I can tell that you are near. Are you in that log?"
   Snow Flower bolted.
   "There you are!" cried the spriggan, and he loped after her like a wolf, "you shouldn't have stolen from me. I would have taken you to the City of the Gods as I promised. Now, I shall eat you whole."
   Snow Flower thought rapidly as she ran.  Spriggans, unholy monsters  dedicated to the Dread gods, once gnomes and now giants!  She should have realised.
   Were all the inhabitants of the City of the Gods spriggans too?
   Where could she go? She ducked down and dove into the bushes.
   The spriggan moved past her. Good, he hadn't seen her!
   Snow Flower scrambled out then ran in the other direction.
   In the gloom she just made out the black mushrooms.
   She had to go back.
   But the spriggan was coming.
   She placed her foot upon one single mushroom, squashing it flat. Then she darted back into the bushes.
   The spriggan stopped, the burning brand raised above him. He was very close, and now she could see that his skin was grey and his hair was red. He sniffed again, but evidently he couldn't smell her, perhaps because the bushes were in flower and masking her with their own scent.
   "I will find you," roared the spriggan, "and I will ..." The spriggan gasped.
   He was looking down.
   He had seen the squashed mushroom.
   Then he laughed, a horrible sound like stones breaking, " Ho! Ho! The fool has crossed the mushroom trail. Now she is truly doomed. I must watch the show." And the giant spriggan and his flaming torch followed the mushroom trail.
   Snow Flower waited until he was out of sight, then she sped off in the opposite direction. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 6
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (4)
   Snow Flower sped through the soft peaty ground around some gigantic fir trees when she suddenly stopped dead 
   Black mushrooms blocked her path.
   She went in a different direction.
   More black mushrooms.
   Black mushrooms everywhere except for the way she came. Snow Flower would have to retrace her steps and find a different way through.
   Dawn broke, and cold light began to penetrate through gaps in the trees. Snow Flower reached the mushroom she had stepped on, then gingerly skirted the mushroom trail, being careful not to cross it.  Soon, she heard a loud voice. It was the spriggan. He seemed to be arguing with someone. Snow Flower snuck closer, blending with the surroundings.
   Some distance away, the huge spriggan had stopped by a large hedge. His torch was extinguished, but he was lit by twin lights, red and blue.
   Snow Flower stealthily moved yet closer. 
   Two figures stood upon each side of the spriggan, guarding a gateway through the hedge wall.
   Two figures in the shape of human skeletons, one blue and one red.
   "Where is the halfling,?" demanded the spriggan, "I know she came this way. Is she dead already?"
   The skeletons remained unmoved.
   "Let me through, " said the spriggan, "I wish to speak with..."
   The skeletons as one came forward. Although the spriggan was over twice their size, he noticeably blanched.
   "I am from the City," pleaded the spriggan, "it was the halfling that crossed the trail, not me."
   The Blue skeleton glanced down.
   The spriggan followed the gaze of the hollow eye sockets. 
   There!
   The spriggan had inverdently crushed the last mushroom. He had crossed the trail...
   "No," cried the spriggan, "it was an accident. I brought you the halfling. I am from the City..."
   The red skeleton touched the spriggan with a finger bone.
   The spriggan opened his eyes as wide as he could. Then he scrunched up in pain and roared.
   For a moment, the spriggan lit up the forest as he immolated in a pillar of fire so bright it hurt Snow Flower's eyes.
   Then, the fire died, and the spriggan was broken pieces of bone and dust strewn across the ground beside the hedge.
   Snow Flower thought that it was time to go. She silently took off before the strange skeletons could see her. 
   Black mushrooms.
   Everywhere.
   She couldn't take another step. The mushroom trail completely surrounded her.
   And the skeletons had seen her!
   They were coming. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 7
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (5)
   Snow Flower followed the only path available to her. Escorted by the skeletons, she was taken through the hedge gateway, and there...
   ...Dancing in a bog was a hut on chicken legs.
   Snow Flower knew what this meant.
   The dancing hut was the home of Baba Yaga the witch.
   Was Baba Yaga the guardian of the City of the Gods?
   Well, Snow Flower wasn't heading there anymore anyway. She had the rings. That was enough.
   She shook her head as the skeletons gestered her towards the hut. No. She didn't want to go in...
... But growing around her on all sides were black mushrooms.
   She had no choice.
   Snow Flower stepped into the bog and quickly found herself sinking down into it. Only her head and neck were free from the awful sucking mud. The hut strode across and the legs folded down. Snow Flower grabbed at the twisting doorknob, the door shot open, and Snow Flower was a brown, slimy blob within a huge room.
   The room wasn't a room. It was a wide hall with a living space, a dining space and a large kitchen. 
   Was Snow Flower in the dancing hut?
   She must be. The door closed behind her with a snap.
   Snow Flower headed towards the furniture. Every chair was outsized, armchairs the size of black bears, a couch as big as a snow tiger, and an enormous rocking chair carved out of Bronzewood big enough for an ogre.
   Snow Flower blinked. The rocking chair was occupied. What she had thought was a heavy blanket draped across it dropped away, revealing a huge, blue skinned ogress dressed in a dirty black cloak, reclining heavily on the heavy seat.
   Baba Yaga.
   Baba Yaga turned her misshapen head slightly.
   "Ah, the girl," she said, "come up to the chair, little halfling. Let me get a good look at you."
   Snow Flower was terrified, but she did what she was told.
   Baba Yaga looked Snow Flower up and down with unoerthly eyes. 
   "You stepped on my mushroom," she growled softly.
   "I'm sorry," stuttered Snow Flower, "I was trying to escape the spriggan."
   Baba Yaga nodded, "I understand. Now, you are here in my hut. Are you going or coming?"
   Snow Flower paused. It was a strange question. What did she mean? Maybe Baba Yaga wanted to know whether she was travelling to the City of the Gods.
   "Going back home," she said, "I have what I need to pay my debt."
   Suddenly the three rings appeared in her hands, bright with colour and heavy with gold. Baba Yaga reached out with a long, large and warty hand, each fat finger the size of a parsnip. Very gently, she scooped up the rings and folded them into her own palm. One black talon as heavy as iron scoured Snow Flower's skin on the way through, leaving a long, thin line of blood.
   "Oh, I scratched you," said Baba Yaga mournfully.
   The scratch was light, and Snow Flower wasn't too bothered about it.  Baba Yaga had taken her rings!
   "Dear little girl, go to the cupboards in my kitchen. You will find some cloth and ointment there."
   "Please give the rings back," pleaded Snow Flower.
   "Nonsense. The rings are part of the City of the Gods. I must bring them to the Mayor. Now, while you are looking, can you get me my bottle of Kirsch? It's over there somewhere too."
                            *****
   With Snow Flower's arm healed and Baba Yaga gently rocking as she sipped her Kirsch, Baba Yaga spoke once more;
   "Little halfling. I am hungry. Do you know how to cook?"
   Snow Flower nodded.
   "Good. I require something from you. Go to the larder and find the ingredients to make gruel. Girl, you must prepare the best gruel in the world."
   Snow Flower went to the larder dismayed. She guessed that she would be able to make gruel alright, but the best in the world?
   What would that even be?   
   As she pulled out a barrel of greenish oats, she called out, "How do you like your gruel? Sweet or sour? With milk or without?"
   Baba Yaga waved her off.
   "You be the judge," she said.
                                  *****
   Snow Flower built a fire then boiled up a pot of thick gruel. Most of  the ingredients in the larder were rancid, and the steam from the gruel gave off an unpleasant scent of cabbage. Snow Flower wrinkled her nose.  Baba Yaga evidently smelled it too, for her voice echoed out from the lounge, "what are you doing girl? Smells disgusting."
   This wasn't going to go well.
   Once the gruel had boiled into heavy sludge, Snow Flower dished up. Baba Yaga climbed out of her rocking chair then wandered over to the kitchen. Her expression reflected her displeasure, and upright, Baba Yaga was truly enormous and terrible.
  Baba Yaga reached out to take the dish when Snow Flower impulsively dashed all the gruel onto the floor with a crash. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 9
A Blackmoor Fairy Tale (7)
   Snow Flower was given a bath in a barrel of tepid water watched over by the blue and red skeletons, then her muddy clothes were replaced with a simple garb of green. 
   She felt dizzy and disoriented, and she couldn't remember much more of her time in the dancing hut of Baba Yaga. The two skeletons stood beside her, saying nothing.
   Then, though everything in the room remained in place, whirling winds dashed about as if in a gale. Baba Yaga rocked back and forth and said nothing. Snow Flower felt the dizziness increase, and she fell back into the great couch, for the hut was on the move, dancing and capering through the strange forest on its two chicken legs.
   When Snow Flower finally emerged from the hut, which had settled just outside of her town,her name was no longer Snow Flower.
   Now she was Green Bark. 
   She looked back through the doorway and nodded one final time to Baba Yaga, who had escorted her to the door. Baba Yaga nodded back. It was time to depart forever.
   Red Death and Blue Death came out with Green Bark, the two skeletons halting on either side of a scraggly tree burdened with snow. Green Bark continued on, soon finding herself on the snow covered road that led straight into town.
                                ****
   "Why are you dressed so strangely, and all in green?" asked the onlookers who recognised Snow Flower. Green Bark didn't bother to answer.  She trudged on until she reached the Shirrif house. She went inside.
                                  *****
     Clever Speck was surprised to see Snow Flower, because he thought that she had fled into the depths of Blackmoor and had been destroyed. He was feeding his winter wolf, who was tearing at a hindquarters of a deer with pure savagery. She looked up when she smelled the strange scent of Green Bark, her storm coloured fur bristling, and her eyes and teeth glittering like lightning.
   "Down, Woe!" snapped her master. Now Clever Speck, dressed in a casual tunic and breeches, addressed the intruder, "You were wise to come back, Snow Flower. I was going to hunt you down eventually. You owe me much, you know. I assume that you have what you need?"
   "My name is Green Bark," said the halfling thief, "and I have a gift for you."
   She pulled out the silver coin and placed it in a table in front of the Shirrif. Clever Speck looked at it with puzzlement.
   "You bring me only one single little coin...?"
   "It is a one kopek piece," said Green Bark, as if that meant everything.
   Clever Speck went red in the face. "You are a fool, girl! Woe will kill you." He tapped the winter wolf's nose and was about to order the creature to attack, when Green Bark laughed.
   "Why are you laughing?" demanded Clever Speck, "you will die in agony for it!"
   "I am laughing," answered Green Bark, "because you have snubbed my recompense and now I am free."
   Woe the winter wolf launched himself at the girl formerly known as Snow Flower. She yelped, curling her body about in mid air.
   Green Bark was no longer a halfling, but a green, wild eyed old looking woman with cracked skin, teeth and claws of iron, and she was as tall as a willow. 
   Green Bark caught the winter wolf by her tail, then threw her across the room. Then she turned to Clever Speck.
                                  ****
   Green Bark left the Shirrif house,  the footprints she made in the snow as she strode along as big as a bear. She took no notice of the aghast and awestruck Blackmoor citizens who stepped away in horror when they saw her. Didn't they know that  Blackmoor was a dangerous place?
   Once she left the town far behind, the green hag turned from the road, heading back to the north.
   Green Bark began to dance as she walked. Dance, and even caper, because the excitement building up inside her could no longer be contained.
   After all, she was on her way to the City of the Gods. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 10
Dalt in the Dungeon (1)
1672 SD
   Dalt noticed the floor of the palace shaking.
   The shaking didn't bother him, because he was a ghost and he hovered, but he was a conscientious soul and he decided to investigate. He sailed down into the dungeon to take a look. 
   The dungeon had expanded into an enormous labyrinth of halls and corridors and cells,, an inverted palace mirroring and at the same time distorting the beautiful, gleaming palace above the ground.
   Everything was brown or grey or dirty. Rats scurried about with frightened eyes. The shaking was even more fierce down here, a heavy vibration that split stone walls and brought down ceilings.
   It was Syrul.
   It had to be.
   Syrul was the former god of the Suel Imperium, and the above ground palace was her creation. Wee Jas, the ex empress who became a god, had deposed Syrul and had exiled her to the dungeon. Syrul then made the dungeon her new kingdom. Dalt had warned Wee Jas that Syrul would not rest until she had regained her power. Wee Jas had shrugged. Syrul could rant and rave, but Oerth had moved on around the sun, and the cosmos was vast. Oerth and the solar system were on a path that Syrul could not change.
   So it was up to Dalt to fix things.
   "Where are you, Syrul," he called out, "it is I, the ghost of Dalt. Let me see you."
   There was a great rumbling crack and a chunk of stone gave way, opening the way into a square black hole.
   Sitting in the hole was Syrul.
   The god was plain looking, with no distinguishing features, and her hair was scraggly and mouse coloured..but her eyes raged.
   "You dare to come to my house, traitor Dalt?"
   "Yes, Syrul. You have already killed me once. I do fear you, but I do dare!"
   Syrul scoffed, "you were always vain, weren't you, Dalt? Well, what do you want of me?"
   Dalt floated down into the black hole. The darkness itself was angry, and Dalt felt his ectoplasm tremble, but it didn't stop him. His white, translucent face looked haunted and lost, yet he faced Syrul as he spoke.
   Syrul listened, or seemed to listen, but her face grew scornful, and finally she broke him off with a micking laugh.
   "You say, ghost, that I have the whole Underdark to play with?" hissed Syrul, "that I should move on and leave my Imperium to its new ownership? No, Dalt, I will shake the ground! I will shake and shake until my dungeon reaches up and brings the palace down." See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 11
Dalt in the Dungeon (2)
   Wee Jas had been very patient with Dalt. She had sat cross-legged upon a cushion and tried to show Dalt how to meditate.
   "You and the Cosmos are one and the same," Dalt remembered that she said, "your spirit form is no different from your former fleshy state. You are Dalt and you are the stars and the void all at once."
   Dalt didn't really understand. It was frustrating to him, being an insubstantial ghost, and he felt vastly different from his mortal days as a young and cocky red headed man. He tried to follow the advice of the serene, young and radiant goddess, but Wee Jas had a distance that Dalt couldn't breach.
   Meditation wasn't for him.
                               *******
   The shaking was intolerable. Andon put down his quill with annoyance. Why wasn't anyone fixing the problem? These tremors weren't natural, and how was he supposed to complete his reports when his ink kept spilling all over the scroll? He rang his bell. His attendant, an Oeridian slave from an island to the south, answered promptly. Andon instructed him to arrange a meeting with the castellan.
   The castellan was sympathetic, but what could he do? The emperor himself had complained about the shaking, but no magic could stop it.
   This was a religious matter.
   Andon met with the high priestess of Wee Jas. Yes, she knew what was happening. Syrul had awoken from her sleep and now wished to return to her former place.
   "Can't you stop it?"
   "We pray to our dear Wee Jas constantly. She is unmoved. She has no fear of Syrul."
   That was all very well for Wee Jas, but she didn't have to live a mortal life where there was a small earthquake every few hours. What was to be done then?
   The high priestess was sympathetic, but her answer was as wise as it was unhelpful, "our lives are rotating around the sun. We are miraculous simply for existing. Tremors and troubles are surely a toll, but a toll worth the price of life itself."
                            *****
   Dalt observed the exodus. The emperor and the officials abandoned the sacred palace to the epistemological, and relocated to another city where they set up a new capital.
   "They have all gone," Dalt complained to Wee Jas.
   "They will return. Have faith."
   "Why don't you just stop Syrul? You are greater than her."
   Wee Jas just smiled.
                               *****
   Dalt returned to the dungeon. It had transformed again, this time looking like flaming pillars and stalactites and stalagmites like gnashing teeth.
   "You are destroying the Suel Imperium, Syrul," complained Dalt, "if you return to the surface you will simply rule a deserted palace."
   "Oh, foolish ghost," said Syrul, "the palace isn't the Imperium. The Imperium is the Imperium. When I break free the entire land will be me." See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 12
Dalt in the Dungeon (3)
   "You have more strength than you know," said Win-Daled the Suel lich to a downcast Dalt, "for you are undead like me, and we undead harness enormous power."
   Win-Daled was an ancient Suel who currently inhabited the body of a Flan once known as Heward. She resided in the palace as Wee Jas's lover, and as Dalt's friend. She had been disturbed also by the shaking Syrul, and was disappointed to see the Suel flee, but she trusted Wee Jas, and she saw the world through the lens of eternity. No, she wouldn't intervene, for her time of trouble had long since passed. 
   It was Dalt's time now.
                              ******
   Dalt decided to test his power. He went to a long disused room and tried to create furniture with his mind. After all, the palace was made from the thoughts of Wee Jas just as the dungeon below was made by the mind of Syrul.
   Nothing manifested. 
   He tried again.
   Nothing.
   Dalt looked inside himself. He was a ghost, and what was a ghost if not the residue of will? He could do this!
   The next earthquake brought down a chunk of plaster from the ceiling. Dalt looked up, shooting an angry glance as his mind cursed Syrul.
   The ceiling repaired itself.
   There! He had achieved something. He looked around the dusty room and tried again.
                            *****
   Dalt once again returned to the dungeon.
   "Syrul!' he called, "Syrul. Show yourself. Your earthquakes shall end."
   The dungeon was even more wretched than before. The walls and ceiling and floor shone with garish red and purple, and bas reliefs of gargoyles with leering tongues and black bat wings jutted about the place as if the dungeon itself was alive.
   Syrul appeared, and she looked sullen and haggard. Her fiery eyes were puffy and bloodshot. Dalt thought that the effort to bring down the palace was tapping her resources. 
   "You don't need to keep doing this, Syrul," said Dalt, "I think that Wee Jas is too strong for you."
   Syrul glared at the ghost. How dare he mention Wee Jas! "No," she snapped, "my will will be the greater in the end. I am getting closer, and when I emerge you will be amongst the first to feel my wrath."
   The gargoyles stirred, and began to climb down the walls.
   Dalt calmed himself, then suddenly produced a silver key. Syrul turned to look at it, puzzled.
   "What's this?"
   "A present for you, Syrul..I don't want the palace destroyed, so I made this key. I can take you to the stairs that will lead you back. Then you can reckon with Wee Jas face to face, if you truly believe that you can best her. But leave me be, great Syrul, and it shall be as it was. You shall rule and I will haunt. I will never cross you again."
   The gargoyles resumed their position in the walls. Syrul held out her hand. "Give me the key then, and I shall not harm you."
   Dalt gave her the key.
   "Now, good Dalt, where are these stairs?"
   Dalt pointed down a long corridor, then glided along it. Syrul followed. Presently they reached a locked iron door. 
   "The stairs are behind this door," said Dalt, "the key will open it."
   Syrul placed the key in the lock. The door opened.
   "Go through," said Dalt, "resume your place on Oerth."
   Syrul went through the door, and found the winding stairs. As she began to climb, Dalt slammed the door shut with his mind.
   From behind the door, Dalt heard Syrul shriek. "What have you done, ghost? These stairs lead to nothing. The key won't work on this side! Dalt, you have trapped me!"
   Dalt grinned. The trap had worked. He had managed to create a little dungeon of his own. He glided back down the corridor and was surprised to see lead bars block his path forward. He tried to float through, but the bars stopped him. And as he vainly attempted to push himself through, more bars appeared behind him.
   Now he was trapped himself!
   Dalt saw movement on the other side of the bars. It was Syrul. She glared at the ghost.
   "Stupid ghost!" she mocked, "this dungeon is of my making. I wasn't tricked for a single second. But,  Dalt, whether I ever break free or not will be of no consequence to you, for you will haunt no more than these twenty feet for the rest of your aeons. This little corridor is now your home forever."
   " See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 13
A Discourteous Look (1)
1686 SD
   Once again, that new slave girl gave lord Spindle a discourteous look.
   Who was this woman? She looked ordinary enough, about eighteen, with reddish hair and a complexion a little lighter than some. She had gone back into the kitchen, disappeared with the rest. Spindle wouldn't have ever noticed her if she hadn't always given him that look.
   Who did she think he was? Secretary Spindle was second only to the emperor himself. Yes, he had changed over the years. Alas, he wasn't young anymore.
   It was doubtful that he was even human anymore.
   Spindle looked down at his enormous leathery belly. He had put on a lot of weight. His single arm was extremely thin and bony, and long, stretching out from his jutting shoulder like an old dead tree branch. His face had become toadish, some said goblin ish, but that would be flattering.
   He was loathsome looking, there was no denying it, but that gave the girl no excuse. None of the other slaves dared to show any expression on their face other than a nervous smile, 
   Administrator Poit was in the office too, checking over some notes.
   "Leave it," said Spindle, "tell me, that girl that just took my order? Did you notice her at all?"
   Poit shrugged, "not really. I think she's from one of the new batches."
   Spindle leaned forward in his stout chair, "yes. Yes. There's always quite a turnover, isn't there? Where's she from?"
   Poit frowned, "shall I organise for you to add her to your harem?"
   Spindle waved his one hand, "no, I don't like her like that. She's not really my type. There's something about her that disturbs me..."
   "I believe she is from one of the Isles of Woe."
   Now it was Spindle's turn to frown, "the Isles of Woe? Oh, that would explain the look she gave me. Likely she's the whelp of some big-note gladiator. Now, administrator, I wish to take a nap before lunch. Find your paperwork and go."
                             *****
   Most of the slaves were rotated regularly, so Secretary Spingle didn't see the girl again for several weeks. In fact, he had almost completely forgotten her when once again his old and tired eyes were stung by a defiant look.
   "Girl," he snapped, "girl! You will come here!"
   The girl quietly stepped over to the desk.
   "I didn't mean to disturb you," she apologized, "I am just bringing you the food."
   "Not that, stupid girl! Why do you stare at me?"
   "Well, I don't mean to," said the girl with a steady voice.
   Spindle rose up, his stout legs shooting pain up his hips.
   "Don't lie to me, girl. You aren't in the arena now. You don't fear me, do you?"
   The girl held the dish of steaming brains, and glanced quickly over to the nearby dining table, but she didn't answer.
   "What is your name, bitch." demanded Spindle.
   "Culber," said the girl, "and no, I don't fear you."
   "Put the dish down, for gods sake. Why don't you fear me?"
   Culber put the plate down then turned back with a glare. 
   "You can kill me if you want, or torture me. I am your slave and you can do to me anything you wish, whether I agree or not. But, Secretary of Vecna, you cannot make me feel what I do not feel. My soul is free." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Part 14
A Discourteous Look (2)
   The punishment hadn't been all that bad, all things considered. Culber returned to her quarters several days later, bruised but intact. She dwelt in a dilapidated old barracks converted into a slave dormitory. Around fifty slaves lived here at any one time. The slaves formed family and friendship groups and went to great pains to give each group some valuable privacy. The dormitory was divided into partitions with ragged blankets or stitched together torn clothes. Cuber went to her section and pushed the blanket across.
   "I was worried about you," said a middle aged woman heating up a stew.
   Cuber went to the pot. "I'll take over the stirring. It's my turn."
   There were several others in the cubicle, an old man, a few young men and a young woman.  One uncle, and the rest were cousins. The older woman was their aunt, and Culber's mother.
   "You're hurt," said one.
   "Not badly," answered Culber, who had already begun to stir briskly, watching the stew bubble, "I told you that being brought to Spar would be better than the Isles. The capital is cloaked in a veneer of civility, being so close to our beloved Vecna. Besides, they didn't know what to make of me."
   "Still, I think you should rest."
   "No. I am happy being at home. In fact, tonight I shall lead the prayers."
                                 ******
   Culber's family was very pious, and several other slave families made fun of their chanting and singing and strange sounding rituals that emanated through the blanket. 
   Culber' kneeled on the bare floor, deliberately letting her knees chafe. The others did the same, forming a half circle. 
   "Beory. Earth Mother. Hear us, O Lord." chanted Culber, "we thank you for our suffering, for without suffering we would be our overlords."
   "Thanks to Beory. Thanks to Beory." echoed the others.
   "And thank you from delivering us from the Isles of Woe, where our martyred ancestors were forced to fight for the pleasure of monsters."
   "Thank you for delivering us. Thank you. Thank you."
   "And now we light the sacred candle for our First Ancestor. The One who went from overlord to sufferer for our glorious future when one day out suffering will purge the last of our sins, and we will be the custodians of Oerik."
   "Yes. We light the candle for our beloved one. Our beloved one."
   "Gavron," intoned Culber," Thank you for your sacrifice . Gavron. Dear Gavron. Our Gavron." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 15
The Olve Above (1)
1695 SD
   Nestled to the east of the Yatil mountains and  hugging the Whyestil lake was the great Vesve forest. Once the northernmost edge of the Celenian empire, the remains of Celene were hundreds of miles to the south. The Vesve was now a holding of Vecna, as was almost the entirety of the Flanaess. 
   Yet, the empire of Vecna didn't control the Vesve. The tall and stout trees of the forest were countless years old, and even the oldest Olve were younger than the tallest trees. Tens of thousands of Olve lived within the Vesve, some remnants of the Celenians, but others were Olve that rejected all manner of civilization, believing in anarchy and living for the moment.
   They were the wild elves. The Grugach. They spoke their own language and wore clothes made from leaves. They hunted with green furred dogs they called cooshee. And they didn't like being disturbed.
   Bhylyu was being bothered right now. She hunched over a thick branch high in the canopy, her anger mounting.
  Below, walking on the brown dirt and dry leaves and old sticks that made up the ground, were a gang of the fox people the Celenians called 'kodge.' The kodge were brutish mercenaries from across the sea. 
   The emperor, Vecna, had brought them to Oerik. Bhylyu had seen them before, but not this close to the mountains. She had seen orcs this close, but the orcs were enemies of the empire and they were naturally going to hide in far away places.
   She notched an arrow. The kodge would be gone in a moment or two.
                              ******
   The cooshee were howling. Bhylyu and the other grugach emerged from the shadows within the moonlit trees and stealthily slipped through the branches like monkeys. Their eyes saw darkness as gold, bronze and silver, so they could make out the cooshee below, their hackles raised, their eyes wild. What was disturbing them? The dogs were usually dead quiet and wouldn't raise an alarm even for a wandering bear.
   Something dangerous was close.
   A flash of gold.
   There! An Ur Flan in robes. 
   Ur Flan? Here? 
   Look! Another. Over there, see?
   And there!
   And is that...
   Dragonels! We are under attack!
   And the grugach hesitated no more, clouds of arrows bursting upon their multiple enemies.
    Arrows that dissolved into sand..The Ur Flan of the empire were well prepared.
   The ancient and beautiful Sylvan trees of the Vesve began to burn. See less
