A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 69
Boy Wonder (1)
1722 SD
   The harpies were wreaking havoc in the villages skirting the Gambodge forest. The Empire was angry, and Vecna had stretched out his Hand. Woodcutters were plucked into the sky and devoured. Wandering travellers were lost. Ur Flan were making their presence felt too, and many people suspected of being in league with the rebels were rounded up and taken to the Isles of Woe. 
   Culber had managed to evade these myriad difficulties, but it had made her extra cautious, and she was forced to stop her smuggling operation. What had made Vecna so angry? The speculation was that his loss of his Mystaran province to the rebel Arik had hit him hard, both personally and economically. Stories were that the Glantri Empire, his supposed ally, wasn't picking sides, and the island of Kodge Land between Oerik and Mystara was wavering, and Vecna's Hand there was losing its grip. 
   Whatever the truth was, the dark times had become even darker. Culber and the Gavronites met extremely infrequently, and isolated, they felt helpless to fight on. Culber knew that even Celene was losing its light. Ur Flan surrounded their borders and trade with the kingdom, nefarious though it was, was almost totally ended. 
   Then there was the boy. He was four or five, his skin like dark copper, his hair black and curly. His eyes were pale and green, and he was staring at Culber like a cat.
   It was very disconcerting. What did the little boy want?
   His mother was laughing. They were preparing a meal when the boy had come in then stood, staring., "Don't mind him. He always does that."
   Culber frowned, "he should be with the other children."
   The mother gave a helpless smile, "the other children hate him "
   "I can see why," said Culber, "he is very rude."
   The boy belched.
   "Is he a simpleton?" continued Culber, "you had best hide him. The Ur Flan will kill him."
   "I am not a simpleton," announced the boy, "I just find you fascinating."
   The mother had stopped laughing. She gave her boy a smack. "Leave us! Go and play somewhere else."
   The little boy shrugged. He turned to go, then strained his neck, and looked Culber in the eye, "I don't want to be here. You have taken other children away. Take me too."
   Culber went red, "whatever are you talking about? I am a laundress. I don't take children anywhere."
   The boy went back into the little kitchen. "When I was one year old, you took Fulig to Celene. When I was two, my mother helped you  take Hulli and Sibby there as well. And there were others. These are the ones I knew."
   "How could you know that?" exclaimed Culber.
   "Fulig used to cuddle me when I was in my crib. Hulli and Sibby gave me sweets and told me that I would grow up to be a wizard!"
   "But how can you remember them? You were too young."
   "What do you mean, Culber? I remember when I was born. The two moons were out and mother was crying. It was a little bit disorientating, if I am being honest."
   Culber looked at astonishment at the boy's mother, who was clearly embarrassed.
   "Your child isn't a simpleton, I take that back, but he is in even more danger than before. If Vecna finds out about him..."
   "I know," interrupted the boy, "that's why you have to smuggle me across the border. Please. I can feel great good within you. I will go now, but I will be back in seven days. Have a plan by then." He turned to his mother as he went to leave, "sorry, Mother." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3
Broken Empires 
Part 70
Boy Wonder (2)
   Culber led the boy through hidden trails in the Gambodge forest. The route had been disturbed. In certain places trees on either side had been brought down, and some of the thick shrubs and berry bushes had been thinned out.   Continuing on was much too dangerous. Soldiers had marched this path. Ur Flan or goblins or kodge were nearby. She stopped mid step, shook her head, then looked down at the boy, who stared at her with an off-putting grin.
   "We can't get to Celene this way," said Culber, "we must head back east, then go south through Welkwood further down.
  The boy looked thoughtful. Culber tried to turn him around, but he was slow to move.
   "Come on, Rao, we could be discovered at any moment."
   "Isn't this the quickest way, though?"
   "No, it certainly isn't. And it's not the safest route either. Let's go."
   "What is the quickest way?"
   "The main road. Filled with checkpoints."
   "Oh," said Rao, "let's do that then."
   Culber believed that the child was mad. She picked him up. He was lighter than she expected, weighing little more than her pack. Still, she couldn't carry him all day. "You wanted me to get you into Celene, didn't you? You have to obey me."
   "You know best, " said the boy at last, and they both turned back.
                                   *****
   The song was hypnotic, seductive and beautiful. The sweet melody drifted through the roanwood trees. Culber froze in her tracks.
   "What is that amazing sound?" asked Rao.
   Culber groaned. "Harpies," she hissed. This was a big problem. Her faith kept her safe from the siren song, but Rao was a sitting duck. "Cover your ears!" she cried, "don't listen to it."
   But little Rao was dancing under the trees with a terrific smile on his face. "I love it. Who are the harpies?"
   Culber found a big stick. She gave it to the boy, then she pulled out a small cudgel. The sweet songs continued. A branch broke from high up in a tree. They were coming.
   "Not who, what. Harpies are flying man-eaters. Use this stick to fend them off." 
   The harpies flew down, singing all the while. Eagles with the upper body and head of a woman, they had piercing red eyes and their talons were hooked like scythes. Three of them lashed against Culber, and two attempted to abduct Rao. Culber hit out with her cudgel, and the impact on one batted it away, smashing it hard against a solid tree trunk.The other two tore at her eyes, so Culber was forced to dive down to protect herself. She desperately wanted to help the boy, but the harpies were relentless. Facing the ground, she heard the flurry of wings and smelt the carrion stench of bloodstained feathers as talons ripped out her hair. 
   The singing stopped, replaced with a triumphant screech.  Culber rolled about, trying to shake the harpies off, and she glimpsed two harpies taking back to the air, and with them, held in their talons, was the boy.
   Culber jumped back to her feet, her cudgel swinging back and forth. Screaming in rage she cracked the oaken club into a harpy head, caving in its skull. The one harpy remaining squaked defiance, then shot up into the canopy above, where it disappeared from Culber's sight. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3

Part 71
Boy Wonder (3)
   Culber couldn't go back to Spar. The harpies were Vecna spies, not mindless monsters, and now his Eye would spy her. Her only hope was to make it to Celene. She went off the trail and plunged into the depths of the forest. The ipp and rieu and  oak trees were large and imposing, and their branches and leaves fractured the light from Sol into diamonds interposed with shadow. Culber had a good sense of direction, but with no landmarks, little light, and with the sun blocked from sight, she soon realised that she had no idea where she was. She sat down on a ground covered in seeds, the scent of acorns calming her. 
   "Beory. Oerth Mother. It is I, Culber, the slave girl," prayed Culber in a whisper, though she was long past being a girl, having grown up children, "If I am to return to  the waiting Gavron in the Seven Heavens I accept, but I have more to offer Oerth, if you will let me. I lost the boy, and for that I will atone. He was the first child that I failed to bring to Celene. He begged me to take him and it was my ego that aquiessed. Let the boy die quickly. Please don't let him suffer. And, if you are to give me leave to stay, please let me find the way."
                               *****
   Little Rao was deposited into a harpy nest made out of bones. The nest was tucked into a shallow cave within a large crag jutting off the side of a hill some miles from the forest. The three harpies clung to the side of the nest, their faces contorted in anger, for two comrades were lost.
   "We are cursed," moaned one, "all we have is this morsel."
   "Eat him quick, I say," said another, "then we go out to hunt again."
   "The club woman is out there!" complained the third harpy, "the woods are teeming with rebels."
   "Why aren't you singing?" asked Rao.
   The harpies stopped their bickering. What was this?
   "Human boy? You understand what we say?"
   Rao looked confused, "of course I can. Aren't you speaking?"
   The harpies looked at their meal in astonishment. The harpy language was all chirps and whistles and shrieks and squawks.
   "Yes, we were conversing," said the first harpy, "but where did you pick up our language?"
   "I don't know what you mean," and little Rao looked even more confused.
   "You speak harpy fluently," said the second, "and I know for a fact that our sounds are extremely difficult for a human thorax to master. Are you working for Vecna?"
   Rao laughed, "Goodness no!" he exclaimed, "I learned how to talk, that's all."
   The harpies jumped off their perch, fluttering about nervously. This was all very strange. Too strange in fact.
   "Will you please sing for me again?"  Rao was smiling.
   The third harpy couldn't take anymore. Without a squawk or a shriek, she suddenly dropped down, snatched Rao out of the nest, then hurled him from the cave. Rao tumbled out of the opening, plunging into the open air. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 72
Boy Wonder (4)
   Rao hadn't fallen before. He tumbled off the ridge, the trees far below. Air rushed over him making him feel cold. His stomach found itself in his throat. It was hard to move in any direction except for down. He realised that he wasn't going to fall for long, because the trees were growing rapidly as he plummeted.
But what was air? Air was made up of molecules. Molecules were made up of atoms. Atoms were matter.  So Rao stopped falling, resting upon the physical building blocks of the Material Plane. As if the sky was a great staircase, he wound his way down to the ground. Then he walked away.
   The harpies flew down to the area where the boy had fallen, but instead of a broken body to feast upon, they saw little footprints in the dirt. Wisely, the harpies decided not to follow, and they returned to their roost.
                                *****
   Ehlonna found Culber resting by a log.
   "Come, friend of Celene, take my hand.I am Ehlonna.
   Culber looked into the face of a beautiful young elf with fair hair. No. She was looking into the face of a beautiful Flan woman with dark hair. This must indeed be Ehlonna. Ehlonna who was both elf and Flan at the same time.
   "I am a long way from Celene, I think," said Culber.
   "Yes. Quite far." answered the princess.
  "The Gnarley forest is too dangerous, princess. The Ur Flan are near."
   "I know it. That's why I came for you. They would find you."
   "You knew that I was here?"
   Ehlonna's eyes shone with amusement, "you think that only Vecna has eyes? The Olve have many friends in the forest."
                              *****
   Ehlonna carried Culber as if she was as light as a loaf of bread. The Olve/Flan slipped  through the forest as if she was oil. Before very long, even before Culber felt hungry, they were crossing the thorn hedges that marked the borders of Celene. Culber was taken up into a bright treehouse surrounded by slender trees with silver leaves. Grey elves attended to her cuts and bruises, and her terrible gash across her scalp. 
   "We know of you, human called Culber," said one of the elves as he applied a poultice to her forehead, "You help the people. You saved some lives."
   "I lost a child today. The harpies took him."
   Ehlonna was conversing with two young Olve in clothes of gossamer, but she overheard Culber, and interrupted her with a bright laugh, "perhaps they took him to a place where he needed to go. Now, dear Culber, it is your time to rest. I will not have you return to be a slave of the Empire. Celene will be your home now." See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 73
Spindle's Satisfying Meal
1725 SD
   The octopuses were large, plump and still alive. Splashed with citrus juices, the score of creatures on the plate thrashed and writhed, their tentacles a moving host of delicate flesh. Secretary Spindle grabbed a handful in his single gnarled hand then tossed them into his maw. He slurped his tongue about, enjoying the astringent flavours of the lime and lemon mixed with meat, salt and sea. He rolled the octopuses around for nearly a minute before swallowing them down whole. Spindle felt the slime and ink slide across his ancient tastebuds, and he sucked his lips in pleasure. But the octopuses didn't slip all the way down. Their tentacles lashed out gripping onto the inside of his throat. 
   Spindle couldn't breathe. He coughed, but nothing dislodged, for the tentacles had wrapped around his insides in a death grip. Choking, his beady eyes watered and began to roll around in his skull. He gripped the heavy table so that he wouldn't fall, the octopuses left on the plate were motionless now, as if they were fixed upon the impending revenge of their comrades. Spindle went rigid. He stopped choking, holding what breath remained. Then,  he consciously compressed his stomach and the  acid from his gut  rose up as a massive burst of heartburn. The toxic gases from his stomach bathed the octopuses in virulent gastric juices, forcing the tentacles to reluctantly release their hold, plunging down at last to their doom.
   Eventually, after the delicious meal was finished, the Secretary went over a final run of the finances of the Empire. It hadn't improved since the meal. He laughed at his own joke, although it was a dry laugh, for he was feeling a little afraid.
   Vecna was going to be disappointed. Again. The Emperor had been patient, his voice always steady and measured, but Spindle could detect that little edge of steel in the timbre. Until quite recently, the Empire was extremely wealthy, with strong trading with Glantri and Kodge Land growing the coffers year by year. Arik's return to Mystara had changed things. His rotten army of pirates had invaded Kodge Land and disrupted the trading routes. Worse, Glantri's fear of Arik on their borders meant that they had become more neutral, no longer a solid ally despite being ruled by Ur Flan. Lord Arik was now growing richer as Vecna's profits slowly retreated. 
   Spindle wanted to open up trade with the Thyatic Empire in eastern Mystara, but the elvish island kingdom of Ierendi blocked the way. And now, the rebels in the Flanaess were disrupting the overland routes around Celene and the Sheldomar valley, despite crackdowns. 
   What was the Secretary to do? He was also the administrator of Spar, and that great city was flourishing. If only that were enough.
   Spindle decided to put the papers away once again. Maybe better news would come in the morning. He called a slave to make him his favourite drink. He was going to relax and enjoy himself in the hour left before bed.
   Nursing the drink, an idea came to him. It was practical, and logistically simple. The Suel Imperium over the mountains was in turmoil. A dark age had come there, a good example of what could happen to an empire without a great ruler. But despite their troubles, great wealth lay within there. 
   Secretary Spindle was pretty sure that he had found a way to extract some of it. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 74
Hellhound Crouch 
1726 SD
   Smoler remembered, when he was only about eight feet tall, climbing up the obsidian wall of Hellhound Crouch then gazing down upon a large city far away on the plains below. Smoler returned to his father, Baron Kash, and asked the fire giant why they never visited the city. 
   Baron Kash smiled indulgently at his boy's naive question. What was a child for, if it wasn't for being wide eyed, inquisitive, and just a little foolish? He answered his son kindly, "dear little one," he said, "The city down below is a Suel city. The Suel are not our friends."
   Smoler smashed his hands together in a very warlike way, "Then why don't we crush them, my father? Then the city will belong to us."
   The Baron patted Smoler tenderly on the head, "Ah, my son, it is not so simple as that. We would need to come down from the Hellfurnaces. We would be seen by the Suel, and they would defend themselves with blasts of cold air and frost conjured up by their wizards."
   "What is cold air, my father? What is frost?"
   Smoler was indeed very small, mused Baron Kash, "Frost you do not know, for I have never seen it form in our mountain kingdom, but do you not sometimes feel discomfort from high winds? That is cold air, dear Smoler."
   And now Smoler understood. He hated high winds. It wasn't at all like the warm smile and ash that tickled his skin when a distant volcano erupted. He would have to be satisfied with just looking down upon that forbidden city.
                                *****
   Yes, Baron Smoler remembered that simple time long ago, when he was just a little boy. Smoler was now over twelve feet tall, newly crowned (poor father slain by a roc) and now he stood upon Hellhound Crouch looking down once again upon that city of the Suel, the city that they called Rhaan. But times had changed. The Suel were in disarray, concentrating their vast armies upon themselves and forgetting the giants of the mountains. The king himself had commanded him to lead his loyal subjects down into the Suel Imperium. Great things would come to the fire giant kingdom if a portion of the Imperium could be seized. The Vecna Empire would shower them with gifts, and new trade routes with Western Oerik would be established.
   Baron Smoler smiled, his iron-black face lit up by his orange-yellow mane. The news he had just received had been very good. The Suel magi of the city had rushed into a neighbouring province to reinforce their infantry. Who was left to defend Rhaan? Perhaps an old wizard, and a few veterans leading stock Men at Arms. High upon the black stone of Hellhound Crouch, Smoler raised his grey sword high and twirled his white furred cape in what he thought was a regal fashion. The Fire Giant Kingdom was at war at last! Even the cold breeze that scorched his face couldn't dampen his euphoria. See less

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik  
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 75 
Hail the Chief 
   Baron Smoler had wanted to lead the attack upon Rhaan but his advisors cautioned against this. What if the city was better defended than expected, or what would become of the realm if by some freak chance, an arrow caught him in the throat or an eye? The fire giant infantry was the best in the world. Let them do their job.
   Smoler had agreed and now he regretted it. He had moved down into the Suel plains to get as close as possible without being drawn into the combat, and he quickly found that he couldn't see anything but the backs of the giants. The king had generously offered his Baron his personal guards of honour, and they were freaks, some reaching upward of eighteen feet high. Their armour was garish and ceremonial, and to make themselves even bigger their hats were heaped up masses of cave bear fur. They seemed barely trained with their great swords, holding them awkwardly, and their gangly bodies were shaped like stalks, and their square, elongated heads made them top heavy. 
   What made them far worse was that they completely blocked Smoler's view. He was ignominiously forced to retreat into the foothills where at least now he could see. Unfortunately, he felt incredibly distant from the melee unfolding below, and his dashing cloak of white furred snow serpent, his scale mail fashioned from hatchling silver dragons, and his mirrored sword seemed faintly ridiculous now. 
   The combatants might as well have been beetles or ants, so distant were they, but at least Smoler could make out the gist of the battle. It was going almost as well as he had expected, though one Suel magi and a few priests had bolstered the defenders (fortuitously only bringing down a couple of the King's guards) for a brief moment before being cut down. 
   Soon it was all over. His fire giants were victorious. The city fell to Baron Smoler.
                              *****
   Smoler entered the smouldering city and was at a loss of what to do with all of the Suel humans. Their were lots of old men, and boys, and thousands of women, girls and little children. Why hadn't they all fought like fire giants did when their halls were invaded? And they all chattered and yelped and wept with cries worse than giant goats. Smoler couldn't understand a word, but fortunately one of his advisors spoke Suel, and he was able to interpret.
   "They beg for their lives," said the advisor.
   "Do they think us barbarians?" exclaimed Smoler, "There is no honour in slaying non-combatants without good reason. Some we will take as slaves, of course. The rest...what do we do with them?"
   "We must organise them by sex. Males and females don't tend to like being heaped up all together. We should separate them and make them swear fealty to our King."
   Baron Smoler nodded in agreement.
                                  ****
   The city had a new name. Smoler, it was called, and the new province was called Kash in honour of the Baron's late father. Many Suel had left, but some had stayed in return for obedience and safety. There was a knock on the door.
   The Black Monks had arrived.
                                  ****
   Baron Smoler was extremely drunk. He staggered about, dishevelled, unshaven and undignified. He didn't care. Vecna's Eye was upon him. The city was not called Smoler. The province was not called Kash. The conquered little realm was Vecna's.
   Vecna offered up his Hand in friendship, the Black Monks had said, and it would be a shame to feel the back of it. See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik 
Book 3 
Broken Empires 
Part 76
The Shephard (1)
1732 SD
   The sheep weren't cooperating today. They were fidgety and fussy, ignoring some of the best grass in order to wander off into the bog. Rao didn't worry about the why's, he just worked harder. Rao wore a kilt and vest of grey wool and wore rabbitskin gloves and boots. His skin glistened like dark copper and his curly hair had lightened in the sun. As he walked he leaned upon a tall, spindly crook.
   There was danger here. Not for Rao. For the sheep. Out past the little bog was a stand of trees. Usually a benign wood with game to hunt and a little brook to fish, the trees sheltered a predator. A particularly large and temperamental tyrg had retreated here to eke out his last chance at survival. Once the leader of a highly successful pack of tyrg that roamed this part of Vol, west of the Velverdyva River, he had been brought low by two young rivals working together. The betrayal stung, for he had saved the pair when they were cubs. But that was how the world turned. He remembered how he himself had become pack leader, surprising his old rival when the beast was bent over to drink. 
   The tyrg was big and scarred and desperate.
   Three young sheep were pounding their feet in the mud, pulling out rubbery weeds then chewing them with expressions of great happiness. Rao smiled. He would give them a few minutes more. A dark shadow slipped out from the trees. It was the tyrg, as large as a tiger, with a savage canine snout and fur both blotched and striped. He came hard, running like a cat, then exploding into the bog with one great leap. 
   The sheep emitted high pitched bleats and tried to run, but two had their necks torn apart before they could gain momentum. The third sheep burst out of the bog and onto the hard ground where it dashed into Rao. The tyrg didn't pursue. He had made his kills. One sheep was devoured on the spot, for he was ravenous, having eaten nothing larger than a hare for weeks, then, seeing himself undisturbed, the tyrg gripped the second sheep with his jaws, then retreated back into the wood.
    Rao patted the surviving sheep, then led her back to the flock, who were now altogether amongst the greenest grass. They looked up at Rao but averted their eyes when his own green ones met theirs. Perhaps they felt guilty at last.
                               ****
   The moons Celene and Luna were high in the night sky when Rao left his hut and went into the woodland. Armed only with his crook, he went out to find the tyrg. The sheep weren't his own, and his master would be unhappy with the loss of two. And he should have done better, for wasn't he fourteen years old and mature for his age?
   Before very long, he found the tyrg, for the wood was small and their were only a few places suitable as a lair. The tyrg, who had been asleep only moments before, was upright, hackles up, and he was already snarling. Rao, unhurried, reached out with his long crook and tapped the animal's nose.
   The tyrg whimpered., then whined. Rao nodded, smiling. 
   Rao benignly watched the tyrg carefully tear off the hindquarters of his prize, then, the meat secured between his teeth, the huge tyrg turned about and left. He wouldn't return. See less

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 77
The Shepherd (2)
1736 SD
The castle on the hill was getting close to being completed, signifying the end of simple life for the land of Vol, for Vecna's Eye was about to open. The master of the sheep had grown fond of Rao, and as Rao matured, he worried for him. Rao never socialised, he never attended local gatherings, never spoke to people his own age. Rao seemed content, but the master thought that was because Rao's last vestiges of childhood had yet to leave and never return.
Rao was very odd, easily distracted by trivial things, but also extremely quick to learn. He needed to become exposed to society for the master had no children, and perhaps Rao would be the one who took over the pastures, and his naivety could easily see him come undone by confidence tricksters or scheming women. Or Vecna.
Rao was sent into town to buy two new rams of that new variety of sheep with pure white wool. The trip took several days and Rao went alone, although the master offered him the chance to go down with a team of merchants.
"Why not go alone upon the road?" asked Rao.
"There are dangers. You know that."
"I know that this road leads to the town, and I know that roads were built to be walked on, so I cannot foresee any problems for me."
And of course, Rao had been right. He reached the edge of town at the end of the third day and slept that night in a hay barn. The next morning he enquired after the farmer with the white sheep. Having been given directions to the man's house, Rao found the farmhouse in a low glen a little away from the town. Rao crossed a miniature bridge spanning a creek and saw his first glimpse of the sheep. Their wool was thick and white and their heads and legs were naked and black. With them was a young woman in a yellow dress. She had an eisel set up, and she was painting. She looked up as Rao went by.
"Hello," she said.
"Hello," said Rao.
"I have not seen you before, " said the woman, and Rao noticed that she was quite beautiful.
"I have not seen you before either," he answered.
"Yes, but you are the wandering stranger, not me."
"I am not a stranger. I am Rao."
"And I am Metty. And you are indeed a stranger."
Rao shrugged, and made to move on, but the woman called out to him, "Hey, stop. Don't you want to see what I am painting?"
Rao decided to have a look. He went over to the canvas, expecting to see a picture of a sheep, or the house, or the glen, or the bridge, or the creek, or all of it at once. Instead he saw the image of a young man with a crooked nose, large teeth and neatly groomed dark hair dressed in expensive gaudy clothes. Rao looked around for the man, but he didn't seem to be around anywhere.
"A good picture," said Rao, "but who is he?"
"My beloved," said the woman, "and we are soon to be married."
"And you see him in your mind's eye? Why paint his likeness out here? Do the sheep inspire you?"
Metty laughed, "you are funny, Rao. Why, I paint him here because this is where he is."
Rao looked around again. He still didn't see anyone. "Where, exactly...?"
Metty pointed to an empty piece of grass several feet away. "Right there," she stated. "He is with me all the time."
"Hello," called Rao to the spot.
No answer.
Rao returned his attention to Metty, "invisible is he? Why doesn't he speak?"
Metty looked confused, "how could I paint my beloved if I could not see him? You must be joking. He is literally standing right there. How rakish he looks!"
Rao looked one more time. No. No one was there. "Hello, sir. Hello!"
A sheep bleat was all that he heard.
"No," said Rao firmly, "you must be painting him from your imagination. He says nothing either."
Metty looked even more confused, "you can't hear him either? He whispers love to me even now."
Rao had another look at the painting. The details were not quite finished, but around his throat was the outline of a necklace with a dangling lead pyramid.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 78
The Shepherd (3)
Count Xert went back into his little room then closed the door. He sat down on his bed and threw off his jacket, hat and boots. They lay where they fell, amongst clothes and papers and books and detritus. Xert was a dissipated, derelict of a man, and he didn't care one whit. He pulled out a crystal ball from his shirt, hanging from a small leather bag below his pyramid necklace. He polished it with a rag. He liked a clear view. Then he peered into it, watching diaphanous figures emerge. What were they all doing now?
*****
Count Xert put the crystal away. He would get addicted to this if he weren't careful. Wasn't he meant to meet the mayor in an hour? He rubbed his bent nose. It had never recovered from that punch by his eldest brother when he was eleven. It hadn't half helped his looks, cursed already with teeth too large for his mouth, and with a weak chin below.
O, to be the third son!
Xert called himself a Count, but he wasn't one really. His father was the Count, and his arrogant bully of his brother would be the next Count, but why not call himself a Count in this godsforssken backwater called Vol? It's not like the Flan here knew any better. Most of the idiots couldn't even read or write. Xert never wanted to come here in the first place. No one important ever came to Vol, and being given the job of administrator of the province was hardly a promotion from his fine life in Spar. He knew that he was sent to Vol to rot.
He bent down to find his jacket, hat and boots. Fine clothing, wrinkled and scuffed. It was funny how things had turned out. Despite still feeling resentment with his family, he was actually rather happy. Xert had never seen so many beautiful women in his life.
Xert resided in the tavern. The best place in town as far as he was concerned. Here he could meet girls, show off his status, eat as much as he liked, and drink even more. He went up to an empty table, then sat down. A couple of ales before his business with the mayor would be perfect. He scanned the room with a supercilious frown. A few surly men who were looking in his direction quickly turned away. Spineless saps!
The chair next to him creaked. Someone else had come to the table. Xert didn't recognise him.
"Do you mind," he snapped. The young man, tall and lean, with darkly tanned skin and curly light hair, dressed in country clothes, stared at Xert's nose with piercing green eyes.
"Actually, I do mind. Very much."
"Are you aware that I am a Count? I can have you destroyed with a click of my finger."
The waitress came over with the first ale. "Dearest, love," she breathed as she gave over the cup to Xert, "I cannot wait until you are mine."
Xert brushed her away. He was feeling too annoyed with the impertinent bumpkin sitting next to him.
"Does every woman in town think that you will marry them?" asked Rao.
The Count looked at Rao with surprise. Who was this strange man? He took a gulp of the ale. "What do you know of my affairs?" he asked.
"No more than anyone else in town," answered Rao, "the men are too afraid to say anything, and the women are all under your spell."
"All the women?" scoffed Xert, "only the good looking ones. I do have some taste."
"You are a very disagreeable man," said Rao.
"So what?" said Xert, "I own Vol. I might as well own the women too."
The waitress came back. "My love, my life. Let us elope, tonight! The moons will be out and the weather is fair. I would hate for another girl to steal you."
"Come, Katt, sit upon my lap," cooed the Count, "let this stranger see that I bring you nothing but happiness. Are you bewitched by my good looks?"
"Oh, yes, quite bewitched!" answered Katt, climbing upon Xert's knee, "for you are handsome exceeding even the grey elves, and you are always with me, night and day."
Rao looked at Katt, studying her face for any sign of unhappiness. He saw none.
"Miss Katt," said Rao, "you must know that many women of the town feel the same way about the Count? He is using you all for his self gratification."
"What other women? I fear that somebody will come one day and snatch my love away, but right now I am the only woman here. Can't you see how much my man adores me?"
Rao shook his head, then he spoke once more, "Count Xert, your magic is very strong."
"Yes," sneered the Count, "I am an Ur Flan."
Rao stood up, smiling. He reached out his hand. "My name is Rao. I am a shepherd. You are a disgraceful, despicable man. But I want to be an Ur Flan too. Will you teach me?"
And to Xert's surprise, he said yes.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 79
The Shepherd (4)
1738 SD
Xert had been commanded to rule from the new castle in central Vol, so his time in town had come to an end. He was having his last meal in the tavern before setting off the next day. His pupil Rao sat across the table eating his stew.
Pupil? Rao wasn't much of a scholar. He was an intelligent young man, and he had an instinct that couldn't be taught, but the simplest things seemed to baffle him.
"Looking forward to living in the castle with me?" he asked Rao, before taking a long swig of ale.
Rao nodded gently, but he didn't speak. Xert became frustrated.
"I've had enough of your sulking. Want to be an Ur Flan? You have to see things in a different light."
Rao looked up. "Light? You live in the dark. You treat women worse than I ever treated my sheep, and you refuse to teach me any real magic."
"Ah, Rao, here's the rub. You don't care about my mistresses, you just think of yourself. You can't just learn spells, boy. I began the magical arts at seven, and I didn't get grips with it until I was more than twenty."
"You mean spells like this?" Rao waved his hand and mumbled some words. Where one Rao sat were now three. Xert frowned.
"How did you learn the Mirror Image spell? I didn't teach you."
Rao slurped his broth. He let the warm meat and peas bathe his mouth before swallowing it down. "You think that I don't read your spell books while you sleep?"
"How...? My wards..."
"Wards are made to be broken. You see, master, I have learned every spell in every book that I know about. So where are the real spells?"
"Real spells?"
"Spells where I don't have to wave my arms around. Spells where I don't have to crush a blue beetle or set fire to a piece of straw or eat a biscuit. Spells where I don't have to utter silly words."
Xert stared hard at Rao. He felt a chill. "But Rao... that's what you must do, if you wish to cast magic."
"Are you telling me that the Emperor upon his Spider Throne needs to crush a nut or throw a rock or split a leaf while muttering words and throwing his arms about too?"
"For certain spells...yes."
Now it was Rao that stared at Xert. "Master Ur Flan, I made a mistake. It is you that should learn from me."
*****
Xert invited Rao into his room for a nightcap. Their professional relationship was at an end. Rao was not going to the castle after all, for there was no point. Yet, Xert did have some fondness for the country boy, and he somehow wanted to try one last time to explain his position to him. He felt that the friendship was only one way, and it would be nice to end on amiable terms. He went down a trapdoor, returning with a bottle of Celenian wine. He poured out two generous serves, then sat down on a chair with a sigh.
"Rao, dear Rao, you have never approved of my relationships with the womenfolk."
"No. I have not. But you never listen to me. You refuse to change."
"But where is the harm in what I do? Look." He pulled out his crystal. "See what I see." Xert peered into the mirrored glass and nubile female figures swam up into view. Rao averted his eyes.
"Oh, Rao!" cried Xert, "Behold my beloveds. Here they all are, each alone, and each believing that they are right now with me. See how they caress thin air thinking that I am there? And I am there! Look, Rao. They are happy. They are very happy, certainly happier than if they had to settle for a local Vol man! They make love to a Count."
*****
The next morning two men shook hands then parted ways, one to administer Vol for Secretary Spindle, and one to see how his sheep were faring. He had heard that his master had been very happy with the two rams.

posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 80
The Shepherd (5)
1741 SD
The sun was unseasonably hot and the grass was shriveled. Rao had to roam the sheep further afield, but he didn't really mind. Further north were low and green hills, and there the breeze was cooler and the grass remained lush. The newly built castle was close by, and Rao took the sheep past it each morning and evening. The walls were black stone and the castle was solid, imposing and functional. There was nothing elegant or beautiful about it. Rao saw ring-mailed soldiers manning the turrets, and to his eyes they looked disinterested. Where did the men come from? Spar? The cities to the east? Did they want to be here?
Probably they were like their master, Count Xert, forced to be here. Xert lived in the castle, Rao knew, and Rao wondered whether he should pop in one day to day hello. Not that he liked Xert. He detested him, but Xert was a neighbour, and Rao had been taught to be amicable to neighbours.
Yet, Rao didn't bring himself to knock on the door. He kept his distance and just watched his sheep.
*****
The hills hid a few shallow caves and Rao found one that suited the sheep. At night he brought them into the cave then lit a fire to keep predators away. The orange and yellow flames cast flowing shadows on the stone walls and Rao found the effects soothing. It was as if he had a companion sitting with him as he sat by the fire, smiling at existence.
Rao never slept. He didn't understand why anyone did. He knew that most everything slept, even the sheep, but why sleep while you are alive? People sometimes asked Rao whether he ever got tired. Rao always answered, "tired of what?" Rao enjoyed being alive, but it didn't mean that he jumped about all day. He appreciated the quiet of the night, because then he could enter his inner world and contemplate... everything.
Rao heard a snapping sound outside the cave. The fire suddenly guttered as a cloud of stench wafted in. Something was out there on the hill. Rao grabbed his crook then padded to the entrance. He looked out into the darkness but only one moon was out, and it was only a sliver. He couldn't see much more than shadows. He blinked a few times then made out several large shapes moving about. They were larger than bears with heads like horned dogs, two huge arms bearing enormous pincers, two smaller arms protruding from their chests, and they smelled of sulphur and rotting mushrooms. A small shrub near the entrance had been trampled. One had passed by moments before.
What were they? Rao could tell that these beings were not part of the natural world. One of the figures stopped moving, head raised, smelling the air. It turned around slowly, its eyes blazing white. It emitted a low rumbling growl. It had seen Rao. Its companions turned likewise. Rao found himself cornered by three of the monsters, who loped and hopped towards him upon two massive legs. Rao retreated back into the cave. He had never felt so uncertain or afraid. It was a strange sensation. The great beasts followed him in, one stomping on the little fire, extinguishing it in a puff of smoke. Rao retreated further, to where the sheep were. They had smelled the great stench emitted by the horrors and were bleating in terror. The sounds in the darkness, accompanied by sour rot and sulphuric acid, overwhelmed Rao. He struck out with his shepherds crook but the thin wood shattered and snapped as it struck the first beast's horned and leathery hide.
Rao fell backwards, the bleating of the sheep bouncing around the walls. The three monsters continued to advance, pincers clacking...

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 81
The Shepherd (6)
Darkness killed the very air, a cold blanket of blind hate that turned the interior of the cave into clacks, thuds and bleats. The sheep were being destroyed. Rao could hear their deaths as they were tossed against walls and sliced up with razor sharp pincers. Rao lay stunned against cold stone, hearing and feeling everything but seeing nothing. What were these monsters that violated the natural world? Rao felt unfamiliar emotions bubble within him. Emotions that overrode his fear, his shock and his pain.
Rage. Naked, unfettered rage.
The darkness shriveled into mist, dissolved by pure light. Rao was incandescent, shining with the brightness of burning phosphorus. The devil's element? No. The pale green and eerie glow that irradiated from Rao was surely from the Seven Heavens.
And with the light came comfort. And with the light came understanding. And with the light came power.
Rao confronted the three enormous beasts, part crab, part dog, part toad...and he knew now their names. The Glabrezu.. demons from the Abyss.
The glabrezu were snarling, leaving off their attacks on the sheep, aware that they were under threat. The one that had attacked Rao at the entrance to the cave was perhaps more confident than the others, for he beat his chest with his smaller arms while swinging his pincer arms at the lit up Flan. The great blades struck Rao on the shoulders, but instead of bringing him down, the pincers burst into an explosion of whiteness, and the demon immolated.
The light was now so bright that the cave may as well have been a sunny beach. The sheep were saturated with colours of brown, grey, white, and red, the survivors gathering together and moving behind their bright shepherd.
The two remaining glabrezu hissed impotently. They wanted to destroy Rao very, very badly.
"Touch me and you die," said Rao. "You are not of this Oerth. Begone from here. Go back to your malestrom. You will slay no more sheep this day."
The glabrezu were whimpering. They were defeated. They retreated, leaving the cave, then hopping and leaping away. Rao went to the entrance and watched where they went.
They headed towards the castle.
Rao dimmed as the danger passed..He glowed pale green, returning to his sheep. Some were dead and some were injured, but most were unharmed, although their eyes were bulging with shock and fear.
"Calm yourself, my lambs," said Rao, "they are gone now, and I shall see that they never return."
Rao bent down, then gathered up the demonic ash of the vaporised glabrezu. He rubbed the black, sulphuric powder over his hands and fingers. He rose, his eyes steel. He now held a crook. A new crook, pure white, and as he raised it up to touch the cave roof, Rao would swear until the end of the Cosmos that the sheep all bowed in reverence.

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 82
The Shepherd (7)
The castle drawbridge was down. Of course it was. Vol was at peace. The courtyard was filled with merchants and beggars and courtesans. It was its own little city. Rao, with his white crook, accosted one of the soldiers. Where was Count Xert?
"Within the castle. You will need to speak with the castellan about making an appointment."
"Do I?" said Rao, and he went to the gates. The gates were guarded, and they were locked. Two guards with halberds stood at either side. Rao studied one of the iron gates. Open or shut, a gate was a gate. He went through. The guards stared in astonishment. They thrust out their halberds to block Rao, but the white garbed man was already walking down the corridor beyond.The guards blew a horn. Rao shrugged. All this fuss!
Guards flooded in. They were all young, and they all wore crude ring mail. Rao smiled warmly. "I am here to see Count Xert," he said, "I am an old pupil of his."
****
Count Xert had sumptuous quarters, the decor all black and red. He wore a purple gown and he lay sprawled over a couch. A slave prepared drinks. Xert looked up when Rao was escorted within. The Ur Flan broke into a grin.
"Ah, Rao, so good to come and visit me. Guard, you may go."
Rao hovered over the couch.
"Rao, please...take a seat. Anywhere. I have Celenian wine, if you like. I am more into brandy these days."
Rao found a small chair then sat down..The cushion was scarlet and plump. His crook stood tall in his hand.
"What drink would you like?" asked Xert, "and you can put away your crook. Relax."
Rao held onto the crook, and he didn't take a drink. He gazed at the Count with steely green eyes. "Count Xert. My sheep were accosted by demons."
Xert took a sip of brandy. He looked up with amusement. "Oh, my," he said, "poor sheep."
"I think that you have something to do with the demons. Did you summon them?"
Count Xert looked shocked, "are you calling me a Demonologist, dear Rao? Well, you are correct. I did, and do, summon demons."
"Why?"
"Well, not to bother your sheep. The crazy creatures, they do tend to have minds of their own. Got hungry, I suppose."
Rao continued to stare.
"Why? Why summon demons, you mean? Unlike you, I have ambitions. I learn to summon and control demons, and then I become very useful for the Empire. Find a speciality like that and a man can go places."
Rao scowled. "I have always known that you were a bad person, Count, but polluting Vol with monsters of the Abyss...? Can't you see how dangerous this is?"
Xert took another swig. "Are you sure you don't want anything? Anything at all? I do understand your concerns, but really, if a handful of demons run amok, what harm to Vecna? And if I do manage to harness them to my will... The Empire will be stronger than it has ever been."
Rao stood up. He glowed. "I accept this castle. I accept that you administer Vol. I even accept the rule of Vecna. I was born under Vecna and perhaps I shall die under Vecna, for I understand that he is immortal, but I shall not accept demons or devils or demodands or daemons. Monsters from the Lower Planes bring nothing but ruin. Put your summoning spells away, or I will oppose you."
Rao reached out to the slave with her table of drinks and snatched a full bottle. Bottle in one hand and crook in the other, Rao left the room, left the castle, then went back home.

posts.title: Broken Empires
posts.text:
A History of Oerik
Book 3
Broken Empires
Part 83
The Shepherd (
A young woman came to the pastures. She said that she was a niece of the sheep master. She had heard about Rao, and she wanted to meet him.
Rao kept a well groomed curly beard, and his wavy hair was neat. His sheepskin clothes were pure white. He greeted the girl cordially, and offered to show her the sheep.
"Truth to tell, I am not really interested in the sheep," said the niece, and Rao suddenly noticed her pale skin flush. She was tall, with hair the colour of wheat. Her skin was the colour of honey and her eyes were bright with irises of hazelnut. She reached out, brushing Rao's bare arm with graceful fingers. "You haven't asked my name, dear sir."
Rao hadn't thought of that. 'Niece' had been enough, but now he asked.
"Yheera," she answered. Then, she asked, "Rao, is it true that you fight demons?"
Rao didn't want to talk about such things. He found it disturbing.
"Oh, I am sorry," said Yheera, "tell me, is there any place that we can sit down? My feet are hurting."
Rao led her to the cave. He lit the fire then brewed some tea. Yheera sat down beside him. She touched his thigh. Rao flinched. Yheera laughed. "Do I make you uncomfortable?"
Rao nodded.
"But why, dear Rao? With all the things that I have heard about you, you must have made love to women before"
"Is that what we are doing?" exclaimed Rao, "No. I never have."
"Why not? You don't like women?"
Rao looked at her with sternness, "I am different to most people. I don't understand them. People are strange to me. And courtship... it's both selfless and selfish all at the same time. I don't want to partake in that world."
Yheera clasped Rao around the waist. "But surely you have kissed a girl before... would you like to kiss me?"
Rao realised that he wanted to kiss her very much. But he pulled away. Was there a hint of distrust in his eyes? For Yheera then said, "no, I am not your master's niece. I am from the castle on the hill. Count Xert told me to find you."
"Xert...?"
"Yes. He says that you and he are good friends. He wanted me to introduce you to some of the pleasures of this world that you had seemed to miss."
"So, who are you then? A courtesan?"
Yheera smirked. "A courtesan? Courtesans make love for money. I make love because I like it! Come, kiss me, shepherd boy. I really have heard all about you. Come...you can't be good all the time...just a kiss. That's all."
The fire went out, but Yheera remained illuminated, her hair glowing, her eyes shining, her lips dark pink, her teeth...
And as Rao was about to capitulate, he saw her steel horns, her fangs and her black bat wings.
Yheera was a succubus.
Rao recoiled as if he had been slapped. He reached for his crook.
"Now, now, silly man," hissed the succubus, "nothing has changed. I am still beautiful and I still wish to kiss you. And, afterwards you will want nothing more than to join with me forever more. The Abyss can be your paradise."
But Rao wasn't listening. He raised his white crook, and the crack of it on stone banished Yheera from Oerth.
*****
Count Xert, who had been watching the entire encounter in his crystal, cursed. How close that had been! He would need to be circumspect for a while, until he was promoted. Apparently Secretary Spindle had indicated that he had been impressed with Xert's progress. The sooner Xert could get away from Vol the better.

Captain Fharlanghan and the Skeletons of Death (4)
   Celestian and Wee Jas were on the Moon. Fharlanghan could see them as two tiny figures waving their arms frantically. Fharlanghan conjured a rope and grapple then threw it up. The hook caught on a crater. 
   "Come on Llerg," said Fharlanghan, and he shimmied up the rope. Llerg looked at the rope, gave a small shrug, then shimmied up after the red faced man.
   The sky was like honey and the two heroes felt like they were pushing through goo. Fharlanghan called out to Celestian as he made his way to the Moon, "Ho, Celestian, we are coming."
   "We are not alone," returned Celestian, his voice breaking upon their ears, "be careful."
   Not alone? Fharlanghan hadn't seen any other figures, and now he couldn't check because of the angle of the rope. Who else was up there?
   Fharlanghan reached the end of the rope and found himself on a spongy surface that smelled of sour milk. He helped Llerg up, who was a little awkward on the rope, then he pulled out from a torn pocket a long staff. He held it out, ready for trouble.
Celestian and Wee Jas were a few hundred yards away and Fharlanghan saw that their legs were buried into the ground. 
   "Careful, brother," called Celestian, he is watching you."
   "Who is watching us?"
   A very thin, very gaunt apparition interposed himself between the rescuers and the two captives. He wore a simple brown tunic but his form was emaciated and skeletal, lemon yellow skin stretched tight over bone. His hair was dirty, black and tied into a topknot. He screeched when he saw Llerg and Fharlanghan, and guttural utterings filled the air, then, as if recalibrating, the noises turned into recognisable words*, "More of you? Betrayers all!"
   Fharlanghan was glad he had his staff, for the psychic energies that struck it and rebounded away would have rendered he and Llerg as helpless as Celestian and Wee Jas. Llerg growled, and a bear would have been impressed. The roar of rage seemed to rattle the skeleton who stepped back and raised up his arms, afraid.
   "I am not afraid of death," he said, though his body language betrayed him, "I expect it to come. But you will regret killing me, ere long."
   Celestian then spoke, his voice steady and calming, "I am sorry to have brought my friends. I thought that I needed more help."
   Fharlanghan moved forward, staff held in front of him, "Please, Mr skeleton man, can we parlay? We don't understand."
   The skeleton looked around, his bloodshot eyes aflame with fear and rage. Then he calmed himself.  "I told you to come alone, Celestian. Alone means alone."
   Celestian nodded, "I said I was sorry. Please, we are here to help you."
   "So you say, but you are probably lying." He crossed his arms and waited for Fharlanghan and Llerg to come all the way to the crater. When they reached him he introduced himself, "I am the Illithid killer, the great Gith. My name is Zerthimon. I am the only being who can save us all."
*What language were Wee Jas, Llerg, Fharlanghan and Celestian speaking? Suel, ancient Oeridian, or some other, lost language? This chronicler does not know. See less

Glossary of Characters
   A History of Oerik contains a lot of characters and it can be hard to keep up. With that in mind, and celebrating the end of Book 2, here are many of the characters in the series.
Arik: appearing in the second half of Golden Age, Arik was an Ur Flan (evil wizards or priests from the Flanaess) who conquered part of Mystara for the Vecna Empire. He was nearly slain by the Elven goddess Sehanine and was rebuilt with magical metal and gems. 
Acererak: The brother of Arik, another Ur Flan of the Empire. He conquered Sunndi but fell in love with the Vast Swamp. Vecna made him a Lich lord.
Baba Yaga: The daughter of Queen Dully of the Suel, she was adopted by Ulaa. She is an extremely powerful witch, plays with Death and lives in a hut with chicken legs.
Bahamet the Platinum Dragon: One of the old Dragons from the Dragon Age. Enemy of Tharizdun.
Boccob: There are two Boccobs, the young one and the seemingly evil older one who interferes from future Oerik. Boccob fell into the Mystical Organ and became imbued with magic.
The Book of Vile Darkness: originally a scroll created by a demon Lord, this extremely evil magical artifact has been possessed by many, including the Queen of Chaos, Lolth, Nerull, Tharizdun and Boccob. Vecna turned it into a book and currently has it.
Celestian: An Oeridian who helped fight Tharizdun and was the navigator of the Sea Stork, he is now the Star Man. The brother of Fharlanghan.
Corellon Larethian: one of the early elves, they are both male and female and represent all Olve. They won battles both with Gruumsh and Lolth. Friend to Moradin.
Dahlver- Nar: Ur Flan priest of Nerull used by Incabulos. His teeth were taken and given to Tiamat in the Empire of Lynn. Now they have magical properties. 
Dalt: A suitor for the Suel Empress, Syrul killed him and he became a ghost that haunts the Palace.
Dully: Dully Maure became a Suel Queen and eventually the first Emperor of the Suel Imperium. Mother of Baba Yaga (the father was a mysterious blue man from Hades) but did not bring her up.
Fharlanghan: The brother of Celestian, he is an Oeridian who captained the Sea Stork against Tharizdun. Became a god.
Garl Glittergold: Greatest of the Gnomes. Friends with Ulaa, Boccob, Heward and Ye'Cind. Fought Maglubiyet and Tharizdun.
Gavron: Ur Flan and loyal companion to Arik. He took issue with the way Vecna ran the Empire and became a rebel. An ancestor to the future saint and god, St Cuthbert of the Cudgel.
The Gith Queen: Appearing in Book 1 (probably to be titled Relics of a Dragon Time), she was once an elf of the Vesve forest kidnapped by Mind Flayers.
Ghost Dragon: Daughter of Tiamat. Mother of Tharizdun. Imprisoned in the Deachensgrab mountains.
Gruumsh: King, Lord and god of the Orcs. Conquered many worlds, including Toril and part of Oerth. Injured by Heward. Defeated by Corellon.
Heward: Flan with Fey blood. Hero. Warrior, Bard and Rogue. Quasi deity. Lived for more than 1400 years. Played the Mystical Organ and founded the Bardic colleges. Fought the Queen of Chaos, Gruumsh, Maglubiyet, Kavoss the Cyclops and Tharizdun. Stole the Ring of Gaxx and the Scroll of Vile Darkness. Father of Vecna.
Incabulos: Once a boy from the Sheldomar valley, evil magic in the Cairn hills turned him into the God of Disease and Suffering. One of the three Death gods.
Kavoss the Cyclops: One of the greatest generals for Gruumsh, he was a clever but brutal magic using cyclops who rode a giant evil beast called Hucephelus.
Llerg: The Lost Emperor of the Suel Imperium. Fled assassination attempt and met demons and orb troglodytes in the Anedio jungle.
Lolth: Demonic Spider offspring of the Queen of Chaos. Sister of Miska the Wolf Spider. Became Queen of the Singing Ones, and later, the goddess of the Drow. Defeated by Corellon Larethian when she tried to conquer Eastern Oerik.
Maglubiyet: Giant goblin general for Gruumsh. Played his own game and financed the creation of the Machine. Fought Heward. Lost in the Rift Canyon.
Miska the Wolf Spider: Demonic Spider offspring of the Queen of Chaos. Brother of Lolth and lover of the Queen of Chaos. He fathered spider demons with his mother. Defeated by the Wind Dukes in Western Oerik.
Moradin: One of the First Dwarves (dwur). Resisted slavery for the elves. Became friends with Corellon Larethian. Nearly slain by Kavoss. Forced to remain in Mount Celestia in the Seven Heavens.
Nerull: Former friend of Incabulos. Corrupted into the God of Death. One of the three Death gods.
Norebo; Appearing in Book 1, friend of Ye'Cind. Gambling kingpin.
Obad Hai: The first and greatest Druid. The Hierophant. Rival of Boccob and Heward. 
Paroclydes: Genius gnome inventor. Created the Mightty Servant, the Machine and the Mystical Organ. Slain attempting to take a piece of Tharizdun.
Pelor: Gnome and Sun god. Instrumental in the creation of the Mystical Organ. Sacrificed himself in the war against Tharizdun.
Pious Grimm Quartztusk: Doughty dwarf (dwur) and devout follower of Moradin. Fought the evil duergar and witnessed the birth of Lolth and Miska. Was captured by the Singing Ones where he became a puppet toy for Lolth. Escaped with iron legs, and ultimately became the thrall of Incabulos (though some say he returned to the Seven Heavens).
Queen of Chaos: Once called Dweomyne the Whip lady, she was a Singing One Olve who was corrupted in the demonic abyss. Mother of Lolth and Miska. Miska was her son and lover. Tried to conquer the Wind Dukes but met her demise in Pesh.
Sehanine: Olve Moon Goddess.suffered during the wars against Gruumsh in Toril. Lives as a recluse in the island of Ierendi in Mystara.
Syrul: Syrul became a Suel goddess by deceiving the Suel to worship her. Unmasked by Ye'Cind and her recorder. Later became the symbol and literal embodiment of the Suel Imperium. Defeated by Wee Jas.
Tharizdun: The Mist God. The god of Entropy. Lover of Nothing. Head of the Death gods. With the help of the Scroll of Vile Darkness, the Throne of the Gods and his mother the Ghost dragon, created the magical stone circles called Tovag Baghru. Nearly became the Multiverse. Trapped by Boccob in the Yatil mountains where he is worshipped by Ur Flan priests.
Th're the Silver Dragon: Friend of Ulaa. Inadvertently helped Incabulos and Nerull.
Tiamat the Chromatic Dragon: A dragon from the Dragon Age. Created the Ghost dragon. Grandmother of Tharizdun.
Ulaa: Half gnome and half dwur. Inventor and  healer and fought Maglubiyet. Became a goddess and founded Ull and Ulek.
Vecna: Magical offspring of Heward , Ye'Cind and the Mystical Organ. Stole the Scroll of Vile Darkness from Boccob. Cousin of Baba Yaga. Became an Ur Flan, then a Lich. Conquered most of the Flanaess and rules an Empire.
Wee Jas: An Empress who found enlightenment from the Star Man in Zindia. Deposed Syrul to become the Palace of the Suel Imperium. Lover of Win Daled. Has two teeth of Dahlver-Nar.
White Baron: Greatest white dragon of the lower Crystalmists  Loyal servant of Gavron. Unwittingly helped defeat Tharizdun.
Win Daled: The First Queen of the Suel. Happily dead when Queen Dully brought her back as a Suel Lich. Former companion of Heward and Ye'Cind. Helped to defeat Dweomyne (the Queen of Chaos) of the Singing Lands. Accidentally killed Heward as the Suel Lich. Now looks like Heward. Lover of Wee Jas.
Ye'Cind: A Singing One who couldn't sing. Created a magical recorder. Helped Norebo. Defeated Syrul. Fought Maglubiyet , Gruumsh and Tharizdun. Mother of Vecna.
Yondalla: halfling High Priestess of Moradin. Fought Gruumsh and Tharizdun. Slain by Tharizdun but raised in the Five Shires in Mystara. See less

A History of Oerik 
Book 1
Interlude
   My history of Oerik is based upon my own campaign that began in the early 1980s. The World of Greyhawk had little published history then and the various states and nations were documented in but a paragraph or two. The DMG had an outstanding chapter on artifacts and relics which gave us a glimpse of the past. Baba Yaga and her hut, the Eye and Hand of Vecna, the Machine of Lum the Mad, Howard's Mystical Organ; these and other strange items were potentially scattered about in dark, forgotten places.
   The early modules gave us tiny kernels too. The archmage Keraptis of a thousand years ago in White Plume Mountain, the tomb of the Demi-Lich in the Vast Swamp, built by  long dead people, the Forgotten Temple of Tharizdun, the brief rule of the witch Queen Iggiliv, the demon-god Iuz...  My imagination caught fire and I went on a personal tour of Oerik's past, indeed, Oerth's past. With little canonical information I freely made the world my own for my players. My table was a true sandbox and the players could and would go anywhere. 
   I came to D&D too late for the original white box and began with the Basic Blue Book. I found myself temporarily straddling the Expert and Advanced rule sets and when I found my feet in AD&D I happily placed Mystara into the Solnor sea east of Oerik and later Kara-tur across the Dramidj ocean. 
   Of course published Greyhawk material did continue to develop into the 90s and beyond even if TSR seemed more invested in Krynn, The Forgotten Realms, Spelljammer and Dark Sun. We began to get more canon on Greyhawk's history and the mysterious Western Oerik.
   But it all came too late for me. My Greyhawk had become my own, and my Heward, my Baba Yaga, my Iuz, my Vecna had a homebrewed history invented  out of necessity because I wanted to know the details and origins of these powerful beings, and needed to for the style of game I was running.
  So this is the origin of the histories I have been publishing on this page. I thought that other people might like to see what had been done with Greyhawk if left to our own devices. Funnily enough although much of my history differs from later canon there are occasionally close similarities. The connection between Iggiliv, Iuz and Baba Yaga coincidentally occurs in my history too, though the details are not exact. 
   The writing of this history has halted for a bit. Health issues and a subsequent loss of confidence made me tentative to continue because in truth these posts are hard to write. I condense down huge events into two or three paragraphs with little dialogue and a real attempt at making it accessible to readers not as invested as I am. I also strive to only include narratives relevant to the history as a whole and attempt to juggle them into a coherent story without contradictions. I believe I have succeeded for the most part (the saga of Heward in the Fey world got a bit too convoluted) and that has placed pressure on me to continue to a certain standard. I am about to continue the history and you of course are free to read it or not and to appreciate it or not. I am not trying to impose my history onto any other Greyhawk campaign and I do not claim copyright on any character not wholly my own. Ideas presented can be cannabilised for parts, changed, altered, fictionalized or ignored. 
   Thanks for your understanding.
   Damien. See less

Part 106
   Moradin was layed out onto an alter, candles lit with ethereal flames at each corner.  One by one the designated priests sprinkled Holy water over his motionless body.  All the while the congregation of clerics intoned the magic verses to  prepare the way to the next, more dangerous part of the ritual...
   Correllon Larethian looked out atop the battlements of the Rockhome defences.  Down below were multitudes of dead and wounded hobgoblins.  Further away in a valley tiny figures had set up rude campsites, the hobgoblins were regrouping.  He looked from horizon to horizon for the winged demons sent to attack from above, but saw nothing.  
   Moradin was now very close to death.  His subconscious will was strong and his heart and lungs refused to give up despite the Godrot ravaging him from within.  But they would have to give up if he was to ascend into his new state.  The verses were repeated six times.  As the congregation began the seventh and final repeat the Highest priest went through the sacred curtain to fetch the sword.
   Correllon came down to the barracks.  Where were the scouts who had warned the king?  The scouts?  But none have returned!
   The sword was not magical.  It was just a sword, but the elderly abbot had blessed it and rubbed it with oil.   He looked up at the Highest Priest and smiled faintly.  O, yes, he was ready.  His feeble body found the sword rather heavy to carry.  Would the priest help.  Good!  The curtain was pulled aside and the Highest Priest with the sword and the hobbling abbot stepped to the alter as the seventh verse was completed.  The abbot took a deep breath and took the sword from the priest.  He raised it to his lips and kissed it.  A little patch of saliva dampened the edge and trickled down the blade.  The abbot took another step and raised the sword high above Moradin's throat.  He paused for a moment, glanced furtively at the clerics and coughed nervously.  Then he plunged the sword down. Part 96
  The Druids were naive in their collaboration with the Ur Flan.  
   The Druids sought to understand the true essence of Existence in order to resonate with and within Nature.
   The Ur Flan sought power over Life itself.
   The Ur Flan  corrupted the spells and rituals that the Druids used to transform their bodies into wild animals. The Druids wandered under the Moons, Luna and Celene, as wolves, bears, tigers, boars, ravens .. but upon the rise of Sol, and as light bathed yellow upon a new day, the Druids, scattered across the Northlands, awoke alone, with little memory of their night crawls..
   They would find themselves in a cave, or lying in a field, or concealed within shrubs, bodies bruised and aching, often covered in blood.
   The Druids assumed that they were hunting other animals, part of the Circle of Life.
   But mostly, they were hunting people.
   The Druids didn't want to believe this, they tried to discount or ignore evidence that their ravages were upon villagers or farmers, not deer or sheep. Sometimes they awoke holding an odd shoe or torn clothes that were not theirs, and sometimes they half remembered seeing men, women and children, sometimes people they knew, running from them, wide eyed and full of fear 
   The Ur Flan used enchanted crystals to watch the Druids wander the night in animal forms 
    Were beasts, they called them. Animal Men, Lycanthropes. 
   And they cast dark spells upon the Druids in secret that caused their corruption to spread, to turn innocent survivors of attacks into were beasts as well.
   The Ur Flan watched and took notes. 
   The Druids wished to be of One with Oerth, but they became outcasts, corrupted by bloodlust, killing for pleasure, not sustenance.
   The wiser Druids, those that did not trust the shadowy Ur Flan, those that knew that the wizards and assassins were lovers of Demons and Devils, the Unnatural, the Uncanny,; these Druids shunned the Lycanthropes and saw them for what they really were.
Instruments against Nature itself.
   The were beasts, no longer Druids, found each other and accepted their fate. Many embraced the wildness and learned to control their transformations. 
   The were tigers loved the thrill of the hunt.
   The were wolves lusted for human blood.
   The were boars simply lusted.
   Only the were bears kept some semblance of their former personalities, but became terrifying and chaotic if angered.
   After around three years , those infected with lycanthropy no longer changed involuntarily with the full moon,  and their dual nature became one, that of the beast.
   The lycanthropes found that they could mate with the same type of were beast,  and that their offspring would be truly wild, filled with animality, not humanity.
   By 520 SD the Curse of Lycanthropy was  forevermore a part of Oerth. See less

The giant form of King Silvervein bore down on Pious Quartztusk and his troops.  He had hoped his vast size and possession of the Fierce Axe would prove his legitimacy as the first mortal king of the dwarves.  However this manifestation of might and power simply compounded his blasphemy as Quartztusk saw it.  Here was a mere dwarf attempting to emulate the God Moradin.  
   With a great war cry, the forces of Quartztusk charged at the giant pretend king.  The first ranks fell quickly to the dancing and slicing Fierce Axe, but the next ranks pressed forward with spears and attacked the feet and legs.  Roaring with pain, Silvervein kicked out at his opponents, then he staggered and tripped over a Dwarven fighter.  His body slammed onto the road crushing some of the normal sized dwarves to pulp.  
   Pious, wielding his blessed hammer, smote the head of the giant and after several blows managed to cave in the skull.  With one last sigh, the spirit of Silvervein Moradinson left the  body and shuddering, the giant reverted back to its normal four and a half foot size.  
   Pious Grimm Quartztusk took the Axe of the Dwarven Lords, the Fierce Axe, and held it up for his soldiers to see.  Along the road and through the gates they then went, to the Palace of Grawn where the axe could be stored in Moradin's Forge so this ridiculous war could be concluded. See less
